fam: Place not named or further east

authors.sig: His letter on the Antichrist became one of the most copied medieval descriptions of Antichrist and shaped all later apocalyptic tradition; the saints' lives here document the cults of Luxeuil- and Toul-region saints.

Bishop of Metz from 855 until his death in 875. He backed Lothar II's effort to set aside Queen Theutberga in favor of Waldrada. His letters to the pope and to Archbishop Theutgaud of Trier defend papal authority over deposed metropolitans.
Merovingian bishop of Metz who succeeded St. Arnulf and built Great St. Peter's there. He was a personal friend of King Dagobert I. Epistles from him and to him survive in PL 87.
His Aurora revision carried Pierre Riga's versified Scripture, with its doctrine that gospel truth dawns beneath the literal sense, into wider circulation.

authors.aff: Archbishop of Canterbury (elected Easter Day 995, installed 996)
authors.sig: The Canons to Wulfin are a window into late Anglo-Saxon clerical reform, enforcing celibacy, residence, and the separation of priesthood from secular office.

Abbot of Rievaulx Abbey in Yorkshire from 1147 until his death in 1167. He wrote on charity and spiritual friendship in Mirror of Charity and On Spiritual Friendship. His life of Saint Edward the King and his history of the Battle of the Standard make him a central witness to twelfth-century English monastic thought.

A Neustrian Benedictine monk who wrote De bellis Parisiacae urbis, the only eyewitness account in Latin verse of the Viking siege of 885–886. It carries events through 896. He also left sermons for the instruction of clerics.

Bishop of Paris from 858 until his death in 870. He wrote the Liber adversus Graecos, a treatise prompted by the encyclical letters of Photius. It answers Greek accusations against the Latins with quotations from Greek and Latin Fathers.

authors.aff: King of the Anglo-Saxons (924–927), King of the English (927–939)
authors.sig: These texts show how the first king of all England legislated for the church and Christian observance as an instrument of unified rule; readers here will find early English canon-royal law on tithes, ordeals, and worship.

The three pieces preserved under his name — a letter on behalf of Archbishop Ralph of Tours, a church-foundation charter, and a judgment against Raginard — show an eleventh-century bishop acting in support of his metropolitan: excommunication for contumacy before ecclesiastical judgment, suspension for disobedience to church authority, and solidarity owed to the metropolitan against bishops like G

The letters here record his deposition of Anthimus and correspondence with Justinian, asserting that the unity of churches rests on the apostolic see of Rome and that imperial faith-constitutions are valid only per the canons — a sixth-century statement of Roman primacy against both Monophysites (Severus, Anthimus) and imperial overreach.

Pope from 946 to 955, when Alberic II of Spoleto held power in Rome. His letters and privileges protect monasteries from bishops and secular rulers and affirm monks' right to elect their abbot under Benedict's rule.

Bishop of Rome from 678 until his death in 681. He sent a dogmatic letter defining two wills in Christ to the Sixth Ecumenical Council at Constantinople (680–681), which the council accepted and which helped end the Monothelite controversy.
His surviving work is a brief Carolingian charter-history of Vabres Abbey that documents monastic claims to immunity, self-governance, and exemption from the rule's property prohibition.

A priest and monk of Corby who counted among his friends Hathumoda, the first abbess of Gandersheim. After her death in 874 he wrote a prose Life of Saint Hathumoda and a verse Dialogue on the Death of Saint Hathumoda. The Dialogue answers mourners who objected to her renunciation and defends her consolatory teaching.

authors.aff: Titular abbot of St. Mary ad Blachernas and St. Bartholomew, Ravenna
authors.sig: His Liber Pontificalis Ecclesiae Ravennatis is a principal narrative source for the bishops, churches, buildings, inscriptions, and religious life of ninth-century Ravenna.

Born in Spain and archbishop of Lyon from 816 to 840, he opposed trial by ordeal and wrote against Felix of Urgell's Adoptionist Christology. He also wrote a Letter on Jewish observance and a Book Against the Law of Gundobad.

authors.aff: Bishop of Roskilde (from 1158); Archbishop of Lund (1178–1201)
authors.sig: Born into the powerful Hvide clan, he became Bishop of Roskilde in 1158 and Archbishop of Lund in 1178. He served as chief adviser to Valdemar I and Canute VI and had Saxo Grammaticus compose the Historiæ Danicæ. A Testament under his name survives in PL 209, and the surrounding material argues over whether it was oral or written.
He is a seminal figure in early Insular biblical scholarship, renowned for his complex mystical and allegorical interpretation of the genealogy of Christ.

His letter is a contemporary witness to twelfth-century Marian piety and pilgrimage rites such as the Chartres cart-pulling, and to how refusal of forgiveness was understood to exclude a person from holy fellowship.

Benedictine monk of Fleury-sur-Loire. He wrote the Historia Francorum at Abbo's suggestion. The history was highly esteemed through the Middle Ages and early modern period. Its historical value is now judged slight.

authors.aff: Abbey of Saint-Victor, Paris; later abbot of Springiersbach
authors.sig: His sermons show Victorine exegetical preaching at work: allegorical reading of Scripture applied to sanctification, grace, and the moral life, arguing against hypocrites, corrupt clerics, and deniers of the bodily assumption.

Monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris, later its chancellor and chief copyist. He taught Abbo Cernuus and wrote hagiography on relics and miracles. His accounts of the translation of St. Vincent's relics say divine revelation guided the move and that episcopal consent was required.

authors.aff: Abbot of La Rivour (1152 or 1153 to about 1167), then bishop of Auxerre (1152–1167)
authors.sig: Cistercian monk and abbot of La Rivour who became bishop of Auxerre in 1152. He wrote the Vita secunda sancti Bernardi, a principal biography of Bernard of Clairvaux that presents his sanctity through piety and visions.

authors.aff: Abbot of Saint-Victor, Paris; later Bishop of Avranches
authors.sig: Second abbot of Saint-Victor and later Bishop of Avranches. A letter to Henry II survives in which he presses the king to force the royal treasurer Richard of Ely to repay money unjustly held from the poor, arguing that neglecting the poor is neglecting Christ.

authors.aff: Prior of Christ Church, Canterbury; later Abbot of Tewkesbury
authors.sig: He served as Prior of Christ Church in Canterbury before becoming Abbot of Tewkesbury. He was a strong supporter of Becket against Henry II. His letters defend Canterbury's rights against Rochester, and his Life of Saint Thomas argues for a fixed date for Becket's translation.

authors.aff: University of Paris, School of Chartres, Cistercian Order
authors.sig: A major figure of the twelfth-century Renaissance. He brought Neoplatonic cosmology, literary allegory and axiomatic method into medieval theology.

Abbot of Fleury from 988 and a teacher at Ramsey in England, he wrote On the Breaking of the Body of Christ. In it he argues that Christ's body is truly broken in the sacrament, drawing on the words of institution and holding that eucharistic mysteries are to be believed rather than judged by natural bodily laws.

Cardinal Bishop of Ostia, created in 1138. As papal legate he presided over the Council of London that December. For Eugene III he acted against the heretic Henry of Lausanne in France. A letter to the monks of Saint-Orientius of Auch argues that settlement saves reserved rights pending the abbot's consent.

authors.aff: Canon of the church of Aachen
authors.sig: His Historia expeditionis Hierosolymitanae is the sole source for the People's Crusade of 1096 under Peter the Hermit and a major, if partly legendary, record of the First Crusade and the Latin Kingdom to c. 1120/1121, later used by William of Tyre.

A tenth-century hermit whose letter to archbishop Heribert of Cologne gathers teaching from the holy fathers. It argues that perseverance in good works merits eternal life and that charity is the chief of all virtues.

Anglo-Latin teacher who led the palace school of Charlemagne. He became abbot of St Martin's at Tours in 796. He wrote against Felix of Urgell on adoptionism, and his works include commentaries on Scripture and treatises on the Trinity.

authors.aff: Abbot of Malmesbury; first Bishop of Sherborne
authors.sig: Abbot of Malmesbury and first bishop of Sherborne, he was the most learned teacher of seventh-century Wessex. He wrote Latin prose and verse on the septenary, virginity and church dedication. A surviving letter to King Geraint of Dumnonia urges Roman observance of Easter.

authors.aff: Archbishop of Sens; abbot of Ferrières
authors.sig: Archbishop of Sens from 828 and earlier abbot of Ferrières, he directed the Palace School at the court of Louis the Pious. His letters defend the pastoral office, arguing that church goods are the patrimony of the poor held in stewardship and that monastic endowments should be immune from episcopal alienation.

Bishop of Rouen from 641, he had served the Frankish king Dagobert I as referendary and promoted monasticism at Fontenelle. He wrote the Life of Saint Eligius after his close friend from court died, a key source for seventh-century Neustrian episcopal life.

As leader of the Gregorian mission he founded English Christianity and the see of Canterbury; the privilege preserved under his name documents early claims of monastic immunity against archiepiscopal and secular control.

authors.aff: Chorepiscopus (auxiliary bishop) to Archbishop Wenilo of Sens
authors.sig: A Frankish monk and chorepiscopus, auxiliary bishop to Archbishop Wenilo of Sens from 847 until he was deposed in 849. He wrote the verse Liber de fonte vitae. The visions he claimed about the civil wars in France were set down in his Liber revelationum.

Abbot of Jumièges from 1171 to 1213 and a doctor of divine and secular letters. He wrote a Letter on the Son of Man that argues Christ's titles are literal and that Christ alone recovers the inheritance Adam forfeited for his seed.

Bishop of Hippo Regius from 396 until his death in 430. He argued in polemic against Pelagius and Julian that grace precedes and enables the will. Against the Donatists he held that valid sacraments do not depend on the celebrant's worthiness.

authors.aff: Bishop of Rome, 1061–1073; formerly bishop of Lucca
authors.sig: His letters and diplomas here are primary instruments of the Gregorian reform: they assert the apostolic see's care of the universal church, excommunication for simoniacal intrusion into churches, and anathema for violation of papal privilege.

Chancellor of the Roman church under Adrian IV, he was elected pope in 1159 in a contested election. He spent much of his pontificate outside Rome, defending papal authority against Frederick Barbarossa and Henry II of England. His letters and privileges assert papal confirmation and exempt monks from tithes.

authors.aff: Abbot of St Augustine's Abbey, Canterbury (from 1213)
authors.sig: Abbot of St Augustine's Abbey, Canterbury, from 1213, and a loyal supporter of King John. He is remembered chiefly as the author of the Life of Hugh, which records Hugh of Lincoln's consecration as bishop in 1185 and is held to outweigh the accounts of Roger and Matthew Paris.

King of Wessex and a studious lawgiver who promulgated an important code after studying earlier codes. He fought Danish invaders and won the Battle of Edington in 878. The invasions ceased around 896. His Ecclesiastical Laws and Preface to His Laws set rules for oaths, sanctuary and penance.

His De Misericordia et Justitia is an important source for pre-Gratian church law and discipline, and has been suggested as influential on Gratian's Decretum. His Eucharistic treatise against Berengarius was highly commended by Peter of Cluny and published by Erasmus in 1530.

Archbishop of Arles from 546 until his death in 551, he received the pallium and was named papal vicar for Gaul. He wrote a Rule for Monks that requires total enclosure, the only early medieval rule of its kind for monks. He also wrote a Rule for Virgins.

Bishop of Auxerre who enforced daily attendance at the Divine Office. He held a diocesan synod whose 45 canons treat marriage and popular superstition. A surviving Epistle I argues that saints' lives should be written in both verse and prose, and he caused the lives of his predecessors Amator and Germanus to be written.

authors.aff: Bishop of Carthage (from about 391 until his death; the Catholic Encyclopedia dates the episcopate 388–423)
authors.sig: Bishop of Carthage who presided over the African plenary councils and led the church through the Donatist resurgence and the first appearance of Pelagianism. He was among the first to denounce Pelagianism, and his epistles and synodal letters insist that every bishop must subscribe to the condemnation of the heresy.

authors.aff: Monk of Saint-Jean de Réôme (Moutiers-Saint-Jean), diocese of Langres
authors.sig: A Frankish monk of Réome who wrote the Musica disciplina, the earliest extant medieval European treatise on music and an early source on the melodic character of the church modes. He wrote it as penance after being dismissed from his community, addressing it to Abbot Bernard in a dedicatory letter.

authors.aff: Professor of grammar and rhetoric at Bordeaux; tutor to the emperor Gratian
authors.sig: Gallo-Roman poet who taught grammar and rhetoric at Bordeaux. He tutored the emperor Gratian and later wrote occasional verse. His Idylls, Letters and Epigrams record the schools and families of fourth-century Gaul.

Bishop of Toul in the fifth century and a saint of the Roman Catholic church. He wrote the verse Epistle to Arbogast, which argues that cupidity is the root of all evils. He held that almsgiving drains cupidity's poison and that Christian faith surpasses pagan virtue.
The single item held is an administrative charter for the monastery of Wallers, evidence of episcopal patronage of Merovingian monasticism rather than theological writing.

authors.aff: Order of Saint Benedict, Abbey of San Vincenzo al Volturno
authors.sig: He is renowned for his extensive ten-book commentary on the Apocalypse (*Expositio in Apocalypsin*) and his foundational contributions to Western Mariology and moral theology.

authors.aff: Abbey of La Couture, Le Mans
authors.sig: Monk and then abbot of the monastery of La Couture in a suburb of Le Mans from after 1061 until 1079. His one surviving work is an epistle to Anselm of Canterbury written while Anselm was still at Bec. It cites Lanfranc and Guimond.

authors.aff: Latin Church / Frankish clergy in Naples
authors.sig: He is historically significant for his treatises defending the validity of ordinations performed by Pope Formosus and articulating early medieval arguments against the repetition of holy orders.

authors.aff: Bishop of Vienne, metropolitan of southern and eastern Gaul
authors.sig: Bishop of Vienne and metropolitan of southern and eastern Gaul, he led a Catholic-Arian conference before King Gundobad in 499. He defended Roman primacy in letters to Pope Hormisdas, and his poem On the Deeds of Mosaic History is among the major works of late Latin verse.

authors.aff: Monk and priest of Hautvillers Abbey
authors.sig: A Frankish monk and priest of Hautvillers Abbey who wrote the Vita of Memmius, bishop of Châlons (BHL 5909). His Rescript, a reply to Theudoinus, provost of Châlons, prefaces that Vita. It argues that charity requires writing a saint's life and that truth outweighs elegance in sacred writing.

Third abbot of Cluny, elected in 942 after Odo's death. He expanded the abbey's property through gifts from wealthy patrons, then resigned after going blind and arranged Mayeul's election. In 948 the papacy confirmed Cluny's direct dependence on the Apostolic See.

Provost of Saint Simeon in Trier, who had earlier headed the cathedral school there. He became a friend and adviser to Archbishop Albero after meeting him at Paris in 1147. After Albero's death he wrote the Gesta Alberonis archiepiscopi Trevirorum, a biography of the archbishop.

authors.aff: Prior and then abbot of Bourgueil, then archbishop of Dol
authors.sig: Archbishop of Dol, he wrote a four-book Historia Hierosolymitana on the First Crusade. It draws partly on eyewitness testimony. He also left poems and a Vita beati Roberti de Arbrissello.

Benedictine chronicler whose De diversitate temporum covers events from about 990 to 1021. He dedicated the work to Burchard of Worms and used history to argue about true worship and irrevocable donations to the church.

Count of Edessa before he became king of Jerusalem in 1100, he reigned until his death at Al-Arish in 1118. His charter raising the church of Bethlehem to episcopal rank cites papal authority and ties the grant to the crusade's success.

authors.aff: Count of Flanders and Hainaut; first Latin Emperor of Constantinople
authors.sig: Prominent leader of the Fourth Crusade, which took Constantinople in 1204. He was crowned the first Latin emperor. Defeated by Kaloyan of Bulgaria at Adrianople in 1205, he spent his last days as a prisoner. His letters and diplomas set out truce terms with the sultan of Babylon and commerce guarantees.

Cistercian abbot of Ford who became Archbishop of Canterbury and died on crusade at Acre in 1190. Before he became a bishop he wrote treatises that argue faith must accept Christ's words over human wisdom and defend the Eucharist as a real union of the believer with Christ.

authors.aff: Bishop of Benevento; monk of S. Sofia, Benevento
authors.sig: Bishop of Benevento and monk of S. Sofia there, documented in a single 781 transaction granting rights at Venticano. His charter of renunciation says a founder's heirs appoint the church's priest and that churches are consecrated only by the bishop.

Archbishop of Salerno from 1058 until his death in 1085. He was a Benedictine monk and physician who encouraged medical study. He wrote Latin verse and hymns, and his Life and passion of Saint Christina stresses the intercession of saints and the eternal reward of martyrs.

The single work held under this name is a two-page account of the institution of a Cistercian order of Saint Michael in Portugal, arguing that the founding knightly fraternity honors God and the saints, that divine favor toward the kingdom requires thankful service, and that each faithful one has a guardian angel whose aid warrants perpetual commemorative institutions; it also gives the abbot sole

Bishop of Laon from 1113 to 1151, he contributed his own money to rebuild the cathedral after the commune's revolt of 1112. His donation charter granted the site of Prémontré to Norbert in perpetuity, and it exempted religious houses from parochial tithes under an anathema on violators.
Referenced in theological literature though not represented by any catalogued texts.

authors.aff: Bishop of Münster (839–849) and Abbot of Werden
authors.sig: Bishop of Münster from 839 and abbot of Werden, he wrote the Vita Liudgeri at the request of the Werdener monks. Though he never knew Liudger, his biography is a valuable source for the mission history of Westphalia.
A foundational architect of Nicene orthodoxy, Eastern Christian monasticism, and liturgical tradition whose works shaped both Eastern and Western patristic thought.
Abbot of Fleury from 988 until 1004. He wrote on grammar, computus, and canon law. His Apologeticus to Kings Hugh and Robert of the Franks defends his abbey against its own bishop.

authors.aff: Monkwearmouth–Jarrow Abbey, Kingdom of Northumbria (Benedictine monasticism)
authors.sig: Known as the 'Father of English History,' Bede wrote the definitive early medieval account of Christianity in Britain. His computistical works spread the use of Anno Domini dating.

His work here is Gregory-centered exegesis: a running exposition treating sin, grace, sanctification, and last things, arguing against Pelagius and Coelestius that grace is not bestowed for preceding merits and that faith without works is dead.

authors.aff: Christian scholar of Córdoba under Muslim rule
authors.sig: Mozarab scholar, poet and polemicist in ninth-century Córdoba. He wrote the Vita Eulogii, a biography of his close friend Eulogius that insists its narration rests on eyewitness truth and defends open confession over dissimulation. He considered Muhammad a precursor of the Antichrist.

A letter survives under his name, dated to the eleventh century. It argues that absolution may be conditional on promised satisfaction. It also states that a sworn surety is required rather than a bare promise. Burial is refused to those under excommunication.

authors.aff: Bishop of Trier (811/812–13), administrator of Lyon (835–38)
authors.sig: His writings on the Mass, offices, antiphonary, and baptism are a principal source for ninth-century Western liturgy and an early, influential example of mystical-symbolic interpretation of the rites.

authors.aff: Abbot of Aniane; monastic adviser to Louis the Pious
authors.sig: Abbot of Aniane and chief adviser on monastic affairs to the Frankish ruler. He wrote On the Harmony of Rules, which reads every known monastic rule as converging on the Rule of St. Benedict, a program that unified Frankish monasticism under that Rule.
Archbishop of Milan from about 685. He wrote a verse medical manual drawing on Pliny and Quintus Serenus. He also wrote an epitaph for Caedwalla, king of Wessex, buried in St. Peter's in Rome.

The letters here assert papal primacy in discipline: synodal decrees ratified by the apostolic see stand permanently, metropolitans answer only to the Roman pontiff, clerics may be summoned to Rome for judgment, and excommunication excludes from the Lord's body and blood while aiming at the sinner's salvation.

Bishop of Rome from 684 to 685, he obtained an imperial decree easing the imperial confirmation of papal elections. He urged the Spanish bishops to sign the Sixth General Council's definition against Monothelitism, arguing that such subscription proves the catholic faith and leads to the heavenly kingdom.

Pope from 900 until his death in 903. He crowned Louis the Blind emperor in 901 and excommunicated Baldwin II of Flanders for the murder of Archbishop Fulk of Reims. His letters and a privilege assert that a canonically elected bishop lawfully keeps his see.
Revered as the father of Western monasticism. His Rule of Saint Benedict became the main guide for communal monastic life throughout medieval Christendom.
His surviving epistle shows a Roman bishop enforcing orthodoxy against Arians in Visigothic Spain, defending the Trinity, baptismal formula, and the church as pillar of truth.

Abbot of Peterborough from 1177 until his death in 1193, after serving as chancellor to Archbishop Richard of Canterbury. His Life X of St. Thomas of Canterbury defends the liberty of the church against Henry II's justices and argues that judgment of bishops belongs to the pope.

authors.aff: Bishop of Rome; pope three times between October 1032 and July 1048
authors.sig: Pope three times between 1032 and 1048, Benedict IX was placed on the see as a youth by his father Count Alberic of Tusculum. He issued diplomas granting monasteries exemption from episcopal and secular jurisdiction and free abbatial election. These documents were central to the eleventh-century contest over church property and jurisdiction.

authors.aff: Monastery of St. Andrew on Mount Soracte
authors.sig: His chronicle is a tenth-century Roman history covering the church above all, the Lombard wars, and the city's deliverance from Greek rule — legendary in detail, but a witness to how a Roman monk narrated Narses, Totila, and Ambrose.

Missionary bishop in the Merovingian kingdom who evangelized Ghent and founded monasteries there and at Mount Blandin. Charters under his name record donations to his monastery and assert perpetual monastic ownership and burial rights.
His surviving letters are brief instruments of tenth-century papal government, showing how the see exercised delegated metropolitan jurisdiction and defended monastic exemption.

authors.n: Benedict of Saint Peter of Rome
authors.sig: He is significant for compiling the Liber Politicus, a primary source for the liturgical ceremonies, papal administration, and urban topography of twelfth-century Rome.

Bishop of Rome from 974 until his death in 983, elected with the backing of Emperor Otto II's envoy Sicco. His pontificate promoted monasticism and opposed simony, as in a 981 encyclical forbidding payment for holy orders. His surviving letters and privileges defend monastic exemption and the authority of the apostolic see.

authors.aff: Bishop of Rome and ruler of the Papal States, 18 May 1012 – 9 April 1024
authors.sig: Pope from 1012, he was a layman when he gained the office by force. He crowned Henry II emperor in 1014 and kept close ties with him. His letters and decrees defend monastic privilege against bishops, asserting that papal protection exempts monasteries from episcopal interdict and that violators incur anathema.

authors.aff: Canon of the Basilica of St. Peter's, Rome
authors.sig: A canon of the old Basilica of St. Peter in Rome and one of four canons who said mass there. Between 1140 and 1143 he wrote the Liber polypticus. It contains an Ordo Romanus that records the institutions, celebrations, and feasts of twelfth-century Rome. His life is otherwise undocumented.

His Apocalypse commentary was widely copied in medieval England (attested in numerous monastic booklists) and was used in the Douce Apocalypse (c. 1270), where French translations of its text accompany the Latin.

authors.aff: Benedictine Abbey of All Saints, Schaffhausen
authors.sig: A priest and chronicler born in Swabia who defended the reforms of Gregory VII. He wrote an Apology for the decrees of Gregory VII. His tracts attack simoniacs, married clergy and schismatics. On Avoiding Communion with the Excommunicated defends the binding force of excommunication.

authors.aff: Pseudonymous author of a forged capitulary collection
authors.sig: Pseudonymous author of a ninth-century forgery in the Pseudo-Isidorian tradition. He wrote capitularies that argue for clerical immunity from secular courts and inviolable ecclesiastical privilege. The work also opposes chorepiscopi, and it shaped Carolingian canon law despite being spurious.

authors.aff: Bishop of Oloron (from 1073), Archbishop of Bordeaux (1089–1101), papal legate
authors.sig: His texts here are instruments of the Gregorian reform in southern France: rulings securing monastic possession of churches, confirming donations, and enforcing clerical celibacy, issued against named opponents such as Duke William of Aquitaine and a simoniac abbot of Saint-Savin.

authors.aff: Abbot of St. Maximin near Trier
authors.sig: His surviving works are early twelfth-century sermons on the finding and veneration of the Holy Cross, a locus where crusade-era piety, the Helena legend, and anti-Jewish polemic meet.

authors.aff: Master of the cathedral school of Angers
authors.sig: His Liber miraculorum sancte Fidis defends the truth of Saint Faith's miracles against those who deemed them fabricated — arguing that faith in them should rest on experience and that the truth of miracles outweighs elegance of style — while also serving as propaganda for the Conques sanctuary.

Abbot of Clairvaux who backed Pope Innocent II against Antipope Anacletus II. He preached the Second Crusade at Vézelay in 1146. He wrote Letters and Sermons on the Song of Songs, and he attacked Peter Abelard.

These are letters of a lay magnate intervening in monastic reform: they argue that simoniacal abbots may be expelled without restitution, that the right to choose an abbot belongs to the reforming abbey, and that placing monasteries under reformed houses guards against heresy.

authors.aff: Abbot of Saint-Martial, Limoges (formerly prior of Solignac)
authors.sig: His single surviving letter here, addressed to Hervey, urges a saintly abbot to persevere in virtue and prayer amid worldly turmoil and argues that hagiography can move kings to patron monasteries.
A Benedictine monk at Cluny under Peter the Venerable. He wrote the verse satire De contemptu mundi and an exegesis on the parable of the unjust steward. The satire is dedicated to that abbot.

authors.aff: Charterhouse of Portes (prior); briefly bishop of Belley
authors.sig: Prior of the Charterhouse of Portes until infirmity forced his resignation in 1147. Three letters survive under his name, urging prayer and penance and warning against those who preach security in late repentance.

authors.aff: Archbishop of Toledo, first primate of Spain
authors.sig: Monk of Cluny and archbishop of Toledo, he was named to that see by Alfonso VI in 1086 and made primate of Spain by Urban II in 1088. Under his episcopate the church of Castile and León broke from isolation and from dependence on Rome. His sermons survive in PL 155.

authors.aff: Monk, born in Paris, settled in Lorraine
authors.sig: His treatise is a witness to how Gerbert's circle transmitted Boethian music theory to the eleventh century, defending numerical division of the monochord against empiricist accounts of pitch.

authors.aff: Premonstratensians (Order of Canons Regular of Prémontré)
authors.sig: He is notable in medieval theology and church history for authoring one of the earliest systematic polemical treatises against the Waldensian movement.
His two works here are principal Latin sources for the cult of St. Hunegund, presenting her virginity as a victory over the devil and her baptismal rebirth as the start of sanctity.

His musical treatises are a primary witness to how Gregorian chant was organised into modes and rhythmically sung in the eleventh century (supporting long and short note-values against equalist theory), and his liturgical and hagiographical works document German monastic reform under Henry II.

Abbot of Monte Cassino from 856. He fortified the abbey against Muslim raiders and founded a women's monastery at Teano. He wrote a life of St. Scholastica, a treatise on fasts, and a poem on St. Benedict.

The Testament printed here is the founding charter document of Cluny: it records Berno's division of his monasteries between Wido (who succeeds to Gigny, Baume and Aethicense) and Odo (who succeeds to Cluny, Massay/Macey and Dôle), asserts royal and apostolic privileges protecting the monasteries, and orders that abbots appoint successors while living — provisions that shaped the Cluniac congregat

Bishop of Clermont in Auvergne, thought with some confidence to have filled part of a sixty-year gap in the episcopal lists. His devotional poem on death and grace teaches that pardon is found at the saint's shrine and that eternal life comes freely through Christ.

authors.aff: Priest/canon of Verdun, monk of St. Vanne
authors.sig: Priest and canon of Verdun and monk of St. Vanne, he wrote a brief chronicle of the bishops of Verdun dedicated to Bishop Dadon. His Gesta is a principal source for the early bishops of Verdun, recording their succession and disputes with Count Sigebert and King Lothair.

authors.aff: Monk of Reichenau Abbey, Lake Constance
authors.sig: Benedictine monk of Reichenau Abbey and friend of Hermann, whose unpublished writings he was entrusted to copy onto parchment. He continued Hermann's world chronicle, a concise and impartial account of the troubled times before Pope Gregory VII's accession.

authors.aff: Priest of Constance; later monk of St. Blasien and All Saints, Schaffhausen
authors.sig: Priest of Constance and later a monk at St. Blasien and All Saints at Schaffhausen. He was an uncompromising opponent of Emperor Henry IV. His annals of his own times are a principal source for the Investiture Contest, and his tracts defend papal supremacy, excommunication, and the reform decrees of Gregory VII.

authors.aff: Grand Master of the Knights Templar, c. 1156/57–1169
authors.sig: As Grand Master of the Knights Templar, he wrote to King Louis VII of France in 1163 for aid. His letter describes the grim state of the Latin East, with captured and slain nobles, earthquake-damaged fortifications, and the death of Baldwin III, and begs the king to help.

Bishop of Le Mans from 586 or 587 until his death around 623 to 626. He was one of the wealthiest prelates in sixth-century Gaul. His testament of 616 names the church as sole heir and frees his slaves. It also provides perpetual alms and lamps for the donor's sins.

authors.aff: Roman senator, consul, and magister officiorum under Theoderic
authors.sig: Roman senator and consul who served the Ostrogothic king Theoderic as magister officiorum. He was executed at Pavia around 524 to 526, and the diocese of Pavia honors him as a martyr. He translated Greek logic into Latin, making him a principal conduit between ancient philosophy and the medieval Latin West.

authors.aff: Abbot of San Vincenzo al Volturno, near Benevento
authors.sig: A Frankish Benedictine monk who was elected abbot of San Vincenzo al Volturno on 4 October 777. His election aggravated disputes between Frankish and Lombard monks. He wrote a sermon on greed that treats covetousness as idolatry and the root of all vices.
Bishop of Rome from his disputed election in 418 until his death in 422. His letters concern the legitimacy of his ordination against Eulalius and appeals of bishops under the Nicene canons.

His treatise is an insider's account of Cathar teaching in Lombardy and one of the earliest Latin refutations of it, arguing against the Cathars, Pasagians, and Arnoldists while defending the Trinity, the sacraments, and creation ex nihilo.

His letters confirm the Council of Orange's doctrine that grace is always necessary for salvation—prevenient, accompanying, and following the will—and assert the primacy of Peter as the ground of ecclesiastical authority.

Bishop of Rome from 608 to 615. He received permission from Emperor Phocas to convert the Pantheon into the church of St. Mary and All Martyrs in 609. He encouraged monasticism and presided over a Roman council on monastic discipline in 610.

Pope from 619 to 625 and a Neapolitan who succeeded Deusdedit. The Liber Pontificalis credits him with rulings on sanctuary rights, and Bede records his letters of encouragement to missionaries in England. Some of those letters survive while others are lost.
His letters are the primary record of how the papal-authorized mission to Germany and the reform of the Frankish clergy were argued and carried out.

Bishop of Milan from 374 until his death in 397. He took a firm stand against Arianism, and his preaching helped convert Augustine of Hippo. He wrote exegetical and doctrinal treatises, letters and moral instruction. Among them are On the Duties of Ministers and an Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke.

His polemical histories defended Gregory VII against Henry IV and argued that persecution purifies and grows the church, that internal heresy may be fought with arms, that external persecution must be endured patiently, and that believers should rejoice under worldly hatred.
His single held work is an eleventh-century ducal law code on moral reform, showing a lay ruler legislating marriage, worship, and public morals by appeal to canon law against local custom.

His letters here are the principal surviving correspondence of seventh-century Hispania, treating prayer for one another, intercession of saintly bishops, almsgiving, and charity, alongside his Life of St. Aemilianus and acts of the Zaragozan martyrs.

A monk at Ramsey Abbey in Huntingdonshire and a student of Abbo of Fleury. He wrote a Life of Saint Dunstan, describing Dunstan's virtues and his conflicts with envious kinsmen and courtiers of King Eadwig. He also wrote commentaries on Bede's book On the Nature of Things and on a book On Speech by Gesture.

authors.aff: Bishop of Segni; monk of Monte Cassino
authors.sig: Bishop of Segni from 1080 and a monk of Monte Cassino from 1102, he denounced lay investiture as heretical. His Gregoriale is an exposition of Job built on Gregory the Great, typical of his scriptural writing in the reform-era church.

authors.aff: Bishop of Segni (consecrated 1080); Abbot of Montecassino (1107–1111)
authors.sig: His scriptural commentaries — Psalms, Pentateuch, the Gospels, Job, Apocalypse, Song of Songs — mark him as an eminent representative of medieval exegesis and monastic theology, and his polemical works defend Gregorian reform against lay investiture and simony.
He founded the Carthusian Order, synthesizing eremitic solitude with cenobitic monastic structure.

His Exposition of the Psalms reads the psalter as 'the whole Christ, head and members,' with Christ speaking in the person of his members — an eleventh-century episcopal commentary that draws heavily on Paul, Jerome, and Cassiodorus.
His surviving letters show a tenth-century bishop preaching penitential reform to his own clergy, grounding confession in Ezekiel, the Gospels, and James.

authors.aff: Bishop of Toul; pope as Leo IX (1049–1054)
authors.sig: Bishop of Toul before he became pope as Leo IX in 1049. His surviving writings are diplomas and a notice on restoring the monastery of Saint Aper. The diplomas record grants and altar dues reserved to the bishop.
His letters are a rare lay voice in the Brunhild–Theuderic controversy, framing resistance to the Frankish regime as defense of Catholic unity and legitimate grants.
His Decretum in twenty books became the canon law manual in cathedral schools and in the curias of bishops and abbots across Germany, France, and Italy before Gratian.

Her testament is one of the earliest surviving documents showing how a Merovingian noblewoman endowed a monastery, pairing pious donation with legal sanctions against infringers drawn from Theodosian law.

Archbishop of Arles for roughly forty years from 502 or 503. He urged his clergy to preach constantly, chiefly on moral topics. His sermons and rules for monks and virgins show a pastor and lawgiver. His opposition to Semi-Pelagianism was among the chief influences on that heresy's decline in the sixth century.

authors.aff: Household of Archbishop Werner of Magdeburg
authors.sig: His History of the Saxon War is the principal contemporary Saxon account of the revolt against Henry IV, justifying the rebellion and the election of Rudolf as anti-king while preserving ten letters of Gregory VII and the 'Saxon letters' exchanged with the rebels — key evidence for the Regnum–Sacerdotium conflict.

Bishop of Rome from 283 to 296 according to the Liberian Catalogue and Eusebius. A four-page epistle printed under his name treats church order and clerical immunity from secular judges. It also treats Christ's two natures. Its authenticity as a third-century papal letter is doubtful.
His two letters are among the few surviving Arian statements on divine generation, preserved because Victorinus answered them at length.

A monk of Fulda who studied with Einhard at Charlemagne's court. Abbot Eigil set him to paint the apse of the new basilica where Boniface's remains were placed in 819. He wrote a prose and a metrical Life of Saint Eigil that is valuable for Fulda's internal history. He also wrote a minor treatise on the Passion.

authors.aff: Collegiate Chapter of St Peter and Paul, Vyšehrad
authors.sig: His continuation is the primary narrative for Soběslav I's reign and the first Czech historical text to name the Czech nation as the 'family of Saint Wenceslaus'.

authors.aff: Pope, February 1119 – 1124; formerly Archbishop of Vienne (from 1088) and papal legate in France
authors.sig: Archbishop of Vienne and papal legate in France before his election as pope at Cluny in 1119. He ended the Investiture Controversy with the Concordat of Worms (1122) and convened the First Lateran Council in 1123. His letters assert papal privilege and his bull Sicut Judaeis forbade forced conversion of Jews.

Priest at Stavoren in Friesland around 920, credited with lives of Lebuin and Odulph and with genealogies of Friesland's princes. His Life of Saint Odulph shows preaching, miracles and prophecy proved by fulfillment. Some called him a writer of fables and others doubted he existed at all.

authors.aff: College of Cardinals loyal to Pope Alexander III
authors.sig: Their letters are primary evidence for how loyal churchmen framed papal authority, excommunication of rulers, and resistance to imperial interference during the Alexander III schism.

authors.aff: Mayor of the palace in Austrasia (741–747)
authors.sig: Mayor of the palace in Austrasia from 741 to 747, he led the Frankish church reform with Boniface and summoned councils in 742 and 743. His capitularies issued at Ver and Compiègne tie royal authority to the worship of God and peace and attach public penance to secular penalties for plunder.
He served as the principal voice of the North African episcopate during the Council of Ephesus (431), upholding anti-Nestorian orthodoxy during the collapse of Roman Africa.

authors.aff: Abbey of Anille (Saint-Calais), Diocese of Le Mans
authors.sig: A hermit from Aquitaine who settled alone on the river Anille. The abbey later named after him may have been built in his honor rather than by him. A copy of his testament survives, securing the monastery's property and its subjection to episcopal authority.

authors.aff: Carolingian Empire (King of West Francia, Holy Roman Emperor)
authors.sig: Charles the Bald profoundly influenced the development of medieval Western theology by fostering high-level ecclesiastical scholarship and directly commissioning pivotal works on the Eucharist, predestination, and Christian Neoplatonism.

Capitularies, diplomas and letters are gathered under his name. Modern study most probably gives the treatise On Images to Theodulf the bishop rather than to the king. That treatise rejects both iconoclast destruction and image-worship.
He shaped Western medieval monasticism by making scribal labor, the preservation of texts and classical learning sacred monastic duties.

authors.aff: Churchman and self-described servant of Charlemagne in Francia
authors.sig: His letter is one of the earliest statements of Carolingian political theology: the king rules as God's minister over a Christian people, with eight virtues marking the just ruler and royal injustice bringing famine, pestilence, and defeat.

Abbot of Saint-Sauveur de Redon from 1019 or 1021 until 1040. Two letters printed under his name are addressed to Hildegard and Letgard and treat intercession by sinners and the duty to keep the monastic rule.

His single extant letter to John Cassian prompted the De institutis coenobiorum (Institutiones Coenobiorum), dedicated to Castor, the work that carried Egyptian and Palestinian monastic practice into the Latin West; the text here praises Cassian as expert in Egyptian monastic doctrine and warns that gifts are distributed variously and presumption without discretion leads to ruin.

Papal chamberlain from 1188 and Vice-Chancellor before his election as pope at Perugia in 1216. He promoted the Fifth Crusade and approved the Dominican and Franciscan orders. Two liturgical works survive under his name: Roman Order XII and a short text on Amen.
Abbot of Wearmouth and Jarrow after Benedict Biscop. A letter under his name defends the Roman Easter computus and the Roman tonsure against the eighty-four-year cycle and against Adamnan.

His Libellus contra Maximum Arianum is a compact scriptural defense of the Son's full divinity written under Homoian Vandal persecution, arguing that Old Testament theophanies refer to Christ and that the Father's superiority pertains to Christ's humanity.

The texts here show a Merovingian king legislating for the church — protecting monastic liberty and endowing bishops — and are read as evidence of early Frankish church-state relations rather than as doctrinal writing.

His Exposition on Matthew, written for beginners, sets out the historical or literal sense as the foundation of all understanding of Scripture, and shows how a Carolingian schoolman compiled and taught exegesis.

authors.aff: Cardinal-priest of St. Damasus, Rome; claimed the papacy 903–904
authors.sig: A Roman cardinal-priest who deposed Pope Leo V in October 903 and was driven out by Sergius's supporters in January 904. He is now counted an antipope. His one surviving act is a diploma confirming the privileges of the Abbey of Corbie, asserting papal headship over all churches.

Bishop of Metz from 742 who kept his civil office at Pepin's request. He organized his cathedral clergy in community life and wrote a rule for them that became an early model for the Carolingian canons' movement. He founded Gorze Abbey in 748 and died at Metz in 766.

Archbishop of Tours and a Merovingian bishop. The Chronicon Turonense credits him with privileges for St Martin's Abbey at Tours. Pope Adeodatus later confirmed those privileges. A work titled Judgment concerning the adulterous woman survives under his name, but the record does not describe its contents.

Bishop of Aquileia from 387/388 until his death in 406/407, he wrote a Treatise on the Gospel of St. Matthew and a Sermon on the Eight Beatitudes. Both present baptism as washing away sin and forgiveness as conditional on forgiving others.

Salian king of Germany from 1024 and emperor from 1027 until his death at Utrecht in 1039. He issued diplomas in 1025 and constitutions in 1031 that granted immunity to church lands from secular judges and confirmed monastic elections. They also set out tithes and the dues owed to bishops.

Bishop of Turin from 817 or 818 until his death toward the end of 827. He wrote commentaries on Paul, including the Enarration on the Epistle to the Galatians. His Apology defends his attacks on the cult of images and relics against charges of heresy.
His Life of St. Ildefonsus is the main witness to the cult of Toledo's great seventh-century bishop, presenting Ildefonsus's holiness as a heavenly gift whose teaching endures after his death.

authors.aff: King of the Franks in Neustria and Burgundy
authors.sig: His diplomas show how Merovingian kingship exercised itself through grants to churches and monasteries — clemency toward petitioners, inviolable donations to saints' shrines, and royal confirmation securing ecclesiastical property.

King of the Salian Franks who united the Franks under a single kingship and was baptized between 498 and 506. His Precept exempts clerics and religious from military plunder and orders captives taken from church persons restored by appeal to the apostolic see.

authors.aff: Bishop of Rome, 1046–1047; formerly Bishop of Bamberg
authors.sig: Bishop of Rome from 1046 to 1047 and formerly of Bamberg, he crowned Henry III emperor. His letters grant privileges to monasteries, including Fulda's precedence among German houses and abbatial consecration reserved to the apostolic see. They assert papal authority over monasteries and against simoniacal bishops.

authors.aff: King of the Franks, sole ruler from 613
authors.sig: King of the Franks who became sole ruler in 613 after defeating Brunhilda and her grandsons. His precepts and edicts legislated for the church, setting rules for asylum in church atria, penalties for theft, and the binding force of council decrees.

authors.aff: King of the Franks, sole ruler from 558
authors.sig: The work here shows a Merovingian king legislating on church immunity, lawful judicial procedure, and marriage — loci later treated under the civil magistrate and true worship.

The letters and privileges here show papal government at work: protection of church property, privileges enforced by excommunication and divine judgment, disputes with Baldwin of Canterbury and other bishops, and settlement of jurisdictional claims between mother and daughter churches.

King of Neustria and Burgundy from 657 to 673, ruling as a child under his mother Balthild's regency. Royal charters under his name restore lands to monasteries and grant exemption from tolls. The grants bind his successors forever and the monks owe prayers in return.
A long-serving papal diplomat turned pope, Celestine III navigated major geopolitical clashes with the Hohenstaufen empire and issued significant decretals incorporated into medieval canon law.

A Pelagian presbyter who studied law in Rome and attached himself to the movement about 405. A council at Carthage condemned his denial of original sin and the need of grace in 412. His Booklet of Faith to Zosimus and Book Against Original Sin survive only in fragments.

Bishop of Rome from 26 September 1143 until his death on 8 March 1144. He studied under Peter Abélard and served as legate to France. His letters and privileges defend monasteries, chiefly Stavelot. They grant free burial and protect church possessions and threaten excommunication for violators.
He is remembered for upholding Christological orthodoxy through his support of the Council of Ephesus and for initiating the formal Christian mission to Ireland.

authors.aff: presbyter (per Isidore of Seville and the Gelasian decree)
authors.sig: His Carmen paschale, a five-book verse summary of the Old and New Testaments asserting Christ's equality with the Father and the world-cleansing power of one baptism, became one of the most read biblical epics of the Latin Middle Ages.

Abbot of Luxeuil and Bobbio, he taught an Irish monastic rule and private confession followed by assigned penances. His Coenobitic Rule, penitential measurements and letters are among the earliest surviving works of a Hiberno-Latin writer.

authors.aff: Most likely associated with the monastery of Kildare, Ireland
authors.sig: His Vita Sanctae Brigidae is the earliest surviving life of St Brigid and a key source for early Irish monasticism, church order, and art; his description of the church of Kildare is specially interesting for the history of early Irish art and architecture.

The Aenigmata became the model for medieval Latin riddle collections, especially in England, where it provoked a literary vogue and served as a school text; Aldhelm is the earliest ancient witness to it.
Abbot of Saint-Trond and a poet, he is linked to a dirge on the death of Charlemagne. Modern scholars doubt that attribution and usually regard the poem as anonymous.
The council decisively rejected Semi-Pelagianism and established the orthodox Western doctrine affirming the necessity of prevenient grace for salvation.

A Christian Latin poet who says he was born a pagan and converted late in life, calling himself a beggar of Christ. He wrote Instructions against the Gods of the Gentiles, an acrostic poem holding that only God is to be worshipped and that pagan gods are demons served through images.

authors.aff: Council of the Western Church held at the Lateran, Rome
authors.sig: Its canons on void ordinations by heretics, canonical election of bishops, clerical celibacy, and lay seizure of church property were incorporated into Gratian's Decretum and so entered the mainstream of canon law; readers here hold the conciliar text itself, aimed at Burdinus and the porticani.
The council is significant for enacting regional Peace of God decrees and formally declaring Saint Martial an apostle rather than a confessor.
A brief conciliar letter showing how eastern synods appealed to imperial authority to enforce doctrinal settlement, preserved among Latin patristic texts alongside Ambrose's correspondence.

Cardinal-bishop of Palestrina and papal legate under Paschal II, he held synods in France and Germany and excommunicated Emperor Henry V repeatedly over lay investiture. His letters defend contested episcopal elections by appeal to apostolic authority and assert that bishops may excommunicate kings.

A physician from Ifriqiya who translated Arabic medical works into Latin at Monte Cassino, where he became a Benedictine monk. His treatise argues that medicine is a true science and the end of all philosophy, taught only from experimentally proven knowledge.

The first Christian Roman emperor: these letters and edicts are primary documents of the legal establishment of Christianity and of imperial intervention in doctrine, including against Arius and the Meletians.

authors.aff: Monk of Brauweiler Abbey near Cologne
authors.sig: A Benedictine monk of Brauweiler Abbey near Cologne who wrote the Life of Wolphelm and dedicated it to abbots Everhard and Hermann. The Life incorporates Wolfhelm's own letter to Abbot Meginhard of Gladbach against Berengar's Eucharistic teaching.
Bishop of Albi, listed among those attending the Council of Rheims in 625. An epistle under his name survives. The record gives no account of its contents.

His surviving work is a verse passion celebrating the martyrs Theopompus and companions, who are said to have suffered at Nicomedia under Diocletian — though Baronius doubted that chronology — and it asserts their intercession for the faithful.

His sermon is an early source for the life of Zeno of Verona; the held text credits Christ with omnipotence over demons, shows miracles converting gentiles to faith, affirms that invocation of saints with faith grants petitions, and that saints intercede for the sick at their tombs.

authors.aff: Abbot of the Abbey of Saint-Symphorien, Metz
authors.sig: His single surviving work is a principal narrative source for Adalbero II of Metz and for episcopal ideals in eleventh-century Lotharingia.

The letters printed under his name in PL 89 concern privileges for Evesham Abbey — confirming royal donations, granting monastic liberty, and asserting the certainty of Egwin's Marian vision — but these documents are regarded as spurious, so they witness to Anglo-Saxon monastic claims rather than to Constantine's own authorship.
Bishop of Rome from 251 until his exile and death in 253. His surviving letters defend his election against Novatian and argue that the lapsed may be restored to communion after penance.

authors.aff: Dean of the cathedral chapter of St. Vitus, Prague
authors.sig: Dean of the cathedral chapter of St. Vitus in Prague and a Latin chronicler of Bohemia. He had close ties with the bishops of Prague and the confidence of the duchy's rulers. His Chronica Boemorum is the first history of Bohemia and treats both providence and the Přemyslid origins of the duchy.
The exact identity of this figure remains uncertain in standard reference catalogues due to multiple early Irish figures sharing the name.
He represents the educated Donatist laity whose literary and rhetorical defenses of Donatism survive as a key source for understanding anti-Catholic polemics in late antique Roman Africa.
The foremost Latin Christian writer before Jerome and Augustine. His doctrine that salvation and one baptism exist only in the catholic church shaped Western ecclesiology.

authors.aff: Archpriest of the diocese of Córdoba
authors.sig: His Epigrams are rare surviving Latin verse from ninth-century Córdoba, and their themes—prayer for the author's salvation, prayers benefiting the departed dead, contemptus mundi rewarded in heaven—show the devotional concerns of Andalusi Christianity.
Bishop of Barcelona in the Visigothic period, he attended the Tenth Council of Toledo in 656. Three of his letters survive, two to Ildefonsus of Toledo and one to Taio of Zaragoza.
His fragment is a contemporary witness to how a Carolingian bishop's see accumulated property through imperial and royal charters, told through the lives of the bishops who did it.

A scribe at the court school of Charlemagne who wrote the golden psalter that bears his name between 782 and 795. Charlemagne meant the book as a gift to Pope Hadrian I. Hadrian died in 795, so it likely never reached Rome. A poem of eighteen lines describes the psalter as a royal gift and presents the king as joining David's choir.

Merovingian king of Austrasia who lived in exile as a monk in Ireland before his assassination near Stenay in 679. His royal grants of imperial baths and estates to Wissembourg abbey present almsgiving as a remedy for the donor's soul. Lorraine venerated him as a martyr from at least the ninth century.

authors.aff: Abbot of Hautecombe (1139–1144), then Bishop of Lausanne (1144 or 1145 until his death)
authors.sig: Cistercian who served as abbot of Hautecombe from 1139 and then as bishop of Lausanne. He wrote eight homilies on the Virgin Mary. The seventh was cited in the 1950 papal definition of the Assumption. A letter to the children of the Church of Lausanne also survives.

His Catechetical Lectures and Mystagogical Catecheses are an important surviving record of how fourth-century Jerusalem instructed catechumens before baptism and expounded the creed throughout Lent, and document the liturgy and sacramental teaching of his day.

Bishop of Rome from 366 to 384 who opposed Arianism, Macedonianism and Apollinarianism and commissioned Jerome's revision of the Latin Bible. His verse epitaphs and letters assert Christ's eternal divinity, his incarnation and his conquest of death.

authors.aff: King of the Franks (Austrasia 623–634; Neustria and Burgundy 629–639)
authors.sig: The precepts show how Merovingian kingship framed pious royal donation as true worship and protection of the church as securing divine favor on the kingdom.

Bishop of Pavia who mediated between the Lombards and the Byzantine emperors. He wrote one surviving work, a letter to Emperor Constantine IV sent in the name of Bishop Mansuetus of Milan. The letter professes two natural wills in Christ against Monothelitism and was read at the Third Council of Constantinople.

Prince-bishop of Liège from 1048 until 1075, named to the see by Emperor Henry III. In 1066 he granted city rights to Huy and endowed its collegiate church of St. Mary. A letter he wrote against Bruno and Berengar survives.

authors.aff: Abbot of Montecassino; later Pope Victor III
authors.sig: Abbot of Monte Cassino from 1058 to 1087, he was made cardinal in 1058 and was elected pope in 1086 as Victor III. He wrote a Dialogue defending miracles worked through the saints and the edifying force of virtuous examples. He also wrote an Epitaph of Apollinaris.

Bishop of Cahors from 630 until his death in 655. He had earlier served as royal treasurer under Chlotar II and kept the office under Dagobert. His letters defend him against accusers, including Felix of Narbonne, and treat prayer, royal judgment, almsgiving, and eternal reward for benefiting the church.

authors.aff: Benedictine abbey of Ligugé, near Poitiers
authors.sig: The Liber scintillarum is a florilegium that made the moral teaching of Scripture, Isidore, Gregory, Paul, Jerome, Augustine, and others available in excerpted form, organizing all virtues under charity as their root.

authors.aff: Cardinal-priest of San Pietro in Vincoli, Rome
authors.sig: Cardinal-priest of San Pietro in Vincoli and one of Gregory VII's chief agents against imperial control of the Church. He compiled a book of canons, completed in 1087 and dedicated to Victor III. Fragments of his work argue that no one may judge or depose a pope.

Bishop of Rome from 615 to 618, he governed during the Lombard wars and favored secular diocesan clergy over monks. Two short texts printed in PL 80 treat baptismal sponsorship as a marriage impediment, but the Catholic Encyclopedia judges these decretals unauthenticated.

Bishop of Laon from 977 and chancellor to King Lothaire. He was accused of adultery with Queen Emma and later delivered Laon to Hugh Capet. He wrote the Carmen ad Rotbertum regem, a satirical dialogue poem to King Robert of France that some read as an attack on Cluniac reform.

authors.aff: Abbot of Bangor Iscoed on the Dee
authors.sig: Dinooth was first abbot of Bangor Iscoed on the Dee. Before he took up religious life, he was a North British chieftain. A Response to Augustine the Monk circulates under his name. It argues that the British church was not subject to Rome.

Head of the catechetical school at Alexandria before he became bishop there in 248. Most of his letters survive only as excerpts that Eusebius preserved. The current note says they defend divine providence against the atomists and Epicurus. He argued against Sabellianism that the Son's generation produces a distinct person of the same nature.

authors.aff: Monk in Rome, from Scythia Minor
authors.sig: Monk from Scythia Minor who lived in Rome and translated 401 Greek church canons into Latin. He compiled the decretals of popes and prepared the 525 Easter reckoning that introduced Anno Domini dating.
His Calendar of 354 is the oldest known Christian calendar and contains the first known reference to the celebration of Christmas, alongside Roman festivities.

His surviving fragments here defend one divine nature in three distinct persons against Sabellius and Marcion, and record the Roman council that absolved Dionysius of Alexandria of doctrinal accusation — an early exercise of conciliar judgment and papal oversight in a christological controversy.

authors.aff: Duchess consort of Septimania and Countess consort of Barcelona, wife of Bernard
authors.sig: The Liber Manualis is a rare surviving work of moral and religious instruction by a Carolingian woman, teaching prayer (uniting mouth, heart, and works), love of God, baptism, and hope of eternal life.

Benedictine monk of Sant'Apollonio at Canossa and later its abbot. He wrote the Vita Mathildis in Latin hexameters. The poem is a principal contemporary source for Matilda of Tuscany and the Investiture Controversy.

Bishop of Le Mans from 559 until his death on December 1, 581. He was first abbot of Saint-Laurent. His Testament argues that church goods do not pass by hereditary right and that violating a church donation brings divine curse.

Bishop of Rome from 676 until his death in 678, after a reign of about seventeen months. He paved the atrium of Old St. Peter's with white marble and received the obedience of Reparatus of Ravenna, ending a schism begun by Archbishop Maurus. His verse epitaph asserts episcopal succession as the mark of the true church.

authors.aff: Bishop of Besançon; monk of Luxeuil
authors.sig: His Rule for Virgins is the oldest witness to the textual reception of the Rule of Benedict, combining Benedict with Caesarius of Arles and Columbanus, and adapts monastic discipline for a women's community — an abbess serving rather than lording, correction kept prudent, no acceptance of persons.

authors.aff: Deacon of the church of Lyon; head of its cathedral school and director of its scriptorium
authors.sig: Deacon of the church of Lyon and head of its cathedral school. He directed the Lyon scriptorium, which produced the only complete Latin version of Irenaeus's Adversus Haereses. He wrote a Book Against John Scotus and minor works against Amalarius.

Benedictine prior of Saint-Nicaise de Reims and first abbot of Saint-Jean de Laon. Innocent II made him cardinal bishop of Ostia. He wrote a sermon on the Lord's Passion and a treatise on the divine offices. Short works on the creation and redemption of the first man and on the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are also his.

Bishop of Beauvais from 1030 and a French prelate who died in 1047. In a letter to a fellow bishop he argued that violence against clergy is sacrilege against God's temple and that excommunication declares a judgment already passed.

authors.aff: Lawyer and Christian poet at Carthage
authors.sig: Christian Latin poet and lawyer at Carthage under Vandal rule. He wrote the Poem on God (De laudibus Dei), whose first book on creation circulated separately as a Hexaemeron. In prison he composed the Satisfaction to Gunthar, an elegiac plea for pardon.

authors.aff: School of San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro, Pavia
authors.sig: His Responses against Claudius is a major Carolingian defense of sacred images against iconoclasm, arguing that honor belongs to God alone while images instruct the illiterate and must not be destroyed or adored.

authors.aff: Canon of Saint-Quentin, later its dean; chaplain and chancellor to Duke Richard II of Normandy
authors.sig: His Historia Normannorum is a primary source for the early history of the Norman state and the founding dukes from Rollo onward.

Archbishop of Lyon from 841 who took part in the Gottschalk controversy over predestination. He pressed anti-Jewish policies at the Councils of Meaux and Paris and addressed his Book against the Jews to Charles the Bald in 846. Some letters under his name may have been drafted by Florus of Lyon.

English Benedictine monk who rose from Abbot of Glastonbury to Archbishop of Canterbury and served several kings as a minister of state. He helped restore monastic life in England and reform its church. The Monastic Agreement of the English Nation sought one rule for all monks under royal authority.
His treatise is one of the earliest replies to Berengar's figurist eucharistic teaching, arguing that denial of sacramental truth destroys Christian discipline.
His Lives of Maximus of Riez and Marius are early Merovingian saints' lives that present ascetic renunciation as bloodless martyrdom and the saint's merits as lasting protection for his city.

A Benedictine monk of Evesham Abbey, active around 1200. His Life of the martyred archbishop of Canterbury defends writing saints' lives for God's glory and edification. It also reports the incorrupt body found at the translation and miracles that followed devotion to the saint.

He is the contemporary biographer of Anselm and chronicler of the Canterbury–York primacy dispute (the Historia Novorum argues for Canterbury's primacy over York), and his Mariological tracts fed the Western development of the Immaculate Conception doctrine.

Archbishop of Reims from 816, who joined Lothair's rebellion against Louis and presided at the synod that deposed the emperor in 833. After his deposition he wrote an Apology and a Confession defending the restoration of expelled bishops and arguing that flight from persecutors follows Christ's example.

authors.aff: Abbot of St. Martin's Abbey, Trier
authors.sig: Benedictine abbot of St. Martin's in Trier, attested between about 1018 and 1036. He wrote a Vita of the recluse Simeon of Trier, which presents patient endurance under persecution as witness to holiness. His works also defend enclosed recluses and argue that monasteries must not be given out as lay benefices.

His single held work is a monastic charter asserting the restoration of church property to monastic use and the perpetual irrevocability of ecclesiastical grants, naming Adalbero as bishop and Hugh, Harduin and Alulf as archdeacons.

His three pages of letters are a primary witness to how a tenth/eleventh-century abbey fought legal and political battles over its advocacy and property, and to monastic teaching on prayer for the dead.

authors.aff: Abbot of Schönau Abbey (Diocese of Trier), from 1166
authors.sig: His Sermons against the Cathars are among the earliest sustained Latin polemics against the Cathars, defending episcopal succession, open preaching, real presence, and purgatory against them.

authors.aff: Canon of the abbey of Watten, county of Flanders
authors.sig: His chronicle is an important source for the early history of Flanders and for the abbey of Watten, founded in 1072 by the priest Olfride for canons regular of Saint Augustine.

King of the English from 959 to 975, he ruled a peaceful realm. He backed the English Benedictine Reform with Dunstan and Æthelwold, and his charters and law codes enforced it against secular canons and clerics.

This text is schism literature from the Innocentian side: it asserts that lawful election confers legitimate papal authority, that the pope rules the whole church by divine disposition, and that kings owe honor and obedience to the Roman church, while defending papal grants of episcopal liturgical insignia to abbots and the relaxation of interdicts at royal intercession.

Archbishop of Reims and chancellor to Kings Lothair and Louis V of West Francia. He declared the Frankish crown elective and crowned Hugh Capet, after escaping trial for treason when Louis V died in 987. His letters and a record on the transfer of monks to Mouzon show him governing his province during the Lothair–Ottonian conflict.

Subdeacon at Regensburg who wrote the two books of the Traditions of Saint Emmeram, a record of gifts to the monastery and the disputes they provoked. Documenta Catholica Omnia dates the work to 899. He names donors and opponents and appeals to ducal tradition and Bavarian law to restore church boundaries.
His letters here document the papal condemnation of Origen and the contested case of Rufinus of Aquileia, whom Anastasius argued against but, by the record's account, passed no sentence against.

Bishop of Rome from 911 to 913, whose pontificate was dominated by Theophylact I of Tusculum and Theodora. A privilege issued under his name gave Hamburg metropolitan jurisdiction over the northern mission churches and argued against the archbishop of Cologne.

Cardinal-bishop of Sabina and vicar of Innocent II in Rome, he was elected pope on 8 July 1153 and reigned until his death in 1154. His brief pontificate restored the Pantheon and granted special privileges to the Hospitallers of St. John of Jerusalem.

authors.aff: Librarian of the Roman Church under Adrian II
authors.sig: Librarian of the Roman Church under Adrian II and the most learned Greek scholar of ninth-century Rome. He translated Greek conciliar texts into Latin, defending image-veneration with the principle that honor paid to an image passes to its prototype. His History of the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs ties the true church to episcopal succession.

authors.aff: Priest of the diocese of Bergamo
authors.sig: A priest of the diocese of Bergamo who continued Paul the Deacon's Historia Langobardorum down to about 877. In 875 he helped carry the coffin of Emperor Louis II from the Oglio river to the Adda. He never states that he came from Bergamo.

authors.aff: associated with the church of Cambrai
authors.sig: A Latin chronicler whose name the sources do not establish. The Chronicle of the church of Cambrai covers the diocese during the Investiture Contest and argues against partisans of Emperor Henry IV.

Abbot of Strumi and a disciple of the deacon Arialdo in the Milanese campaign against simoniacal clergy. He wrote a Life of John Gualbert, the Vallombrosan founder. It presents the order's fight against simoniac bishops as a matter of publicly confessed truth and grace-given vocation.

authors.aff: Monk and priest, identified by Trithemius with Saint-Vincent de Metz
authors.sig: Monk and priest who compiled the Speculum Gregorii, a four-book selection of 193 excerpts from Gregory the Great's Moralia in Job. It was copied widely and listed in many English monastic catalogues, and his prologue to his friend Hermann defends the humble 'mirror' against envious critics.
His Life of Arialdus and Hertembald (PL 143) is an eyewitness-adjacent account of the Milanese Pataria reform, denouncing simony and the corrupt clergy under Guido of Velate.

His three surviving commentaries—on Genesis, Kings, and the Song of Songs—read historical books typologically, treating kings as prefiguring Christ and the gospel typically, and compiling patristic 'mystical treasures' for readers who want a window into ninth-century exegesis.

authors.aff: Bishop of Metz (768–791); royal archchaplain to Charlemagne (784–791)
authors.sig: The works under his name here — charters of donation securing monasteries against advocates, and a collection of canons on episcopal rights — belong to the Carolingian defense of episcopal authority that later fed the pseudo-Isidorian decretals.

authors.aff: Abbot of Saint-Riquier (Centula), diocese of Amiens
authors.sig: Abbot of Saint-Riquier (Centula) in the diocese of Amiens, trained under Fulbert of Chartres. His versified Life of Saint Richarius argues that verse is a fitting way to recite Scripture and that reading saints' lives kindles love of God.

Frankish noble who served Charlemagne's court as secretary, diplomat, and poet, and later became abbot of Centula. His On the Restoration of the Monastery of Saint-Riquier describes three churches dedicated by twelve bishops and relics recorded by name.
His letters are evidence of Gregorian positions on investiture and episcopal discipline from the archbishop who did most to defeat Henry V's design on the German church.

Abbot of Centula and a Frankish noble educated under Alcuin at Charlemagne's palace school. He wrote Latin verses addressed to Louis. The verses argue that God made all things in measure and number and sustains them by his power.

Archbishop of Milan from 824 until his death in 859, he acted as intermediary between Lothair I and the emperor and funded the renovation of the Sant'Ambrogio basilica. His rescript to Emperor Louis and his privilege for the Ambrosian Basilica defend episcopal authority, including lawful election and a proper hearing for accused clergy.

Archbishop of Lyon who succeeded Viventius between 652 and 654 and served as a royal councillor. Bede records that he welcomed Wilfrid of York in 653 and offered him the government of a large part of Gaul. He was put to death after being slandered as a traitor. A charter under his name survives.

Archbishop of Cologne from 1056 to 1075 and regent of the empire from 1063 to 1065. In 1062 he led the abduction of the young Henry IV. His diplomas forbid the sale of donated property and found a monastery exempt from secular service under anathema.

Archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen and missionary to Denmark and Sweden. A Life of Willehad, first bishop of Bremen, survives under his name, and so does an epistle. Both present saints as models for imitation and treat the conversion of the pagan Frisians and the veneration of saints.

authors.n: Ansell the Cantor of the Holy Sepulchre
authors.aff: Cantor of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem
authors.sig: His letters are firsthand evidence of relic circulation between crusader Jerusalem and Paris, arguing that many signs of Jesus are unwritten in scripture, that dividing relics preserves them from destruction, and that fragments of the True Cross survive in many churches.

Bishop of Prague who was martyred in 997 during his missionary work. A homily for a saint's feast and a profession of the Rule of Saint Benedict survive under his name. Both are short devotional texts linked to his cult rather than major theological works.

authors.aff: Abbot of Bec; Archbishop of Canterbury (1093–1109)
authors.sig: Abbot of Bec and Archbishop of Canterbury from 1093 until his death in 1109. He is credited with originating the satisfaction theory of atonement. His treatises include Monologion and On the Procession of the Holy Spirit against the Greeks.
King of the English and son of Æthelred II, venerated as a saint for his piety. Laws attributed to him govern tithes and sanctuary, and they condemn withholders of tithes and usurers.

Archbishop of York and author of one of the earliest Anglo-Saxon penitential manuals. His Penitential sets graded penances by the gravity of sin and requires confession to a priest first. Modern scholars doubt that he wrote some other works printed under his name.
He is renowned as the primary eyewitness biographer of Thomas Becket whose narrative shaped the medieval cult and hagiography of the martyred archbishop.

authors.aff: Court of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious
authors.sig: Court official under Charlemagne and private secretary to Louis the Pious from 814. He wrote the Life of Charlemagne, the principal contemporary biography of the emperor. Letters and charters survive under his name. So does an account of the translation of the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter.

Fourth abbot of Fulda from about 818 until his death in 822. After Abbot Ratgar was deposed and banished, Eigil was elected and sought Ratgar's return from Louis the Pious. He wrote the Life of Saint Sturmius.

authors.aff: Deacon of the Roman Church (if identified with Johannes Hymonides)
authors.sig: Identified only tentatively with John the Deacon of Rome, a figure of the ninth-century Roman Curia. If that identification is correct, he wrote a four-book life of Gregory the Great at the request of Pope John VIII.

authors.aff: Abbot of Aura on the Franconian Saale, near Kissingen, Bavaria (from 1108 or 1113, per conflicting sources)
authors.sig: Benedictine monk and abbot of Aura who took part in the Crusade of 1101 and reached Jerusalem briefly. He began the Chronicon universale as a revision of Frutolf of Michelsberg's chronicle and carried it to the death of Emperor Henry V in 1125. The chronicle is an important source for the First Crusade and the Crusade of 1101.

Archbishop of Toledo from 657 until his death in 667. He was a theologian of Visigothic Spain. He wrote a short expository work on the Trinity, the sacraments and the angelic orders. It argues against apocryphal writings and cites Ezekiel and Athanasius.

First bishop of Tournai, probably appointed in the years after Clovis's conversion. The sermons printed under his name are considered spurious. They are read as anonymous texts on the Trinity, Christ's natures, the Spirit, and last things.
His identity remains uncertain and known only through bibliographic citations rather than extant authored works in the collection.
A historical figure whose record is preserved solely through secondary citations.

authors.aff: Abbot of Tegernsee (1017–1026, restored 1031; deposed again 1041)
authors.sig: Benedictine abbot of Tegernsee who was installed in 1017 and deposed in 1041 after being forced out in 1026. His letters are polemical defenses of episcopal authority and of the rights of benefices. They were written chiefly against Bishop Nitker of Freising during the disputes that cost him his abbacy.

authors.aff: Queen consort of England (wife of Æthelred II and Cnut)
authors.sig: Queen consort of England to Æthelred II and then to Cnut, she was mother of Harthacnut and Edward the Confessor. A letter under the title 'Letter to his children' is attributed to her, though its contents and circumstances are not established.

A Latin poet and hymnographer who died young at Padua around 504. Two hymns praising the apostles Peter and Paul are traditionally attributed to her, though the attribution is uncertain. Her verse treats prayer to the apostles and faith that shall see God face to face.

Goldsmith and master of the mint under Kings Chlothar II and Dagobert I, he was ordained priest after 639 and became bishop of Noyon around 641–642. Homilies attributed to him treat grace, sin and the eucharist as a true sacrifice for daily sins.

authors.aff: Bishop of Soissons; monk of Corbie
authors.sig: The single work here, Verses to Abbot Radbert, is a witness to the literary circle of Corbie in the mid-ninth century rather than a theological argument.

Archbishop of Toledo from 782. He first condemned Migetius of Seville for Sabellianism. In that dispute he formulated Spanish Adoptionism, which holds that Christ is the adopted Son of God in his human nature. Councils at Ratisbon and Frankfurt condemned the teaching. He never recanted.
