A bridge figure who deployed late Roman rhetorical learning in the service of the post-imperial Catholic Church, and whose letters, panegyrics, and saints' lives are among the richest sources for the ecclesiastical culture of Theoderic's Italy.

authors.aff: Bishop of Avranches (1060–1067), then Archbishop of Rouen (1067–1079)
authors.sig: The charter here shows an eleventh-century Norman bishop allocating jurisdiction: the abbot exercises delegated archidiaconal authority, marriage dissolution rests on witnessed testimony, ordination, degradation, ordeal judgments, chrism, and excommunication all remain anchored to the episcopal see.

Bishop of Liège from 959 until his death in 971, he founded the collegiate churches of St Paul and St Martin. He wrote an Epistle and a Report of a Miracle of Saint Martin that credits the saint with a personal healing.
Bishop of Freising from 835 or 836 until his death in 854, he came from the Bavarian Huosi nobility. A short epistle to his own people and a fragment on Martel's rise survive under his name.
Bishop of Strasbourg from 965 to 991, he attended the Synod of Ingelheim and the Diet of Speyer. His Municipal Laws for the city of Strasbourg set rules on sanctuary and on clergy bearing the sword.

Poet at the court of Pippin of Aquitaine who was banished from court and wrote In honorem Hludovici imperatoris from exile to win back favor. The poem holds that Christ grants kingship and that a ruler must love Christ, care for the church, honor relics, and rule justly.

His history is a near-contemporary account of the violence among the Lombard princes of southern Italy, read here for its treatment of providence, princely anointing, compelled oaths, and the civil magistrate.
He is primarily remembered as a key biographer of Bernard of Clairvaux and as the author of influential 12th-century spiritual treatises on the Passion and the Virgin Mary.

His single work here is a short polemic against heretics — printed under the title Against the Waldensians — defending sacraments, baptism, lawful oaths sworn by God rather than creatures, and Christ's observance of the law as true God and man, largely through proof-texts from Paul and John.

Bishop of Rochester from 1114, he had trained at Bec under Lanfranc and was counted an expert in canon law. A letter on incestuous marriages survives under his name, applying patristic authority and conciliar decrees to marriage law. He also wrote a history of the affairs of the church of Rochester.

authors.aff: Bishop of Lyon, from c. 434/439; Metropolitan of Lyons by the Council of Orange (441)
authors.sig: Bishop of Lyon and Metropolitan of Lyons by the Council of Orange in 441. His Formulae of Spiritual Understanding teach allegorical reading of Scripture through the nations of Genesis 10 and the Trinity in both Testaments. His letters on the desert and contempt of the world made him a model of Gallic asceticism.

A ninth-century Anglo-Saxon monk and author of the Latin poem Carmen de abbatibus, which recounts the history of his own house in 819 hexameters. Canons on church order, ordination and duties to the dead survive under his name in PL 96. Their Irish provenance is noted.

Bishop of Rome from 824 to 827, elected after a divided vote in which the Roman nobility prevailed. He accepted the Constitutio Romana with Lothar I, and his council of 826 targeted simony and untrained clergy. His decrees set rules on excommunication, clerical celibacy, lay involvement in church business, and tournaments.

Bishop of Carthage from 480 who defended the divinity of the Word against Arian theologians at a royal conference under the Vandal king Huneric. He was exiled to the desert of Tripoli and wrote a letter of consolation to the faithful of Carthage before he left. A Profession of Faith survives under his name.
Known only through external citations in theological references, with no distinct extant corpus identified.

Archbishop of Toledo from 647 until his death in 657, he attended the synods of 653 and 656 and reformed the chant of the Divine Office. Letters and a preface attributed to him oppose simony and the usurping of chrismation by deacons and presbyters.

authors.aff: Priest and head of the chief ecclesiastical school at Córdoba
authors.sig: Priest and head of the chief ecclesiastical school at Córdoba, he was executed there on 11 March 859. He wrote the Memorial of the Saints and the Apologetic Book of the Martyrs in defense of Christians who had publicly denounced Muhammad. His works argue that their witness restores catholic truth to the faithful.

Bishop from December 1047 and a pupil of Berengar. He wrote a letter to Berengar arguing that bread becomes Christ's true body at consecration by divine omnipotence alone. Contemporary writers classed him among Berengar's followers.

authors.aff: School of Augustodunum (Autun); formerly magister memoriae (private secretary) to Constantius Chlorus
authors.sig: Rhetorician of Augustodunum (Autun) and a pagan who served as private secretary at court. He wrote two speeches to Constantine: the Panegyric and the Act of Thanksgiving. They praise his rule as resting on heredity and merit and pair his victories with clemency.

authors.aff: Bishop of Rome (1145–1153); formerly abbot of Tre Fontane
authors.sig: A Cistercian monk and abbot of Tre Fontane who was elected pope in 1145. He was the first Cistercian to rule the church and a disciple of Bernard of Clairvaux. His letters and privileges show papal authority protecting monastic houses and enforcing papal privilege with excommunication against bishops, counts and chapters.

authors.aff: Presbyter of Cremona; for a time abbot of a monastery at Bethlehem
authors.sig: Presbyter of Cremona and a disciple of Jerome, who served for a time as abbot of a monastery at Bethlehem. He wrote On the Death of St. Jerome and Life of St. Jerome, which present Jerome as a teacher chosen by God whose Latin translations founded scriptural authority in the West.

Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine from about 313. He wrote the Life of Constantine to show God granting victory to a pious ruler and destroying persecutors such as Licinius and Maxentius. His Gospel Canons, tables for reading the four Gospels together, shaped biblical study for centuries.
Abbot of Corbie and cousin of Charlemagne. He also served as prime minister to Pepin, King of Italy. His Statutes for his monks set out rules on provisioners, bell-ringers, and alms.

Bishop of Vercelli and the first Western bishop to unite monastic and clerical life, according to Ambrose. He refused to condemn Athanasius as Pope Liberius's emissary at the Council of Milan in 355. For this Constantius exiled him to the East.

His sole held work is a short chronicle continuing Maximus of Saragossa's continuation of Dexter's chronicle down to his own time, touching on the Church and Scripture and citing Isidore, Ildefonsus, Elipandus, Charlemagne, and Trithemius.
Bishop of Rome from 275 until his death in 283. An Exhortation to Priests transmitted under his name is not accepted as his. Its penitential canons and tithing rules belong to a later period.

authors.aff: Bishop of the Eustathian party at Antioch
authors.sig: Bishop of the Eustathian party at Antioch and translator of the Life of Blessed Anthony the Abbot into Latin. That version replaced an earlier one and circulated widely in the Middle Ages. He also wrote On the Ten Names of God.

A leading Nicene opponent of Arianism whose Hexaemeron commentary, preserved here in Latin paraphrase, treats creation, providence, Scripture, and anthropology while arguing against astrologers, Chaldeans, Greek philosophers, and allegorizing interpreters.

Bishop of Rome from 309 to 310, he required penance before readmitting Christians who had lapsed under persecution. He died in exile in Sicily in 310. An appendix printed in PL 7 is attributed to him but cannot be shown to be his.

His epistle defends Christian liberty in matters of food against heretics and schismatics, arguing that all foods are clean to the pure, that defilement comes from the heart not from foods, that the apostolic decree of Acts 15 was a temporary accommodation, and that the blood prohibition is to be read spiritually as forbidding works of iniquity.
His extant De fide contra Manichaeos, preserved with Augustine's works, is the principal surviving treatise by this correspondent and dialogue partner of Augustine.

authors.aff: Bishop of Havelberg, later archbishop of Ravenna
authors.sig: Premonstratensian canon and bishop of Havelberg, later archbishop of Ravenna. Sent to Constantinople as an ambassador, he held theological discussions with Nicetas of Nicomedia and later wrote them up as three Dialogues.

Taught theology and exegesis at the cathedral school of Laon, which became the most famous in Europe for those subjects. Peter Abelard studied there around 1113 and 1114. Expositions on Matthew, enarrations on the Apocalypse and the Song of Songs survive under his name.

Ninth abbot of Iona from 679 until his death in 704. He wrote the Life of Saint Columba. Built on eyewitness testimony that he names, it is the chief source for early Iona. On the Holy Places draws on the Frankish bishop Arculf for its account of Jerusalem and other pilgrimage sites.

authors.aff: Canon and dean of St. Lambert's Cathedral, Liège
authors.sig: Canon and dean of St. Lambert's Cathedral in Liège. He wrote the Gesta Episcoporum Tungrensium, Trajectensium et Leodiensium for his godmother Ida. She was abbess of St. Cecilia in Cologne. The Gesta continues Heriger of Lobbes's chronicle to Bishop Wazo and is the principal source for the diocese's history to 1048.

Bishop of Lucca, he wrote a polemic against the antipope Guibert and canonical collections defending Gregory VII's reform. He argued that the church must be purged of simony and that sinners be cast out.

Archbishop of Milan from 1097 until his death in 1101. He held a reforming synod in 1098 that condemned simony and led the Lombard contingent of the Crusade of 1101. A set of privileges confirming the rights of the monastery of St. Protasius survives under his name.

authors.aff: Castellain of Bouchain, Ostrevant and Valenciennes
authors.sig: His letter to Manasses II of Reims is a firsthand report from the crusade, attributing victory over Corbaran and the Turks to God's favor, intercessory prayer, confession, and the eucharist rather than knightly merit.
His history is a primary witness to Leo IX's Reims council of 1049 and the dedication of the church of Saint-Remigius, including its canons against simony, clerical marriage, and contumacious clergy.

Bishop of Constantina (Cirta) in the Roman province of Africa. Around 437 he wrote a letter to Arcadius, a Spaniard exiled for refusing Arianism. The letter urges the exiles to endure suffering for Christ. It argues that martyrdom brings remission of all sins.

His defense of the Three Chapters is the principal African argument that condemning Ibas and his fellow authors undermined Chalcedon itself. It also asserts the church's independence from imperial power in matters of faith.

Abbot of Clairvaux from 1157 and of Cîteaux from 1161, he backed Pope Alexander III against Frederick Barbarossa. His Letter on the Council of Toulouse and Letter on Observing Regular Discipline are among the few of his writings that survive.

Abbot near Paris from 792 until his death in 806, he was a Lombard who served Charles after the conquest of the Lombard realm in 774. The verses preserved under his name include inscriptions for buildings and a church of John the Baptist, and his Carmina commemorate royal benefaction.

Bishop of Meaux from 627 until his death around 675, honored as a saint in the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches. A noble Burgundian raised at the Frankish court, he served three kings before taking holy orders. His surviving charters, printed in PL 87, concern the Church, true worship, and the sacraments.
His works are the principal surviving voice of the Luciferian schism: anti-Arian theology joined to polemic denying the legitimacy of Damasus and defending Ursinus as lawful bishop of Rome.
Fastidius is historically significant as one of the few attested authors and witnesses to the theological and ascetic culture of fifth-century sub-Roman British Christianity.

An anonymous pilgrim from Piacenza wrote an Itinerary in the 570s, long misattributed to a martyr of the same city. The work records relics and holy places, including the onyx chalice at the Holy Sepulchre and the Holy Lance on Mount Zion.

His anti-Catholic capitula survive solely through Augustine's book-by-book citation and refutation, making him the best-attested voice of Latin Manichaeism and a principal foil of Augustine's polemic.

authors.aff: Bishop of Riez; abbot of Lérins
authors.sig: He is one of the chief surviving exponents and defenders of the semi-Pelagian position on grace and free will in fifth-century Gaul, and the treatise here is a classic statement of it.

authors.aff: Notary and scribe of the papal palace at Benevento
authors.sig: Notary and scribe in the papal palace at Benevento. He wrote a chronicle of southern Italy from 1102 to 1139, much of it from eyewitness observation. He was proud of Benevento and hostile to the Normans. He backed Pope Innocent II against Roger II of Sicily and the antipope Anacletus II. That loyalty cost him exile in 1134.

Bishop of Rome from 269 until his death in 274. A dogmatic letter on the Trinity and the unity of Christ's person circulated under his name, but the Catholic Encyclopedia identifies it as spurious and later interpolated in the interest of a sect.

authors.aff: Bishop of Riez; abbot of Lérins
authors.sig: He is one of the chief surviving exponents and defenders of the semi-Pelagian position on grace and free will in fifth-century Gaul, and the treatise here is a classic statement of it.

authors.aff: Archdeacon of Rome; installed as bishop of Rome (antipope) 355–358
authors.sig: Archdeacon of Rome who was set up as bishop of Rome by Arian bishops in 355. The Roman laity rejected him, and he withdrew to Porto after Liberius returned.

Bishop of Rome from 526 to 530, chosen under Theodoric the Great and governing under Amalasuntha's regency. His letters and decrees set rules for clerical discipline, including the testing of ordinands and the use of episcopal revenues. Some works printed under his name are disputed with Felix II and Felix III.

Archbishop of Ravenna from 709, who asserted independence from Rome after his consecration. Justinian II had him blinded and exiled to Pontus, and he returned after Justinian's deposition in 711. He collected the sermons of his predecessor Peter and wrote a prologue to them.

Bishop of Urgell and, with Elipandus of Toledo, the chief proponent of Spanish Adoptionism. Summoned to the Council of Regensburg in 792, he was induced to recant. A Confession of Faith survives under his name.

authors.aff: Archbishop of Toledo (from 693); earlier Archbishop/Bishop of Seville (688–693)
authors.sig: Archbishop of Toledo from 693 until his death probably in 702, and bishop of Seville before that. The Chronica Muzarabica records him celebrating councils under King Egica and Witiza. His Life of St. Julian argues that saintly friends possess one soul in charity. A Confession of Faith also survives under his name.

authors.aff: Deacon of the Church of Carthage
authors.sig: His letters defend Chalcedonian Christology against Arians, Eutychians, Nestorians, and Acephali, and his Breviatio canonum condenses the canons of Nicaea, Laodicea, Carthage, and other councils into 232 prescriptions — a key source for early canon law in North Africa.

Bishop of Rome from 483 to 492 who repudiated Zeno's Henotikon and excommunicated Constantinople's patriarch in 484. His letters and decrees defend episcopal succession as the mark of the true church and press the emperor to uphold Chalcedon.

authors.aff: King of the Visigoths in Hispania
authors.sig: His decree is an early royal intervention fixing Toledo's metropolitan primacy, a step toward the see's later dominance in the Visigothic church.

The single held epistle is an imperial letter on the Monothelite dispute, arguing that the five synods and approved fathers completed the faith, that faith must be persuaded rather than compelled, and that providence overrules human deliberation.

Desert ascetic of Egypt who gave up his inheritance and withdrew into the desert about 270. His Rules and Precepts on prayer, fasting, humility, and avoiding temptation survive under his name. Athanasius' Life of Anthony made him a model for monks across the Christian world.

Bishop in Merovingian Gaul and praised for his sanctity by Gregory. He founded a monastery and wrote a monastic rule for its monks that leans on the Rule of Benedict and makes obedience the foundation of monastic virtue. A later compilation under his name, PL 103, is not by him.

authors.aff: Priest and canon of the cathedral church of Reims
authors.sig: A priest and canon of the cathedral church who wrote the History of the Church of Reims and the Annals. He defended the canonical election of bishops against Hugh, who was installed as archbishop at four years old in 925.

authors.aff: Praetorian prefect of Italy (395); proconsul of Asia under Theodosius I; son of Pacian, bishop of Barcelona
authors.sig: Spanish official who served as proconsul of Asia under Theodosius I and as praetorian prefect of Italy in 395. Jerome reports an Omnimoda Historia by him that Jerome had not seen. The Chronicle and the Daniel treatise printed under his name are forgeries by Jerónimo Román de la Higuera, first published in 1619.

authors.aff: Monk and disciple of Simeon Stylites
authors.sig: His Life of Saint Simeon is an eyewitness account of the pillar ascetic, presenting Simeon's endurance as imitating Job's suffering, his miracles as converting the nations to faith, and his cross-signing as routing demons.

authors.aff: Monk of Saint-Bertin; later set over Thorney Abbey
authors.sig: A Fleming and monk of Saint-Bertin who came to England under Edward the Confessor, later set over Thorney Abbey without receiving abbatial benediction. He wrote the Life of St. John of Beverley for Archbishop Aldred of York, and his lives and miracles of St. Bertin commend worthy predecessors and defend the saint's cult against critics.

His Epistle XIV to Emperor Henry is a polemical letter defending Saint Peter's abbey against its advocates — including the castellan, the countess of Mons, and Henry of Marbais — arguing that royal grants secure the monks' ancient liberty, that the advocate's fee is fixed at the third denarius by joint appraisal, and that mercy and judgment please God more than sacrifice while justice departs the

Bishop of Poitiers and a Latin poet whose hymns and occasional verse combine classical models with a medieval tone. He is best known for hymns still in use. A short piece of his occasional verse is titled Verses to Bertichramnus.

authors.aff: Monk of Saint-Bertin; abbot of Lobbes
authors.sig: A deacon and archivist at Saint-Bertin from 948, he was made abbot of a second monastery in 965 by Bishop Everaclus of Liège. He wrote histories of the abbots of both houses and relied on documentary evidence over oral tradition. His Life of Saint Folcuin of Thérouanne is also among his works.

authors.aff: Bishop of Rome (891–896); formerly cardinal bishop of Porto
authors.sig: Bishop of Rome from 891 to 896 and formerly cardinal bishop of Porto. Letters and privileges under his name protect monasteries with free election of abbots, immunity from episcopal exaction and the rule that orders from a condemned bishop confer no grace.

A Latin poet who left Italy and settled in Gaul, where he became bishop of Poitiers. He wrote the lives of Saint Martin and Saint Radegund the Queen, which present the sign of the cross as expelling demons and saints as working healing miracles and interceding after death.

authors.aff: Second abbot of Afflighem Abbey (between Brussels and Ghent)
authors.sig: His twelve-book treatise on grace is the main surviving statement of early twelfth-century Afflighem's theology, treating grace as God himself given to man and obedience as supplying what natural ability lacks.

authors.aff: Saint Lambert's Cathedral, Liège (chancellor, later scholaster)
authors.sig: Chancellor and later scholaster of Saint Lambert's in Liège, he wrote De quadratura circuli around 1050. In it he attempts to square the circle and openly reports the problem as unsolved. Sigebert of Gembloux credits him with saints' lives and a poem on the cross.

authors.n: Fredegisus of Saint Martin of Tours
authors.sig: Abbot of Saint-Martin of Tours and an Anglo-Saxon monk who studied under Alcuin. His letter De nihilo et tenebris answers Charlemagne's question whether nothing is something. It argues that every finite name signifies something and that God created all things from nothing.

Bishop of Lisieux from about 824, he was sent to Rome by Louis that year to negotiate with Pope Eugene II over the veneration of images. His Historiarum libri XII is one of the few ninth-century attempts at universal history from Creation onward and a source for Frankish history.

Frankish cleric who served as chancellor of the Prince of Galilee in 1119 and later as archdeacon, probably of Antioch. His Descriptio de locis sanctis survives in over a hundred manuscripts and explains the holy places through biblical history and exegesis.

Archbishop of Cologne from 1100 until his death in 1131, appointed by Emperor Henry IV. His letters and diplomas defend monastic rights and church unity, arguing that communion with excommunicates cuts one off from the church and that an old synodal grant secures monastic tithes.

authors.aff: cleric (deacon) in the household of Oda, Archbishop of Canterbury
authors.sig: A deacon probably of Frankish origin served in Archbishop Oda's household at Canterbury. Oda commissioned him to render Eddius Stephanus's prose Life of St. Wilfrid into heroic verse. The result is the Breviloquium Vitae Wilfridi, so dense with Greek vocabulary that William of Malmesbury said it needed a sibyl to interpret.
The single item under this name is a chancery diploma of Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa printed in PL 188, not a patristic or theological text.

His single surviving letter to Berengar defends prayer for the dead: the prayers of the faithful avail for others' souls and the intercession of saints aids souls after death — a position taken against Berengar's circle amid eleventh-century disputes over Eucharistic and doctrinal rigorism.

authors.aff: Bishop of Chartres (1006–1028); canon, master and chancellor of the cathedral school of Chartres
authors.sig: Bishop of Chartres from 1006 until his death in 1028 or 1029. He ran the cathedral school there, where his pupils included Berengar of Tours. His letters argue for episcopal election over imposed abbots and for permissible diversity of rites where faith is one. He also wrote sermons, hymns, and a treatise against the Jews.

authors.aff: Bishop of Dumio, then Archbishop of Braga
authors.sig: Archbishop of Braga from 656, he founded the monastery of Complutum and nine more. Two monastic rules survive under his name, one in twenty-five chapters with an appendix of consecration formulas and vows. They legislate constant prayer, restricted speech, and nightly inspection of conduct.

A Benedictine monk of Tegernsee who worked as a scribe, scholasticus and poet. His poems and letters treat sin, grace and prayer for the dead. He also defends himself against those who urged him to accept the priesthood.

authors.aff: Bishop of Toul from 813; formerly abbot of St-Evre, Toul
authors.sig: His letters show a ninth-century bishop's dealings with the imperial court and monasteries: restoring alienated church lands, defending monks against abbots who broke the rule (monks may appeal to imperial authority against an abbot violating the rule), and resisting royal envoys over ecclesiastical rights.

Benedictine abbot elected in 1142 to lead Engelberg Abbey in Switzerland. He built up the abbey's possessions and founded a school teaching philosophy and theology. He wrote On Free Choice to Adelbert, which argues that free will is the glory of rational nature and bears God's image as a mirror.

authors.aff: Count of Anjou (1109–1129); King of Jerusalem (1131–1143)
authors.sig: These charters show how a twelfth-century prince expressed piety through endowment—founding a monastery under Benedictine rule, claiming church lands immune from secular exaction, and treating alms as goods converted from temporal to eternal.

authors.aff: Subdeacon (also styled archdeacon); associated with Meaux and Beauvais
authors.sig: His surviving pieces here are short historical and epistolary fragments from PL 150 — an enumeration of the diocese of Meaux, a letter to Hugh, and an epitaph — valued chiefly as evidence of eleventh-century clerical verse and reform-era correspondence.

Archbishop of Reims from 883 until his death in 900. He backed Guy II of Spoleto for the throne in 888 and later crowned the young Charles at Reims in 893. His letters defend the primacy of Reims over Gallican churches and argue that bishops may excommunicate an erring emperor.

authors.aff: Chaplain to Baldwin of Boulogne / Baldwin I of Jerusalem
authors.sig: Priest and chaplain to Baldwin of Boulogne, who later became Baldwin I of Jerusalem. He wrote the Historia Hierosolymitana, a principal Latin source for the First Crusade and the reign of Baldwin I.

Bishop of Ruspe in Byzacena, exiled twice by the Vandal kings for defending Nicene faith. He wrote Books to Trasimund against the Arians and Books to Monimus, which argue that grace comes before the will to believe. Against the Sermon of Fastidius the Arian is also attributed to him.

authors.aff: Functionary in the administration of the count of Flanders
authors.sig: His chronicle is a near-contemporary witness to the murder of Charles the Good and the Flemish succession crisis of 1127–1128, read here for its theology of rulership, betrayal, and divine judgment.

authors.aff: Canon and magister scholarum, Bremen cathedral
authors.sig: Canon and magister scholarum of Bremen cathedral, he wrote History of the Archbishops of Hamburg. The work is the chief source for the history and ethnography of the North before the thirteenth century.

Bishop of Clermont from 527 to 551, a noble Gallo-Roman who was taken prisoner by King Theuderic I and later enjoyed royal favor. His nephew Gregory wrote his Life, which presents him as a model sixth-century Gallic bishop. One epistle survives under his name.

His two short pieces here are administrative acts of Gregorian-era church government: they assert that pastors must correct immoral subjects or be condemned, that broken chastity vows justify expelling monks, that papal authority authorizes reform of corrupt monasteries, and that episcopal jurisdiction survives a monastery's transfer to another abbot.
His epistle is a witness to Gregorian-era conflict over simony and monastic jurisdiction, and his life of Anastasius to eleventh-century hagiography.

authors.aff: Chancellor of the Principality of Antioch
authors.sig: Chancellor of Antioch under Roger of Salerno. He wrote the Bella Antiochena, an eyewitness history of the principality's wars against Bursuq in 1115 and Ilghazi's victory over Roger in 1119. He meant it to show divine will at work in victory and disaster.

authors.aff: Abbot of Auberive, then Abbot of Clairvaux, later Bishop of Langres
authors.sig: Cistercian abbot of Auberive and Clairvaux who was elected Bishop of Langres by 1193. He preached the Third Crusade and resigned his see in 1199 at the demand of Pope Innocent III. His surviving sermons preach Christology and grace to hearers at their own level. They read Proverbs 8:22 as foretelling Christ rather than describing a creature.

authors.aff: Abbey of Saint-Victor, Paris (Canons Regular of Saint Augustine)
authors.sig: He preserved and systematized early medieval patristic exegesis for twelfth-century Victorine theology through his influential compendium of Gregory the Great's writings.

His sermons here defend Nicene faith against Arians, Marcionites, and Manichaeans (and argue against the Jews), and argue for a springtime dating of Easter bounded between the fourteenth and twenty-first moon, citing Paul heavily.
Bernard's secretary and constant companion, who became fourth abbot of Clairvaux (1162–1165). He wrote against the chapters of Gilbert de la Porrée and compiled a dialogue from Bernard's sermons.

authors.aff: Abbot of Fleury; Archbishop of Bourges
authors.sig: Abbot of Fleury and later archbishop, he attended the councils of 1022 and 1024. His letters argue that death comes at an appointed, unchangeable hour and that prayers for the dead help their souls. A sermon on Saint Martial touches the debate over his apostleship.

Archbishop of Lyon from 1077 until his death in 1082, after his election at the Council of Autun. His letter to Rudolph argues that humility casts down the proud and exalts the lowly. It also urges obedience to mother church, which binds the faithful together in charity.
His Vita Bernardi is the main narrative source for Bernard of Tiron and the early twelfth-century eremitical and monastic reform movement in western France.

Archbishop of Salzburg from 1060 who backed Gregory VII against Henry IV during the Investiture Controversy and was driven from his see in 1079. A letter to Bishop Hermann of Metz defends Gregory's cause against the German bishops who rejected him and the antipope Guibert of Ravenna.

Bishop of Rome from 492 to 496, he refused to accept the Henotikon and pressed papal authority against the emperor and the patriarch of Constantinople during the Acacian Schism. His letters and decrees survive, along with the Sacraments of the Roman Church printed under his name.

His continuation of Jerome's De viris illustribus is the sole surviving source of biographical and bibliographical information on many late-fourth- and fifth-century Greek and Latin Christian authors.

authors.aff: Pope (1118–1119); formerly cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church
authors.sig: The letters here are curial documents from the height of the investiture struggle: rulings on the pallium, burial rights, due process against accused bishops, and the duty to shun the emperor's intruded antipope as excommunicate.

authors.aff: First abbot of La Sauve-Majeure (Grande-Sauve), near Bordeaux
authors.sig: Cellarer of Corbie Abbey and first abbot of La Sauve-Majeure, founded in 1079 near Bordeaux. He fostered the cult of St. Adalhard and directed a Life of him. Life of St. Adalhard and Miracles of St. Adalhard survive under his name.

Bishop of Cambrai from 1012 to 1051 and chaplain to Emperor Henry II. He studied under Gerbert of Aurillac. His letters rule that the impenitent excommunicate may not be absolved or buried and argue against selling absolution for money.

authors.aff: Bishop of Cambrai and Arras, prince-bishop of the Holy Roman Empire
authors.sig: Bishop of Cambrai and Arras, elected canonically in 1076 and invested by Emperor Henry IV that July. He held the see as the Investiture Controversy opened between emperor and pope, and an account of his episcopacy survives in the Gesta Gerardi secundi episcopi. His Charter on the Foundation of Anchin also survives.

His writings are principal witnesses to the cult and memory of Stephen of Muret, arguing that disciples must imitate their founder's life and that the community lives by the founder's merits and rule.
He is an important representative of late twelfth-century Cistercian mysticism and spiritual direction.

authors.aff: Priest in Hispania under Constantine I
authors.sig: Juvencus produced the first substantial Latin biblical epic, making him an early witness to how the Gospels entered Latin Christian literary culture.

authors.aff: Pope Sylvester II (999–1003); formerly schoolmaster of Reims
authors.sig: The most learned mathematician of tenth-century Latin Europe before becoming pope, Gerbert's letters here document the contested election to Reims that shaped the reforming church, while his treatises show geometry extended from practice into speculation.

authors.aff: Pope Sylvester II; formerly abbot of Bobbio and archbishop of Reims
authors.sig: He taught at the cathedral school of Reims and became archbishop there before he reigned as Pope Sylvester II from 999 until his death in Rome in 1003. A letter addressed to Charles brother of King Lothair survives under his name from his political correspondence of the 980s.

authors.aff: Subdeacon of the Roman Church under Pope Vigilius
authors.sig: His De Actibus Apostolorum is a verse retelling of Acts that deliberately supplies the mystical and moral meaning of the narrative — allegorical readings of numbers and names, and a marked preference for Peter over Paul — making it a document of early medieval allegorical exegesis rather than mere versification.

A Gregorian reformer and provost of Reichersberg Abbey who wrote on clerical reform and the investiture conflicts under Henry IV and Henry V. His Commentary on the Psalms reads the psalms as spoken in the person of Christ, and his letters take up simony and church discipline.

Bishop of Paris from 555 until his death in 576. He tried to restrain the Merovingian kings and mediated their family wars without success. A brief exposition of the Gallican liturgy survives under his name and describes the two lessons before the gospel.

authors.aff: Archbishop of Reims (formerly Bishop of Le Mans)
authors.sig: He crowned Philip I in 1059 as archbishop of Reims. His surviving diplomas and letters grant tithes and altar rights to canons and assert clerical exemption from archdeacons.

authors.aff: Bishop of Tortona; abbot of Bobbio; royal chancellor to Hugh and Lothar of Italy
authors.sig: His De corpore et sanguine Christi is a tenth-century eucharistic treatise that transmits Paschasius Radbertus's doctrine on the Lord's Supper, arguing that the mass profits the souls of the dead and that the eucharist confers eternal life on believers.

authors.aff: Benedictine (Cluniac), Bishop of Hereford, Bishop of London
authors.sig: Gilbert Foliot is primarily remembered as a leading 12th-century English canonist and bishop who served as the primary ecclesiastical adversary to Thomas Becket during the Investiture and church-state disputes of Henry II's reign.

authors.aff: Bishop of Limerick (Lunicensis); formerly abbot of Bangor
authors.sig: His De Statu Ecclesiae maps the church's hierarchical orders onto the sevenfold Spirit and treats baptism and eucharist as the means by which the faithful pass to heaven, while his letter to the Irish bishops argues against divergent Irish liturgical customs.

His letters here are administrative evidence for twelfth-century monastic claims on church property: that religious men rejoice in others' holiness, that converting secular churches to monasteries is lawful, and that alienated church revenues require compensation.
His Disputatio Iudaei et Christiani is an early recorded Christian–Jewish dialogue, and his Vita Herluini is a principal source for the origins of Bec.

authors.aff: Monk of Elnone (Saint-Amand), diocese of Tournai
authors.sig: His History of the Miracles of Saint Amand records that relic procession through France and defends the healings worked at the saint's relics against skeptics who dismissed the cult as vulgar rumor.

Abbot of Aniane from 814 until his death in 843. He wrote a life of his master Benedict of Aniane in 822 at the request of the monks of Cornelimünster. It is the principal contemporary witness to the monk whose reform shaped Carolingian monasticism.
Gilbert of Hoyland is significant in medieval monastic theology for his continuation of Bernard of Clairvaux's mystical and allegorical commentary on the Song of Songs.

A sixth-century British monk and abbot who wrote On the Ruin of Britain, a religious polemic against corrupt priests and noblemen. He names Maglocunus and Maximus among them and recounts Britain's history before and during the Saxon coming.
Bishop of Gap in the late sixth century and venerated as a saint with a feast on May 1. A life and testament survive under his name. Duchesne judged the earliest life to be contemporary.

authors.aff: Cardinal-bishop of Tusculum; monk of Cluny
authors.sig: He wrote most of the Historia de via Hierosolymitana, the earliest Latin verse epic of the First Crusade, running from the siege of Nicaea to Godfrey's election at Jerusalem, plus a prose life of Abbot Hugh of Cluny and legatine letters.

Bishop of Poitiers from 1142, he taught logic and theology at Chartres and wrote On the Six Principles. He defended his doctrine of the Trinity against Bernard of Clairvaux's objections before Pope Eugene III at the councils of Paris (1147) and Reims (1148). The dispute ended without a definite verdict.

authors.aff: Western Roman emperor; later bishop of Salona
authors.sig: Western Roman emperor proclaimed at Ravenna in March 473 by Gundobad. The Eastern emperor Leo I refused to recognize him and sent a rival against him, and he abdicated in June 474 without a fight. An imperial edict in his name survives.

authors.aff: Monasteries of Burgundy; died at Cluny
authors.sig: A Burgundian Benedictine monk who wrote the Historiarum libri quinque, one of the few narrative sources for France in the tenth and early eleventh centuries. It covers 900 to 1044 and is dedicated to Abbot Odilo of Cluny. He also wrote a Life of Saint William of Volpiano.

authors.aff: Monk of Saint-Bertin at Saint-Omer; household of Herman, Bishop of Ramsbury/Salisbury
authors.sig: A Benedictine monk of Saint-Bertin who spent his life visiting English monasteries and cathedrals to gather material for many saints' lives. His Life of Saint Augustine describes the translation of the saint's relics at Canterbury in 1091 and argues that Rome is mother of the British church.

authors.aff: Abbot of Admont Abbey, Styria, from 1137/38
authors.sig: Benedictine abbot of Admont in Styria from 1137/38 who introduced the Hirsau reform and rebuilt the monastery after a fire in 1152. Many homilies are attributed to him, though scholars doubt that all are his. Some of these may be by his brother Irimbert, who succeeded him as abbot.

authors.aff: Bishop of Amiens (1104–1115); formerly abbot of Nogent-sous-Coucy
authors.sig: Bishop of Amiens from 1104 until his death in 1115. His surviving letters and charters concern the abbey of Saint-Martin-des-Champs. They also deal with excommunication of those who seize church property and with episcopal rights against monastic encroachment.

authors.aff: Duke of Lower Lorraine (1089–1100); first Latin ruler of Jerusalem
authors.sig: Leader of the First Crusade and first Latin ruler of Jerusalem, he declined the title of king and ruled as Advocatus Sancti Sepulchri until his death in 1100. The Assizes of Jerusalem, said to date from his rule, governed fiefs, summons, and military service in the Latin Kingdom.

authors.aff: Bishop of Hildesheim; formerly abbot of Niederaltaich
authors.sig: Bishop of Hildesheim from 1022 and earlier abbot of Niederaltaich, he enforced Benedictine observance in his cathedral chapter and built schools for youth. His letters defend monastic discipline, including the right of monks to elect their own abbot and the duty of religious to answer their bishop personally.

authors.aff: Chancellor of the Cathedral School of Rheims
authors.sig: Chancellor of the cathedral school at Rheims from 1076 or 1077 until his death around 1094. Four Latin poems survive, and they show the influence of Virgil and Ovid. His dream poem revives classical poetic forms before the twelfth-century renaissance.

authors.aff: Abbot of La Trinité, Vendôme; cardinal-priest of St. Prisca
authors.sig: Abbot of La Trinité at Vendôme and cardinal-priest of St. Prisca, he made twelve journeys to Italy under three popes. His letters defend the Gregorian view that lay investiture is simony and that a bishop is made by election and consecration together.

authors.aff: Chancery of King Henry IV of Germany
authors.sig: Monk and notary in the chancery of King Henry IV from 1071 to 1104. He drew up eighty surviving diplomas and at least nine royal letters. He drafted two letters of 1076 against Pope Gregory VII, arguing that God alone can judge a king.

authors.aff: Chaplain to Conrad III and notary to Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa
authors.sig: Chronicler who served Frederick I Barbarossa as notary and chaplain. The record cautions that the notary may be a different man from the historian. His Memoria saeculorum treats the church and civil magistrate and argues that persecution brings divine retribution.

authors.aff: Monk of St Bertin's, Saint-Omer; later in the household of Bishop Herman of Ramsbury in England
authors.sig: Benedictine monk and hagiographer who served Herman, bishop of Ramsbury. He wrote lives of English saints and the History of the Translation of St. Augustine of the English. That work argues that God preserves saints' bodies incorrupt and that bishops may sanction the opening of tombs.

His single held work is an acrostic poem of devotional exegesis asserting that tearful prayer surpasses worldly delights, that love of God outweighs the wealth of kingdoms, that eternal life is the highest beatitude, and that faithful fighters are written in the book of glory, citing Paul and the Lord Jesus.

authors.aff: Benedictine monk of Orbais, Diocese of Soissons
authors.sig: A Benedictine monk who taught double predestination, the view that God predestines some to punishment as well as some to glory. Condemned at Mainz in 848 and Quierzy in 849, he spent his last decades confined at Hautvillers. His Longer Confession and Epistle defend the predestination of the reprobate from Augustine.

Benedictine abbot of Tegernsee from 982 who brought the Gorzer reform to flower there. His letters ask for perpetual prayer, annual masses and vigils for departed souls and written remembrance of benefactors. Empress Adelaide supported his reform.

authors.aff: Domscholaster of Mainz, formerly of the Liège cathedral school
authors.sig: The Letter to Valcher is a rare first-person witness to eleventh-century schooling: it argues that virtue suffices for a blessed life in any place, that seeking self-improvement is not vanity, and that contempt for a spiritual father forfeits eternal inheritance, while answering detractors who cite Horace and Diogenes against him.

Monk of the Abbey of Farfa who proposed to Abbot Berard II a full reorganization of the abbey's archives in 1092. By Berard's death in 1099 he had compiled two volumes of its charters, which he titled the Regestum Farfense.
One of the four original Latin Doctors of the Church. Gregory I shaped medieval Christian spirituality, liturgy and pastoral theology.

authors.aff: Monastery of SS. Felix and Nabor, Bologna
authors.sig: Monk of the monastery of SS. Felix and Nabor in Bologna. Around 1140 he compiled the Concordia discordantium canonum, which arranges nearly four thousand canonical texts to reconcile their contradictions. This Decretum made canon law a discipline distinct from theology and served as the standard textbook of church law for centuries.

Bishop of Rome from 731 to 741, he remonstrated with Emperor Leo III over image-breaking and held two Roman synods in 731 condemning it. He faced the Lombard advance and appealed for aid without success, while his letters show him governing the western church through canonical discipline.

Bishop of Rome from 827 until his death in 844, he spent much of his pontificate caught in the quarrel between Louis the Pious and his sons. He backed Lothar's revolt of 833, which cost him standing among the Frankish clergy. His letters claim papal authority over deposition, restoration of penitent clergy, and monastic exemptions.

Pope from 1227 to 1241, he was a nephew of Innocent III and studied at Paris and Bologna. A short record of miracles wrought through saints and their relics is printed under his name in PL 197. Its style does not match the canonist pope, so that attribution is doubtful.

Bishop of Rome from 715 to 731 who defied Emperor Leo III's iconoclasm and so opened the Iconoclastic Controversy. He encouraged the mission of Boniface and Corbinian in Germany and consecrated them bishops in 722. His letters and canons set rulings on preaching, baptism and communion.

Bishop of Rome from 590 to 604 after serving as papal ambassador to Constantinople. Two short pieces survive under his name: rubrics for gathering canons and a dedicatory letter. They preserve teaching that no bishop may be called universal and that ordination requires consent.
His Ten Books of Histories is the primary narrative source for the Merovingian Franks. His miracle collections document the cult of the saints, especially Martin of Tours, in sixth-century Gaul.

Pope of Rome from 1073 until his death in 1085, he drove the Gregorian Reform against simony and for clerical celibacy. His Register records his conflict with Emperor Henry IV and Henry's excommunication. In it he insists that churches cannot be corrected without papal authority.
His brief, scandal-marked pontificate prompted imperial intervention that opened the way for the Gregorian reform; the privileges here show him granting monastic rights against secular despoilers.

His surviving letters show an Ottonian papacy asserting papal privilege, monastic immunity from secular jurisdiction, and supreme pastoral care over all churches against metropolitans and royal interference.

Pope for less than two months in 1187. He reconciled the papacy with the Holy Roman Empire and launched the Third Crusade after Saladin took Jerusalem. His letters and privileges rule on the Church, worship, sacraments and the civil magistrate.

authors.aff: Abbey of Saint Gall, Carolingian Court
authors.sig: Grimaldus was an influential Carolingian statesman and abbot who established the Abbey of Saint Gall as one of the preeminent centers of learning, manuscript production, and liturgy in early medieval Europe.

authors.aff: Priest and monastic writer (Lotharingian / Carolingian region, possibly associated with Metz)
authors.sig: He authored the 'Regula solitariorum', the earliest comprehensive Western monastic rule designed specifically for enclosed solitary religious (anchorites).

Archpriest of Pontecorvo in Italy and venerated in the Roman Catholic Church. He is believed to have been of English descent. A brief appendix under his name survives, and his feast falls on 29 September.

Prior of Saint-Victor Abbey from about 1173 until his death. He attacked the dialectical method in theology in his Contra quattuor labyrinthos Franciae, a polemic against four masters of early scholasticism that targets Peter Lombard's Christology.

authors.aff: Archdeacon of the diocese of Thérouanne
authors.sig: His Vita Karoli comitis Flandriae is a narrative of Charles the Good's life and murder, reading the assassination as divine justice — divine judgment publicly executing sins hidden in God's foreknowledge — and treating the count's death at traitors' hands as making a martyr.

authors.aff: School of Reims, Canon of Amiens Cathedral
authors.sig: He was a prominent 12th-century Latin poet and theologian whose works span major Latin epic poetry, anti-Jewish polemical theology, and ecclesiastical satire.

His surviving letters show a twelfth-century abbey head operating through papal authority—appeals to Alexander III, legatine intervention (legates Theoderic and Alexander), and canonical argument—in conflicts over jurisdiction, monastic custom, and promises extorted by deceit.

authors.aff: Abbot of Igny Abbey (diocese of Reims), a house dependent on Clairvaux
authors.sig: One of Bernard's first disciples at Clairvaux, he left fifty-four liturgical sermons that expound Scripture through the church's feasts, treating sanctification, grace, Christology, faith, sin, virtues, last things, and hope of salvation, arguing against the Jews, nominal Christians who neglect works, and slothful religious who prefer private devotions to the rule.

authors.aff: Abbot of Gembloux and Florennes; secretary to Hildegard of Bingen (1177–1179)
authors.sig: Abbot of Gembloux and secretary to Hildegard of Bingen from 1177 until her death in 1179. He wrote letters and an account of the burning of Gembloux Abbey. These texts argue that the sins of subjects come from negligent, luxury-loving, and simoniacal prelates.
His sole surviving work is a versified funeral lament from Luxeuil that pairs grief over creation with doctrinal claims about the soul after death.

Benedictine abbot of Nogent-sous-Coucy from 1104. He wrote Moral reflections on Genesis and Tropologies on the Prophets Hosea and Amos and the Lamentations of Jeremiah, which argue that sin enslaves the will. His history of the First Crusade is God's Deeds through the Franks.

Bishop of Amiens from 1058, he inherited a long dispute with the abbey of Corbie. His letters and charters from that quarrel assert episcopal authority over monasteries and the need for clerical confirmation of valid acts.

authors.aff: Cistercian monk; abbot of Pontigny (from 1137); Archbishop of Lyon (from 1165)
authors.sig: Cistercian abbot of Pontigny who became Archbishop of Lyon in 1165. His Ancient statutes of the Church of Lyon argues that reform restores the institutes of the ancient fathers and that negligent canons who scorn church order deserve severe discipline.

authors.aff: Benedictine monk; taught singers at Arezzo Cathedral under Bishop Tedald
authors.sig: Benedictine monk who taught singers at Arezzo Cathedral under Bishop Tedald. His Micrologus and rules for singing unknown chant at sight are the works that set out his practical teaching on music.

Bishop of Le Puy from 985 until his death in 996. He succeeded his brother Drogon. His Peace of God statutes protect churches and forbid clerics to bear arms. They also require restitution of wrongfully seized goods before repentance is accepted.

authors.n: Guigo I, Prior of the Grande Chartreuse
authors.sig: He provided the Carthusian Order with its definitive constitutional and spiritual foundation by writing the *Consuetudines Cartusiae*.

Canon of Châlons-sur-Marne who wrote chronicles, poems and many letters. His letter to Pope Gregory VIII defends the bishop of Laon against his accusers, a source on ecclesiastical politics in twelfth-century France. He also took part in the Third Crusade.

authors.aff: Deacon of the church of Milan
authors.sig: Deacon of the church of Milan and leader of the Pataria, a movement against simoniacal and married clergy in the city. His two sermons to the clergy of Milan are documents of the eleventh-century campaign for clerical reform that came before the wider Gregorian movement.

authors.n: Guigo II, Prior of the Grande Chartreuse
authors.sig: He formulated the classic four-rung structure of Christian contemplative prayer (lectio, meditatio, oratio, contemplatio) in his influential spiritual treatise Scala Claustralium (The Ladder of Monks).

authors.n: Guigo V, Prior of the Grande Chartreuse

authors.aff: court of Roger Borsa, Duke of Apulia (probable)
authors.sig: His Gesta Roberti Wiscardi is one of the principal contemporary sources for the Norman conquest of southern Italy and the only epic-historical poem dealing with that conquest, covering the Normans' arrival in southern Italy through Robert Guiscard's Balkan campaigns against the Byzantines (1081–85).

His two surviving works are early hagiographic and historical sources for the Grandmontine order and its founder Hugh of Lacerta; the Vita presents Hugh as pre-elected by divine grace from infancy and as practicing voluntary poverty and perfect abstinence.

Abbot of Saint-Bénigne at Dijon who spread the Cluniac reform across Burgundy, Normandy, and Lorraine. He founded Fruttuaria in Lombardy (1001–03), and his letters and privilege for it argue that the house was free from episcopal and secular control.

authors.aff: Abbey of Saint Victor, Paris (Canons Regular of Saint Victor)
authors.sig: He is recognized as one of the greatest Latin liturgical poets of the Middle Ages, whose sequences brought the rhymed Victorine poetic form to its theological and structural peak.

authors.aff: Abbot of St. Arnoul, Metz; briefly bishop of Metz
authors.sig: Abbot of St. Arnoul at Metz and briefly bishop of Metz in 1085. He was elected abbot of St-Remi in 1073 but was persecuted by its archbishop. His seven letters and an oration in commemoration of St. Augustine argue that moral fitness must come before the exercise of canonical power.

A Benedictine monk and scholasticus at Liège who wrote De musica between about 1060 and 1075, dedicated to Bishop Ellenhard of Freising. Its first part sets out his own theory of music and its link to the universe, and its second part critically comments on Guido of Arezzo's teaching.

authors.aff: Duke of Aquitaine, Count of Poitou
authors.sig: He matters to readers of this shelf as a lay ruler whose surviving letters document how royal power negotiated with bishops and monasteries around the year 1000.

authors.aff: Abbot of Saint-Thierry near Reims; later monk at Signy
authors.sig: Abbot of Saint-Thierry near Reims and later a Cistercian monk at Signy. He was a close friend of Bernard of Clairvaux. Book I of his history of Bernard presents Bernard's early life and entry into monastic life as a pattern of grace restoring the church through its saints.

authors.aff: Abbot of Saint-Thierry near Reims; later monk at the Cistercian abbey of Signy
authors.sig: A twelfth-century mystical theologian whose works here defend Trinitarian orthodoxy against Abelard, read the Song of Songs morally of Christ and the soul, and treat faith, grace, and the love poured out by the Holy Spirit.

authors.aff: Archbishop of Tyre and chancellor of the Kingdom of Jerusalem
authors.sig: Archbishop of Tyre and chancellor of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, he wrote a chronicle of Outremer that is the main narrative source for the period. He held that hiding or corrupting the truth breaks the duty of a historian.

authors.aff: Bishop of Châlons-sur-Marne (from 1114); formerly master of Notre-Dame and archdeacon of Paris
authors.sig: Bishop of Châlons-sur-Marne from 1114 and earlier master of the school at Notre-Dame. A charter on parochial rights and tithes survives under his name. So does a short treatise holding that Christ is whole under each species of the altar.
Prior, known only from a short notice. Letters are printed under his name, but no birth, death, order or see is recorded.

He was a pivotal 11th-century sacramental theologian whose treatise on the Eucharist significantly shaped medieval orthodoxy regarding the Real Presence and anticipated the scholastic framework of transubstantiation.
His Vita Vencezlavi is an early Latin account of St. Wenceslaus of Bohemia, framing the Slavic conversion as divine grace transmitted through written ecclesiastical tradition.

Archbishop of Cologne from 850 until his deposition in 863, he led the Aachen synods of 860 that let King Lothair II set aside Queen Teutberga. His Diabolical Chapters argue that consent makes a marriage and that resistance to papal condemnation is justified.

Bishop of Rochester from 1077 until his death in 1108, he was a Norman monk who came to England with Lanfranc to help reform English monasticism after the Conquest. He is chiefly remembered as a builder, credited with Rochester Cathedral and the White Tower of the Tower of London.

Bishop of Eichstätt from 1057 until his death in 1075, after serving as chaplain to Empress Agnes. He prepared the Gundecarianum, a book of rites and liturgy for his clergy that includes a catalogue of the bishops of Eichstätt. His historical record of those bishops names him the eighteenth bishop of the see and dates Willibald's death to 781.

authors.aff: Monk and schoolmaster, Abbey of Saint-Vaast, Arras
authors.sig: A monk, schoolmaster and pupil of Alcuin at the abbey of Saint-Vaast. He is known chiefly for the Miracula sancti Vedasti, and letters and a sermon on the feast of St. Vedast survive under his name. His works defend the reality of saintly healing and intercession and argue that miracles signify the spiritual grace they prefigure.

Bishop of Le Mans who succeeded Bertram around 623 and attended the councils of Clichy and Reims. In 643 he made a testament naming the church of Le Mans his heir, and his surviving work concerns testamentary mandates and precarial usufruct.

Cistercian monk at Pairis Abbey in Alsace who wrote the Historia Constantinopolitana on the Fourth Crusade. It is the only western account to say the crusaders pillaged Greek churches. He wrote it to celebrate Abbot Martin and to justify the sack as directed by God.

authors.aff: Abbot of Saint-Denis; archchaplain to Louis the Pious
authors.sig: Abbot of Saint-Denis and archchaplain at a Frankish court, he sided with the sons of his master in the war of 830 and was banished to Paderborn and Corvey. He wrote verses for the tomb of St. Remigius, a minor work.

authors.aff: Archbishop of Lyon (1046–1052); abbot of Saint-Bénigne, Dijon
authors.sig: The letters here document how an eleventh-century abbot defended monastic property rights by appeal to the pope, prayer over canvassing in choosing a successor, and anathema as legal protection.

authors.aff: Abbot of Saint Peter's, Oudenburg; monk of Saint-Riquier
authors.sig: His chronicle preserves information lost when Saint-Riquier's archives burned in 1131, and his Arnulf writings document a twelfth-century canonization process from within.
His penitential superseded earlier handbooks alongside those of Hrabanus Maurus and shaped confessional practice, especially in pre-Norman England.

Abbot of Saint Gall and a Benedictine monk, he died in 885. Two short Latin verse pieces survive under his name: an epitaph for Grimaldus and inscriptions for the temple of Saint Othmar, which treat true worship, the splendor of wisdom, and pardon for the contrite.

authors.aff: Abbot of the Abbey of Saint Gall (elected 922)
authors.sig: Abbot of Saint Gall, elected in 922 and dead by 925. Ekkehart IV reports that he attended to the school and choral singing but neglected the abbey's goods. He is thought to have written a lost account of the history of his times. His poems survive under PL 116, though hymns attributed to an author of the same name are considered unlikely to be his.
His letter is a window into Carolingian episcopal politics: defense of bishops against lay accusation, appeals to Rome, and the alliance of secular princes with ecclesiastical discipline.

authors.aff: Monk of Saint-Riquier; abbot of Saint Peter's, Oudenburg
authors.sig: A Benedictine monk of Saint-Riquier who was elected abbot of Saint Peter's in Oudenburg in 1105. His Life of Angelrannus defends that abbot's election against rival claimants and presents him as teaching his monks by example and word.

Bishop of Halberstadt from late 840 until his death in March 853. A Fulda monk who studied under Alcuin at Tours and taught in the monastery school. Commentaries on Paul, the Psalms, Isaiah and the Apocalypse are printed under his name. Much of that material is probably spurious or by Haymo of Hirschau.
His surviving letter is a rare early-twelfth-century record of a jurisdictional dispute over the segregation of lepers, pitting episcopal petition against monastic opposition.

authors.aff: Abbey of Fleury-sur-Loire; chaplain to King Robert II the Pious
authors.sig: Benedictine monk of Fleury and later chaplain to King Robert II the Pious. He wrote the Epitoma vitae regis Rotberti Pii, which presents Robert as a saintly ruler and defends his salvation against critics. The record also links him to a work asserting monastic rights over donated property under the Rule of Benedict.

authors.aff: Cistercian monastery of Froidmont, diocese of Beauvais
authors.sig: Cistercian monk of Froidmont and noted preacher, who gave sermons at the Council of Toulouse in 1229. He wrote a world chronicle and festival sermons that argue a faithful Christian king surpasses all other kings.

authors.aff: Provost of the collegiate church of Reichersberg on the Inn, diocese of Passau
authors.sig: Provost of Reichersberg on the Inn from 1169 until his death in 1175. He wrote the Shield of the Canons, defending the canons' common life as equal to monasticism in apostolic perfection. A fragment survives of his treatise against Provost Folmar of Triefenstein on whether the man assumed at the Incarnation is strictly the Son of God.

His De computo is a practical textbook of computus, teaching the solar year of 365 days and a quadrant, the bissextile intercalation every fourth year, and the displacement of seasons and solstices when it is neglected, against those who delay the saltus to November or keep Easter with the Jews.

His cartulary and Life of St. Wulstan are the principal witnesses to Worcester's lands and to Bishop Wulfstan, arguing that lands taken by French invaders and powerful men ought to be restored and that written charters secure the church's rights.

authors.aff: Archdeacon of Huntingdon, Diocese of Lincoln
authors.sig: Archdeacon of Huntingdon and historian of the secular clergy. His Historia Anglorum was begun around 1129 and revised through successive editions down to 1154. It reads English history providentially, as God alone raises up and casts down kingdoms and ordains national calamity as punishment for sin.

authors.aff: Bishop of Beauvais (1149–1161); Archbishop of Reims (1161–1175)
authors.sig: The letters and diplomas here are chiefly administrative and polemical: instruments of metropolitan jurisdiction and of loyalty to Pope Alexander III during the 1159 schism, not doctrinal treatises.
His diplomas show how an eleventh-century king exercised judgment over church property and framed royal protection of churches as pious duty.
His diplomas are primary evidence for Ottonian-Salian royal church policy — the theology of kings as donors and protectors of ecclesiastical property — rather than doctrinal treatises.
The constitutions here show an emperor legislating for religion and clergy—canons given force of imperial law—typifying the sacral exaltation of kingship that preceded the Investiture Contest.

authors.aff: King of the Romans and Holy Roman Emperor
authors.sig: His charters show how a king embroiled in the investiture conflict used grants to churches—free abbatial election, immunity, protection—as instruments of rule, making them primary evidence for royal-ecclesiastical relations before and during the Gregorian crisis.

The work is a partisan history from the investiture conflict, arguing that God turns persecutors' malice to the good of the elect and that the church of Salzburg remained free of schism through fidelity to the pope.

authors.aff: Priest, benefice of Calenzano near Florence
authors.sig: His De diversitate fortunae et philosophiae consolatione is a Boethian consolation in verse arguing that fortune is unstable and treacherous by nature (like Proteus), that true nobility lies in probity rather than lineage, and that death can be salvation for the sufferer.
His Tractatus de Purgatorio Sancti Patricii is the earliest known account of the knight Owen's vision and did much to spread belief in Lough Derg as purgatory's entrance across medieval Europe.

authors.aff: Rhetorician at Sicca Veneria, Proconsular Africa
authors.sig: His Adversus nationes, a major Latin apology from before Constantine, answers the pagan charge that Christians caused calamities. It attacks idolatry, anthropomorphism and pagan myth and defends monotheism and Christ's divinity.

authors.aff: Cistercian Order, Cardinal Bishop of Albano
authors.sig: He was a major twelfth-century Cistercian administrator and papal legate who played a central role in church efforts to suppress Catharism and mobilize Europe for the Third Crusade.

authors.aff: Archbishop of Torres (Sardinia), former third abbot of Mores and monk of Clairvaux
authors.sig: His Liber miraculorum et visionum, recording what he saw at Mores, Clairvaux and Torres, circulated widely in the Middle Ages (22 manuscripts survive) and was edited by Chifflet in 1660 and reprinted by Migne in PL 198.

Herbert of Bosham is distinguished as a primary biographer of Thomas Becket and as one of the rare 12th-century Christian theologians to integrate rabbinic Hebrew scholarship into biblical commentary.

Abbot of Lobbes from 990 until his death on 31 October 1007, and a close friend of Bishop Notger of Liège. At Notger's instance he wrote the Deeds of the Bishops of Liège, and he also wrote lives of Landoald and Ursmar. His pupils included Burchard of Worms and Adalbold of Utrecht.
He is primarily significant as the author of the *De miraculis*, one of the most important surviving collections of twelfth-century Cistercian hagiographical narratives and monastic folklore.

Bishop of Eichstätt from 1022 until his death in 1042, he was installed by Emperor Henry II and accompanied the king on several journeys through the Reich. He wrote hymns that survive in many manuscripts, on the cross, sin and cleansing, the Trinity, baptism, the intercession of saints, and eternal life.

A monk of Saint-Germain d'Auxerre who taught in the abbey school until his death. He wrote a metrical Life of St. Germanus dedicated to Charles the Bald and the prose Miracula sancti Germani, which asserts that relics of saints work healing miracles.

authors.aff: Monastic author active in Rome (possibly of African or Gaulish origin)
authors.sig: He represents the fifth-century Roman resistance to strict Augustinian predestinarianism alongside a firm defense of Chalcedonian Christology.

authors.aff: Third abbot of Saint Martin of Tournai
authors.sig: Third abbot of Saint Martin of Tournai, expelled in 1136 by a faction claiming the Benedictine rule was not kept. While at Rome he wrote an account of his abbey's refounding and fortunes. His works include a charter restoring market revenue taken from the monastery by faction and an account of the translation of St. Clement's relics.

His chronicle here is a citation-heavy universal history from creation to his own century, drawing on Fulda and Metz annals, Bede, Paul the Deacon, and others, while his astrolabe and music treatises show the same eleventh-century monastery joining history, polemic against Arians and Ptolemy, and technical science.

authors.n: Hermann of Saint Martin of Tournai
authors.sig: He is significant as an important twelfth-century chronicler whose historical narratives document the revival of monastic life and religious reforms in the diocese of Cambrai-Tournai.

authors.aff: Prior of Saint Emmeram's Abbey, Regensburg
authors.sig: Prior of Saint Emmeram's Abbey in Regensburg, he judged the existing Latin Vita of Saint Emmeram inadequate and proposed a revision. Monks of the abbey opposed him, and he fled to Magdeburg. His works argue that corrupt texts may be emended and that saints' relics deliver from peril.

Archbishop of Reims from 900 until his death in 922, he had served as a notary in the royal chancery under King Odo. A letter to Wito survives under his name and defends tearful repentance and enjoined penance for grave sinners.

Documents from 1116 to 1119 attest him as cathedral canon and scholasticus of Strasbourg. He wrote accounts of the peace negotiated between Callistus II and Henry V. His works argue that renouncing lay investiture costs the king nothing in temporal rights and ends the simoniacal heresy.
He is renowned as the ostensible author of the *Opusculum de conversione sua*, one of the most famous medieval Latin accounts of conversion from Judaism to Christianity.
His single surviving letter here is a concrete case of Ottonian episcopal jurisdiction and church-order polemic between bishops.

authors.aff: Bishop of Basel and Abbot of Reichenau
authors.sig: Bishop of Basel and Abbot of Reichenau, he went on Charlemagne's 811 embassy to Constantinople. He issued capitularies on priestly discipline, liturgy and marriage law for clergy and people. He also wrote On the Vision and Death of Wetti.

authors.aff: Monastery at Bethlehem; formerly secretary to Pope Damasus I
authors.sig: Latin Father who served as secretary to Pope Damasus I in Rome. He later settled at a monastery in Bethlehem, where he translated the Old Testament into Latin from the Hebrew. His commentaries on Isaiah, Ezekiel and Matthew rest on his view that the Hebrew text corrects the Septuagint's errors.

A Benedictine monk at the abbey of Bourg-Dieu who spent his life studying Scripture and the Fathers. He wrote Commentarii in Isaiam prophetam and commentaries on the Epistles of Paul. Commentaries on Matthew and Revelation sometimes assigned to him were written by Anselm of Laon.

authors.aff: Monk of the abbey of Hirsau in Swabia; styled 'Haimo Prior Hirsaugiensis' in the sources
authors.sig: His Life of William is a narrative source for Abbot William of Hirsau and the Hirsau reform; the text as preserved argues that monasteries ought to be freed from lay lordship by imperial and papal privilege and records how monastic customs were adapted from Cluny to local conditions.

Bishop of Lisieux from 1141, a Norman churchman who defended Pope Innocent II against Gerard of Angoulême in a violent letter. His treatise on the schism that followed a papal death argues that lawful election and consent mark the true pope, while the false shepherd persecutes the church under pretense.
He is one of the foremost twelfth-century monastic theologians of northern Britain, noted for his treatises bridging Premonstratensian canonical reform and Carthusian contemplative mysticism.
Bishop of Lisieux from 1141 to 1181. His letters are a primary record of twelfth-century papal politics. The record says his works argue that episcopal fitness is the condition of valid election.

authors.aff: Probably a cleric of Milan (perhaps a subdeacon)
authors.sig: His chronicle is a primary source for the Gregorian Reform, the Patarene movement, and the Investiture Controversy as seen from Milan.

The texts here show the archbishop as a defender of monasteries against plunderers at Reims and officials of Mouzon, asserting that donated property is perpetual, immune from reclamation, and remedies the donor's soul.

Gallo-Roman bishop who claimed metropolitan authority beyond his province, a claim Pope Leo I curbed in 444. His Sermon on the Life of Honoratus is a funeral eulogy arguing that praise of the just belongs only after death.

Bishop of Poitiers from about 350, he learned Greek and carried Eastern trinitarian theology into Latin debate. His On the Trinity was the West's first full treatise on the subject, and he wrote against Arianism even while exiled by Constantius.

authors.aff: Pupil of Peter Abelard at the Paraclete; later possibly at Angers; an Orléans connection is conjectural
authors.sig: A Latin elegiac poet who studied under Peter Abelard and addressed verses to him. Abelard's pupil wrote one verse with a French refrain. His poems survive in a Paris manuscript and were edited in 1838 as Hilarii versus et ludi. After about 1125 no certain trace of him remains.

His Speculum monachorum is a compact twelfth-century manual of monastic self-examination, prescribing weekly confession and inward correction of thoughts, words, and deeds; the other works here extend the same program of prayer, meditation on Christ's passion, and discipline against temptation.
His letters are primary evidence for how the fifth-century Roman see asserted binding authority over episcopal appointments and canonical discipline in Gaul and Spain.

authors.aff: Bishop of Le Mans, then Archbishop of Tours
authors.sig: A major figure of the twelfth-century Renaissance whose sermons, letters, poems, and eucharistic treatises here treat sin, grace, the sacraments, and penance against Arius, simoniacs, and other opponents.

Metropolitan Archbishop of Toledo, who governed the church there for a little more than nine years until his death in 667. He wrote On the Perpetual Virginity of St. Mary, along with On the Knowledge of Baptism and On the Journey of the Desert.

Abbess and visionary who founded the monasteries of Rupertsberg and Eibingen. Her Scivias and Book of Divine Works teach that humility is the queen of the virtues and that God overcame Satan through humility rather than power.

Benedictine monk and teacher at Saint-Germain d'Auxerre until his death in 876. His two surviving poems are a metrical letter and an epitaph that set out doctrine in verse on the Trinity and redemption through Christ's blood. The poems also treat creation from nothing and the saints' prayers for the faithful dead.

authors.aff: Monk of Corbie; abbot of Civitate (Civate), Lombardy
authors.sig: His letter is a Carolingian witness to how punctuation and accent theory governed liturgical reading; his commentary on the Benedictine Rule was widely transmitted in several recensions.

authors.aff: Abbot of Saint-Denis; archchaplain to Louis the Pious
authors.sig: His Passio Dionysii identified the patron saint of Paris with Dionysius the Areopagite, a conflation that shaped Western devotion and scholarship on the Pseudo-Dionysian corpus; the Passion here presents Dionysius as a noble Athenian judge converted by Paul's preaching and martyred under Domitian.

Benedictine monk of Saint-Remi placed in the archbishopric of Reims by King Ralph in 931 or 932. His Epistle is a polemic against Count Heribert and the bishops gathered at Soissons. It argues that clergy and people elect bishops and that ordination without the rightful bishop's consent is invalid.

Archbishop of Reims from 845 until his death in 882, and the most powerful churchman at the court of Charles the Bald. He wrote against Gottschalk's teaching on predestination and against his nephew Hincmar of Laon, and his letters and political writings defend the king's authority.

Nephew of Hincmar of Reims, he became bishop of Laon in 858. From 868 he invoked the Pseudo-Isidorian decretals to assert the rights of suffragan bishops against metropolitan authority. He was deposed at the Synod of Douzy in 871 and blinded.

authors.aff: Monk; spent much of his life in southern Germany, ending at the Scots Monastery, Regensburg
authors.sig: A twelfth-century monk and encyclopedic writer who studied under Anselm in England. He spent much of his life in southern Germany and ended at the Scots Monastery in Regensburg. His works together form an allegorical encyclopedia of doctrine, liturgy and cosmology. They circulated widely through vernacular translation.
His Life of Hilary of Arles is among the few surviving Gallic saints' lives of the period, presenting humility, mortification, and contempt for worldly goods as the substance of sanctity.

The chief fourth-century opponent of Arianism, called the 'Father of Orthodoxy'. His writings argue that the Son is begotten, not made, and consubstantial with the Father, shaping Trinitarian doctrine.

Pope from 1124 to 1130, he had negotiated the Concordat of Worms (1122) as legate to Henry V. His letters and privileges protect monastic houses and grant free burial to all but excommunicates. They also threaten excommunication for anyone who violates papal privilege.

Bishop of Rome from 625 to 638, he sent Birinus to the West Saxons and granted palliums to York and Canterbury. His letters to Patriarch Sergius of Constantinople concern Christ's operations and wills. The Third Council of Constantinople anathematized him posthumously in 681 as a Monothelite.

Bishop of Rome from 514 to 523, he ended the Acacian schism with Constantinople. Reunion was ratified in the cathedral of Constantinople on 28 March 519. His letters and decrees assert the apostolic see's authority over distant provinces.

The first dramatist of the Latin West after antiquity and the first known female writer of the Germanosphere; her six comedies answer Terence with Christian heroines whose virginity and martyrdom triumph over pagan persecutors.

authors.aff: King of Deheubarth and most of Wales
authors.sig: King of Deheubarth who ruled most of Wales and is recorded as King of the Britons. His Leges Ecclesiasticae opens with his account of gathering six laymen and the clergy of each cantref at Ty Gwyn to draw up the laws. The work treats clerical immunity from homicide-price and vengeance and synodal judgment of injuries to priests.

One of the leading music theorists of the Carolingian era: the treatises here classify intervals, tones, and organum (holding that equisonance is not true consonance and that all inequality derives from equality), while the remaining works are saints' lives and liturgical pieces from the same abbey milieu.

As abbot of Cluny from 1049 to 1109 he founded the first Cluniac house of nuns at Marcigny in 1056 and stood with Gregory VII against Emperor Henry IV at Canossa. His letters and statutes present Cluny as an asylum of penitents under Peter and Paul and insist on monastic obedience to the abbot.

Abbot of Vallombrosa and later Bishop of Pistoia. He wrote a life of St. John Gualbert, founder of the abbey, which traces its origins to Itta's 1039 grant. In it he presents Gualbert's virtue as a work of grace against simoniacs.
His single surviving letter documents how relic authentication was conducted through named clerical witnesses and seals in the twelfth-century Latin East.

Bishop of Grenoble from 1080 to 1132 and a partisan of the Gregorian reform. He welcomed Bruno of Cologne to La Grande Chartreuse in 1084 and defended Grenoble's property against Archbishop Guido of Vienne. His cartulary excerpts and letters argue that long possession and royal grants prove the church's title.

authors.aff: Bishop of Lincoln; Carthusian monk of La Grande Chartreuse
authors.sig: Bishop of Lincoln and a Carthusian monk before that, he was canonized in 1220. His surviving diplomas confirm monastic possessions and grants in alms, and his letters of visitation defend those grants against simoniacal encroachment.
Abbot of Flavigny and a partisan of the Gregorian reform. His Chronicle preserves material found nowhere else. Historians rate Lambert, Berthold, and Bernold above him.

A canon regular who wrote the Otium for his sister Helvide, a four-book set of moral and theological reflections. He also wrote a Little Book of Miracles of the Blessed Virgin Mary that records wonders worked through her intercession.

Count of Troyes and Champagne who took Troyes, Vitry and Bar-sur-Aube on his brother Odo's death in 1093. He led crusading ventures in 1104–1107 and 1114–1116 and gave the valley where Clairvaux Abbey was built. A one-page epistle on synodal arbitration between monasteries survives under his name, but its authorship cannot be settled.

His anti-Berengarian treatise is an early eleventh-century defense of a real change in the eucharistic elements: the eucharist is a true body not incorporeal, the bread must cease in nature to be Christ's body (for persistence of the bread's essence would entail no consecratory change), the change is received by faith in divine omnipotence as the incarnation is, and God's word and will exceed all

authors.aff: Court of Manuel I Comnenus, Constantinople
