authors.sig: A Pisan who lived at Constantinople at the court of Manuel I. He took part in disputes between Greeks and Latins on the procession of the Holy Spirit and wrote Adversus Graecos, a defense of the Filioque sent to Pope Alexander III. He later became a cardinal.

authors.aff: First Abbot of Pontigny; Bishop of Auxerre (1137–1151)
authors.sig: First abbot of Pontigny and then bishop of Auxerre from 1137, he is described as the first Cistercian raised to the episcopate. Letters to Suger survive under his name, arguing that hereditary right passes lawfully to a wife and children. A charter also survives from him.

authors.aff: Archbishop of Rouen; first abbot of Reading Abbey
authors.sig: Cluniac monk, first abbot of Reading Abbey, and archbishop of Rouen from 1130. He wrote Dialogues, Against the Heretics of His Time, and a Treatise on Memory.

authors.aff: Abbey of canons regular of Saint-Léon, Toul
authors.sig: The letters here are twelfth-century eucharistic polemic asserting that the consecrated host is no longer bread but Christ's body, venerable by faith rather than argued by reason, with Augustine cited as teaching the real presence.

authors.aff: Bishop of Die (1073); Archbishop of Lyon and papal legate
authors.sig: His letters and privileges here are Gregorian-reform polemics: suspension of simoniacal and irregularly ordained bishops pending papal judgment, canonical examination before election, perseverance for final salvation, and the intercession of departed saints — argued against Ivo of Chartres, the abbot of Cluny, Daimbert of Sens, and the king of the Franks.

Bishop of Vercelli from 924 to 961 and Grand Chancellor to kings Hugh of Provence and Lothar II. He wrote an Exposition of the Epistles of St. Paul and On the Afflictions of the Church, along with letters, sermons, and a capitulary of canon law. His exegetical and canonical writing survives in quantity, unusual for a tenth-century Italian bishop.

Benedictine monk of Vézelay Abbey who wrote its History of the Monastery of Vézelay for Abbot Ponce between about 1140 and 1160. The work defends the abbey's liberties against the counts and the bishop of Autun, and records its claims to exemption from exactions and to the rights of founders and advocates.
His surviving letters are brief documentary evidence of episcopal loyalty to the crown and papal arbitration in the Norman disputes of the mid-twelfth century.
Hugh is notable for his moderate treatise on church-state relations during the Investiture Contest, which sought to balance episcopal consecration with royal investiture.
His single surviving work is an Angevin legal-historical proof text asserting the counts of Anjou's hereditary claim to the seneschalcy and judicial primacy of France.

authors.aff: Abbey of Saint Victor, Paris (Canons Regular of Saint Augustine)
authors.sig: A foundational figure in medieval theology who bridged monastic mysticism and early scholasticism, above all in his systematic theology, De sacramentis christianae fidei.

authors.aff: Canons Regular of Saint Augustine; Prior of Saint-Laurent-au-Bois
authors.sig: He is renowned for his influential allegorical treatises, especially the *Aviarium* and *De claustro animae*, which used animal symbolism and architectural metaphors for monastic and moral formation.

Cardinal-bishop of Silva Candida and papal legate under Leo IX. He was sent to Constantinople in 1054 and excommunicated Patriarch Michael Cerularius there. His epistle argues that vigilant teachers are formed by Scripture read with patristic authority, and that brief open exposition is better than prolix obscure speech.

authors.aff: Benedictine Order, Cardinal-Bishop of Silva Candida, Papal Curia
authors.sig: A key architect of the eleventh-century papal reform movement whose 1054 mission to Constantinople formalized the Great Schism between the Western and Eastern Churches.

authors.aff: Countess of Boulogne; founder of the abbey of Wast (Wastensis)
authors.sig: Countess of Boulogne and mother of Godfrey of Bouillon. She founded the abbey of Wast and wrote no theology herself. Her lives survive with a letter to her from Bishop Osmund of Astorga and a genealogy of her house.

Bishop of Aquae Flaviae (Chaves), he wrote a Chronicle that continues Jerome's from 379 to 468. For the years after 427 it rests on his own eyewitness, making it the principal evidence for fifth-century Hispania. In 431 he joined a delegation to Aëtius seeking imperial help against the Suevi.

Innocent III brought the medieval papacy to the height of its administrative and geopolitical power, leaving a lasting theological and institutional legacy through the decrees of the Fourth Lateran Council.
Innocent I significantly advanced the doctrine of universal papal primacy through his influential decretals and his decisive intervention in the Pelagian controversy.
He preserved the canonical succession of the papacy through the schism of 1130 and presided over the Tenth Ecumenical Council (Lateran II) in 1139.
He is renowned as one of the most philosophically sophisticated 12th-century Cistercian thinkers, particularly for his integration of Neoplatonic anthropology with monastic theology.

authors.aff: Abbess of the convent at Oeren (ad Horreum), near Trier
authors.sig: Abbess of the convent at Oeren near Trier. She gave Willibrord land for his monastery at Echternach and founded the convent she ruled. Her parentage is disputed, and a three-page appendix under her name appears in PL 87.

Bishop of Langres from 857 until his death in 880. He wrote a Capitula of 151 canons, chiefly penitential. The canons treat penance and clerical immunity from secular service and courts. They also set the limits of secular jurisdiction over the church.

A monk of Scetis in Egypt, also called Isaiah of Gaza, who wrote brief ascetic counsels on sin, prayer, humility, and confession. His Precepts or Counsels reached Western readers in Latin through the monastic tradition.

Archbishop of Seville who succeeded his elder brother Leander in the metropolitan see. He wrote the Etymologies, which gathered classical extracts that would otherwise have been lost and stood among the most used reference books in Europe. His treatises On Ecclesiastical Offices and On the Catholic Faith argue against the Jews and Arians.

authors.aff: Schoolmaster at St. Gallen and Münster-Granfelden; monk of St. Gallen
authors.sig: His De miraculis S. Othmari records the miracles at St. Othmar's tomb and argues that prayer there heals the sick, that such miracles manifest the saint's holiness for the faithful's edification, and that relic translation belongs to episcopal authority rather than private initiative.

His Chronicle is one of the few contemporary Christian narratives of the Arab conquest of Spain, recording figures such as Abdalla's conquest of Africa, the defeat of Constans by Moabia at sea, and civil war dividing the Arab army between two princes.
His Decretum and Panormia were foundational collections of canon law for the Latin church. His letters document a bishop's practice during the Investiture Crisis.

authors.aff: Bishop of Girona; formerly abbot of Biclaro
authors.sig: Bishop of Girona, he continued the chronicle of Victor of Tunnuna from 567/568 to 590. It is a primary source for the reign of Leovigild and the conversion of Reccared from Arianism to Catholicism. The work argues that conversion should come through reason and that God grants victory to the Catholic faithful regardless of numbers.
His surviving correspondence in PL 105 is a minor witness to Carolingian episcopal writing on Christian moral formation.

Frankish noble who studied with Alcuin and served as head deacon at Charlemagne's court in Aachen. He was a frequent imperial envoy, deposed, restored, and exiled before he died in 836. A letter on baptism survives under his name.

authors.aff: Prior of Santi Bonifacio ed Alessio, Rome
authors.sig: The Life of St. Adalbert long attributed to him is regarded as the first hagiography of the Prague bishop-missionary, contrasting true worship with pagan idolatry and nominal Christianity, and recording Adalbert's route along the Vistula to Gdańsk.

Archbishop of Constantinople and a Greek Father whose homilies on Genesis, Matthew and John press each passage toward conduct. His teaching that love of money is the root of evils angered the wealthy. He also wrote against Jews, Arians and pagans.

authors.aff: Theological school at Paris; later recorded at Amiens
authors.sig: His Rationale divinorum officiorum is a manual of twelfth-century liturgy and now a principal source for how the divine offices were explained and defended in his time.

Abbot of Tarouca in Portugal and credited with bringing the Cistercian reform to the Iberian Far West. He is also credited with drafting the Rule of the Military Order of Aviz, binding its knights to Benedictine observance. The Rule sets hope in faith over arms and gives spoils to the poor.

The first to bring the rules of Eastern monasticism into the Latin West. His Conferences and Institutes record the teaching of the Egyptian monks on prayer, virtue, sin and grace. His On the Incarnation argues against Nestorius.

authors.aff: Theology master at Paris; later taught theology in England, probably at Oxford
authors.sig: His Eulogium to Alexander III (written c. 1177–1179) is a major twelfth-century Christological treatise defending that Christ is 'someone' — a true man — against nihilian denials of Christ's humanity and against positions associated with Abelard and Peter Lombard.

authors.aff: Abbot and founder of the Vallumbrosan Order at Vallombrosa
authors.sig: Florentine noble who became a Benedictine and withdrew to Vallombrosa around 1030, founding a monastery there in 1038. He opposed simony, and his Prayers and Letter to the brothers assert that baptism remits original sin. Canonized by Celestine III in 1193.

Abbot of Fécamp from 1028, and invited to Dijon as abbot in 1052 while holding both houses until he resigned Fécamp in 1056. He wrote letters on church privilege, discipline and monastic obedience. He also wrote Meditations under Augustine's name, which circulated widely before the Imitation of Christ.

Bishop of Rome from 523 to 526, he was sent by King Theoderic to Constantinople. In 525 he helped standardize the Western calculation of Easter. He was imprisoned at Ravenna and died there. A letter on despoiled bishops and church property survives under his name.

Bishop of Rome from 533 to 535 who took a new name on his election, the first pope to do so. His letters affirm that one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh and that Mary is truly Mother of God, against the Acoemetae. Canons penalizing simony in episcopal elections are also attributed to him.
His surviving correspondence is among the few witnesses to his pontificate and shows sixth-century Roman claims about episcopal succession and the suppression of chorepiscopi.
His letters are early Roman responses to Monothelitism, insisting on one will in Christ's humanity rather than two contrary wills.

Bishop of Rome from 898 to 900, he was elected over Sergius, whom he excommunicated. At the councils of Rome and Ravenna in 898 he undid the Cadaver Synod of Stephen VI and forbade re-ordinations. His letters and conciliar texts assert papal authority over all churches.

His Life of Saint Odo is a work of sworn-eyewitness hagiography presenting Odo's sanctity as granted in answer to prayer and his intercession as effective with Christ; the short On Miracles defends such miracle reports against those who cite solitaries' quiet.

authors.aff: Monk of St. Theodosius Monastery near Jerusalem
authors.sig: His Spiritual Meadow is one of the earliest collections of hagiographical anecdote, recording the sayings, miracles, and ascetic practices of monks he met across the Middle East, and it became a model for medieval ascetic literature.

His complaint against the Farfenses is a concrete record of episcopal-versus-monastic jurisdiction disputes in eleventh-century Latium, asserting that a diocesan bishop holds jurisdiction over churches in his see.
His Vita of John of Gorze is a principal source for the tenth-century Gorze monastic reform and for contacts between Ottonian Germany and Muslim Spain.

A leading figure of the twelfth-century Renaissance whose Policraticus shaped medieval political thought, whose Metalogicon defended the liberal arts against Cornificius, and whose letters and lives of Thomas of Canterbury record the Becket conflict from inside it. He professed to follow the moderate skepticism of Cicero and the New Academy.

Archbishop of Rouen from 1067 to 1079. He pressed clerical celibacy from 1074 and was stoned at a provincial synod for it. His work On Ecclesiastical Duties to Maurilius explains the eight daily offices and the symbolic meaning of clerical tonsure and habit.

authors.aff: Palace School of Charles the Bald
authors.sig: Regarded as the most significant philosopher of the Carolingian era. He brought Greek Christian Neoplatonism to the Latin West through his translations and through his speculative treatise, the Periphyseon.

Author of a single Latin letter from around 990. The letter is addressed to Wladimir, king of the Rus. It argues against the Greeks and their patriarchs and urges the Rus toward the Latin church. He asserts that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone.
The letters here assert Roman primacy in episcopal disputes — that appeal to the apostolic see settles them and contempt of conciliar summons brings deposition — addressed to the Anglo-Saxon church.

authors.aff: Deacon of the church of Venice
authors.sig: His Chronicle of Venice and Grado is the earliest Venetian history and the source later chroniclers drew on for the city's origins: the flight from the Lombard invasions to the islands, the translation of the patriarchal see from Aquileia to Grado, and Grado's metropolitan rank by synod and papal consent.

Pope from 1024 to 1032 and a member of the Counts of Tusculum. He was a layman when elected and crowned Conrad II emperor at Easter 1027. His letters and diplomas confirm bishoprics and property. They record rulings in disputes with the patriarch Poppo of Aquileia.

authors.aff: Bishop of Rome, November/December 983 – 20 August 984; formerly Bishop of Pavia (971–983)
authors.sig: The letter to Alo of Benevento is his only surviving document, setting out episcopal duties: shepherds answer for negligent oversight, justice must be impartial between rich and poor, discipline tempered by paternal love avoids cruelty, and outward honor requires inward observance.

Pope from 931 until his death in 935 or 936. His mother Marozia controlled Rome during his early years. He issued privilege charters placing monasteries under direct papal authority. These include the Cluny privilege, which freed the house from episcopal and secular lordship.

authors.aff: Archbishop of Lyon (1181–1193), formerly Bishop of Poitiers (1162–1181)
authors.sig: Bishop of Poitiers and later Archbishop of Lyon. He banned Waldensian preaching in Lyon. His surviving letters defend the see of Lyon's full temporal jurisdiction against Richard, duke of Aquitaine. They also argue that executioners are barred from holy orders.

The privileges printed here show an early tenth-century pope asserting canonical election by clergy and people, free abbatial election belonging to the monks themselves, and papal protection of ecclesiastical property under anathema.

Bishop of Rome from 872 until his death in 882, he faced the Saracen threat in southern Italy. His letters and decrees assert papal primacy and claim jurisdiction over Bulgaria. They also impose anathema for violating papal privilege.
The works held are papal privileges and letters showing tenth-century Rome's exercise of jurisdiction over monasteries and its dealings with Greek churches, not doctrinal treatises.

authors.aff: Priest of the church of Würzburg
authors.sig: His Description of the Holy Land is a firsthand account of the Jerusalem holy places before their later renovation, linking each site to Old and New Testament events and noting the condition of churches, monasteries, and hospitals under Frankish rule.

Bishop of Narni, raised to the papacy by Emperor Otto I in 965. His letters and decrees assert that Peter's authority founded metropolitan sees and that a bishop guilty of heresy and rebellion could be canonically deposed.

The single work held is a set of papal letters and diplomas asserting apostolic authority over monastic property: anathema on violators, exemption from secular dominion, and perpetual confirmation of imperial endowments — documents of early eleventh-century papal privilege-granting rather than doctrinal treatise.

Bishop of Rome from 985 to 996, he was elected after the usurper Boniface VII died and spent much of his pontificate under the control of the patrician Crescentius II. He issued letters and privileges for monasteries, granting free election of abbots, exemption from bishops, and royal protection.

authors.aff: University of Paris; early master of the University of Toulouse
authors.sig: Master at the University of Toulouse and a teacher in Paris, he wrote word-books for the study of Latin. His Book of Synonyms and his books on equivocal terms and orthography were used to teach the language. A fragment on the mysteries of the Church reads the Church as a house built on Christ the rock.

authors.aff: Deacon of the Roman Church, formerly monk of Monte Cassino
authors.sig: His Vita Gregorii Magni is considered the best biography of Gregory the Great written in its period; its extensive quotations from Gregory's register remain important for the study of papal registers, and its four-book structure mirrors Gregory's own order of material.

authors.aff: University of Bologna; later archdeacon of Santarém
authors.sig: A canon lawyer who taught at Bologna for over twenty years and later became archdeacon of Santarém. His Penitential warns simple priests about hearing confession and sets rules for penance, including for the sick and for different classes of sinners.

Deacon of the Roman Church under Pope John VIII, he wrote a four-book Vita Gregorii Magni that preserves extensive extracts from Gregory's register. His On the Lateran Church claims the Lateran's primacy over all churches and recounts Constantine's conversion through Sylvester's baptism.

authors.aff: Bobbio Abbey; later abbot of an unidentified monastery
authors.sig: A Columbanian monk who entered Bobbio in 618 and probably served its abbots as secretary. He later settled in Gaul and wrote the Life of Columbanus between 640 and 643. His other saints' lives include the Life of Eustasius, the Life of Attala and the Life of Burgundofara.

authors.aff: Fonte Avellana; later Bishop of Gubbio (1104–1106)
authors.sig: Disciple and secretary of Peter Damian at Fonte Avellana, later Bishop of Gubbio. His Life of Peter Damian is the earliest biography of him and a main source for his childhood, monastic career, and conflicts with Milanese objectors, secularized canons, and the archbishop of Ravenna.

Bishop of Orléans from 818 until 843 or 844, he served at court and advised his son Pippin. He wrote De Institutione Laicali and De Institutione Regia, mirrors of Christian conduct for laymen and princes built from Scripture and the Fathers.

authors.aff: Bishop of Limoges, from 1023 until his death
authors.sig: Bishop of Limoges, elected in a disputed contest in late January 1024 with the backing of Duke William V of Aquitaine. Works printed under his name are not securely his, since a fictional account of the 1031 Peace-council debates was published as his conciliar minutes.

Irish monk and diplomat who studied under Alcuin at York and followed him to the court of Charlemagne. Charlemagne sent him as an envoy to Rome, Spoleto, and Benevento in 787/8. He later became an abbot, and two brief verse pieces survive under his name.

authors.aff: priest in the Frankish church under King Charles
authors.sig: His sole surviving work is a Carolingian relic-translation narrative defending the move by appeal to divine visions, scriptural curse on scoffers, incorrupt vestments, and miracles worked at the saints' bodies.

A bishop from 1126 until his death in 1152, he opposed Peter Abelard and sat as a judge at a council in 1140. He wrote an Exposition of the Creed and the Lord's Prayer, which treats the creed as twelve articles of faith and grounds bold prayer in faith.

authors.aff: Monk of Cluny, later associated with Saint-Claude
authors.sig: His Vita Odilonis is the principal early witness to Odilo of Cluny and to eleventh-century Cluniac ideals of monastic sanctity, prayer for the dead, and commemoration.

He is described by multiple sources as the most learned/intellectual leader of the Pelagian party, and Augustine answered him in three different works; the volumes here are his own side of that controversy.

authors.aff: Archbishop of Toledo, primate of the Iberian church (Jan. 680 – March 690)
authors.sig: Primate of the Iberian church and archbishop of Toledo from 680 to 690. He presided over four Councils of Toledo. His Prognostic is a manual on death and the future life that enjoyed immense influence in the Middle Ages.

authors.aff: Roman African chronographer and computist; possibly a monk
authors.sig: He is one of the last vocal proponents of Latin millenarianism: his Libellus predicts the Second Coming in 498 followed by Christ's thousand-year reign, a view soon classed as heresy, yet the work circulated in medieval chronological manuscript groups.

authors.aff: Priest and teacher of rhetoric at Arles
authors.sig: His De vita contemplativa is described by Suelzer as the oldest surviving pastoral instruction in the West and a principal channel of Augustinian thought to sixth-century Gaul.

A Roman Latin writer and public advocate who wrote an astrological handbook before turning Christian apologist. His De errore profanarum religionum was addressed to two joint emperors. It attacks the mystery cults and argues that Christianity is superior to pagan worship.

authors.aff: Quaestor of the Sacred Palace under Justinian I
authors.sig: His Instituta regularia divinae legis introduced Western theologians to the Antiochene school of exegesis and influenced the early Middle Ages, being praised by Cassiodorus in his Institutes (1.10).
Julius I played a decisive role in upholding Nicene orthodoxy and establishing early precedents for the universal appellate authority of the Roman see.

Justinian I defined late antique Christian imperial rule and church-state integration, significantly impacting Christological dogma through the Fifth Ecumenical Council and leaving an enduring architectural and legal legacy.

Last emperor of the Heraclian dynasty, who reigned twice and was killed by mutinous soldiers in 711. He would not accept the supremacy of the Roman see and so came into conflict with the papacy. His one-page imperial text Copy of a Divine Command asserts that the emperor is guardian of the faith and that conciliar definitions are inviolable.

His allegorical commentary on the Song of Songs is among the earliest exegetical works from Visigothic Spain, reading the bride as the Church nourished by apostolic doctrine and reconciled to God through Christ.

authors.aff: Professor of rhetoric at Nicomedia under Diocletian; later Latin tutor to Crispus at Trier
authors.sig: Professor of rhetoric at Nicomedia under Diocletian, he lost that post after the edict of 303. He later tutored Crispus at Trier. His Divine Institutes is the first systematic Latin account of the Christian attitude toward life, and it refutes pagan philosophy in classical style.

Bishop of Arras from 1094 until his death in 1115. He studied canon law under Ivo of Chartres. His letters, deeds and privileges defend his canonical election and clerical control of sacraments and revenues.

His single surviving work records early twelfth-century fasting discipline: seasonal fasts attributed to a Master Bruno, dispensation for the infirm, monastic fasting after Benedict's rule, and abstinence from lacticinia beginning at Septuagesima.

authors.aff: frater of Saint Peter at Pult (Pultariensis)
authors.sig: His one surviving work is a ninth-century letter on correct Latin, showing how Carolingian monks taught usage, reason, and authority as the tests of correctness.

Bishop of Paris, once chief clerk of the royal chancery, who succeeded Audobertus around 650. During the famine of 650–51 he sold his possessions and church vessels to feed the poor. In 653 he subscribed to Clovis II's charter exempting Saint-Denis Abbey from episcopal jurisdiction.

Archbishop of Canterbury under William the Conqueror, he reorganized the English church. He wrote a treatise On the Body and Blood of the Lord on the Eucharist and a Commentary on all the Epistles of Paul that served as a standard medieval textbook.

authors.aff: Benedictine abbey of Hersfeld; from 1077 Hasungen
authors.sig: Benedictine chronicler at Hersfeld and a convinced opponent of King Henry IV. His Annals are a major source for the reign of Henry IV and the opening of the Investiture Controversy. They are written from a firm papalist standpoint.

authors.aff: Acolyte of the church of San Paolo, Milan
authors.sig: His Liber Historiarum Mediolanensis Urbis is the chief narrative source for Milan's conflict-ridden years 1097–1137, written from a partisan Pataria standpoint against Archbishop Jordan and Grossulanus.

His History of Milan is a partisan anti-Gregorian chronicle defending Milan's precedence beside the apostolic see and clerical marriage against the Patarenes, and it preserves the losing side of the Milanese reform struggle.

authors.aff: Monk of Winchester, disciple of Bishop Æthelwold
authors.sig: A monk of Winchester and disciple of Bishop Æthelwold who wrote the earliest account of St Swithun's cult, the Translatio et miracula S. Swithuni. He says he knew little of the saint's life and wrote mainly of his miracles, which he argues God worked through the merits of the saints against unbelievers and envious critics.

His surviving homilies here treat grace, sin, faith, baptism and penance, arguing two times of remission of sins: original sin washed away in baptism, post-baptismal sins remitted by penance rather than water.

His Gesta records Verdun's episcopal succession and defends its church's rights against named opponents such as Richard of Verdun, Henry of Grand-Pré, and Emperors Henry II and IV, arguing that deeds of the fathers must be written down for imitation before mortality erases all memory.

Bishop of Seville from 579. He helped convert Hermenegild and Reccared to Catholicism. He wrote a Regula (Libellus ad Florentinam) for his sister Florentina and her nuns on virginity and prayer. He also wrote a Homily in Praise of the Church.

Bishop of Seville from 579, he led the Visigothic conversion to Catholicism and helped bring Prince Hermenegild and King Reccared into the Catholic faith. His brother Isidore succeeded him at Seville. A rule for nuns addressed to his sister Florentina is part of his wider work.

He led Saint-Vaast's adoption of the Cluniac reform in early eleventh-century Flanders, and the record here preserves a charter-like constitution governing the abbey's public plea and its men's exemptions.

His surviving treatise on baptism is a Carolingian episcopal instruction on the sacrament's prefiguration from the beginning of the world, its doctrine, and its rites (including catechumenate instruction and the salt rite), grounded in Paul, Augustine, Gregory, and the ancient fathers.

Bishop of Atina, whom no surviving record describes. The Translation of the Body of Pope Mark and two sermons on St. Mark of Atina are attributed to him. They present Mark's martyrdom under Domitian and the power of his relics.

Bishop of Rome from 440 until his death in 461. His letters and sermons assert Rome's teaching authority. They attack Manichaean, Eutychian, Priscillianist, Pelagian and Arian teaching. His Tome to Flavian of Constantinople is a major foundation for Chalcedon's definition of Christ as one person in two natures.

authors.aff: Bishop of Rome (pope from 26 December 795 to his death in 816)
authors.sig: The letters here assert papal primacy — obedience owed to Roman commands, reception of papal envoys as reception of Christ, the faith spread from the Roman see — and include privileges such as the transfer of the London pallium to Canterbury.

Bishop of Rome from 682 to 683. He ratified the acts of the Sixth Ecumenical Council against the Monothelites. His letters affirm Christ's two natural wills and operations. They call for the deposition of obstinate heretical bishops and uphold Agatho's orthodox confession as transmitted through Peter.

authors.aff: Bishop of Rome (pope, 1049–1054); previously Bishop of Toul
authors.sig: Bishop of Toul from 1026, he was elected pope in 1049 and pursued reform through synods at Reims and Mainz. His letters and decrees assert papal privilege and jurisdiction, and his conflict with Patriarch Michael Cerularius of Constantinople helped precipitate the East-West Schism.

Bishop of Rome from 847 until his death in 855. He rebuilt Rome's walls and organized Italian cities that defeated the Saracen fleet at Ostia in 849. His letters and decrees cover episcopal jurisdiction and ordination, and a homily also survives under his name.

authors.aff: Monk, librarian, and archivist of Monte Cassino; cardinal bishop of Ostia
authors.sig: His chronicle is the principal source for Monte Cassino's history to 1075 and a valuable mine of information for southern Italian affairs generally; Peter the Deacon continued it to 1139, and modern scholarship distinguishes Leo's own revised recension from later Cassinese reworkings — the very questions the texts here address.

Marozia arranged his election as pope in June 928 after she deposed John X. He held the see until his death in February 929. A bull he issued to Dalmatia grants the pallium to Archbishop John of Spalato and keeps bishops within their ancient limits.

Elected pope in 963 by a synod convened under Emperor Otto I. His Privileges and constitutions concern episcopal election, the pallium, and Aquileia's rank among Italian churches. His pontificate is a test case of imperial control over papal elections after the saeculum obscurum.

authors.aff: Abbot of Santi Bonifacio ed Alessio, Rome
authors.sig: Benedictine abbot of Santi Bonifacio ed Alessio on the Aventine from 981, he was often sent as a papal legate after 992. His letter to Kings Hugh and Robert treats the Church, true worship and Scripture.

Bishop of the see of Sens in sixth-century Gaul, successor to Saint Paul there. He defended his see's rights against King Childebert I in a letter arguing that no second bishop may be ordained while the first lives.

Bishop of Autun, he was raised at the court of Clotaire II and introduced the Rule of St. Benedict as abbot. He led the Burgundian faction against Ebroin, and his dying Testament transferred villas to the church of Autun and bound successor bishops to keep the donation.

Pope from 936 to 939, elected while Alberic II of Spoleto controlled Rome. His letters and privileges grant monasteries exemption from all authority save the apostolic see and free election of abbots under Benedict's rule.

Archbishop of Vienne in the eleventh century, he issued charters asserting that the power of binding and loosing passed from Peter to bishops. Those charters also required that alienated church property be restored and placed anyone who disturbed church donations under anathema.

authors.aff: Monastery of Saint-Mesmin de Micy, near Orléans
authors.sig: Benedictine monk at the abbey of Saint-Mesmin de Micy near Orléans in the later tenth century. He wrote Latin saints' lives and miracle collections, among them a Book of Miracles of Saint Maximinus and a Life of St. Julian of Le Mans. He argued that God works miracles through his saints.
The single page preserved under his name is a legal-ecclesiastical formulary showing how Merovingian bishops managed landed property held by petitioners on the church's terms.

His sole surviving work is the donation charter to Cluny printed in PL 133, cols. 841–844A, an early witness to Cluniac landholding and to the theology of almsgiving as liberation of souls from hell's punishment.

authors.aff: Priest of the Christian community in Córdoba under Umayyad rule
authors.sig: A priest of ninth-century Córdoba under Umayyad emir rule, recorded as dying in 852 under Abd al-Rahman II. He wrote the Book on the Attire of Clerics (De habitu clericorum), which argues that clerical dress bears mystical meaning and that clergy must not adopt the garb of the Ishmaelites.

Roman deacon elected bishop of Rome on 17 May 352, succeeding Julius I. He resisted imperial pressure under Constantius II during the Arian controversy and was exiled. A Letter to Lucifer survives under his name but its authorship is unverified. He is omitted from the Roman Martyrology, while the Greek Menology venerates him.

Bishop of Utrecht and counselor of Emperor Henry II, he defended his see against Norman raids and lost the Merwede dispute with Dirk III of Holland. He wrote a life of Henry II whose preface sets out the qualifications of a historian, along with a Life of St. Walpurga and short treatises on music and on the thickness of a sphere.

authors.aff: Bishop (later tradition: archbishop) of Cartagena under Byzantine rule
authors.sig: His three surviving letters are among the few witnesses to theological debate in Byzantine-ruled Spania, defending against opponents who denied that angels are spirits and engaging Augustine's and Origen's positions on the soul and creation.

Bishop of Cambrai from 1051 until his death in 1076, he led a pilgrimage toward Jerusalem in 1054 that reached only Cyprus before turning back. His charter establishing regular canons argues that common life without private property restores proper divine worship and opposes secular canons who keep their property.

Bishop of Rome from 352 to 366, whose pontificate fell under the Arian emperor. He asked the emperor for a council at Aquileia on a disputed case and was exiled for refusing to abandon it. Letters and sayings printed under his name are largely documentary and polemical.

Abbot of Saint-Ruf in the diocese of Avignon around 1100. He wrote the Liber ecclesiastici et canonici ordinis, a customary grounded in Augustine's monastic teaching that shaped later houses of Augustinian canons. His letters defend the divine institution of the clerical order and the power of priests to absolve sins.

His Breviarium causae Nestorianorum et Eutychianorum is a principal narrative source for the Nestorian and Monophysite controversies from Nestorius's ordination (428) to the Fifth Ecumenical Council (553), written from a Chalcedonian, anti-Three-Chapters standpoint.

authors.aff: Bishop; apostle of Flanders and Brabant
authors.sig: The epistle here, addressed to Florbert of Ghent, is one of only two texts on which any claim to Livinus's existence rests (the other being an epitaph on St Bavo), and its genuineness was first challenged by Rettberg.

authors.aff: Bishop of Cremona; diplomat at the court of Otto I
authors.sig: His histories — Antapodosis, Historia Ottonis, and the Relatio — are primary sources for tenth-century Italian politics, the Ottonian intervention in the papacy, and the Byzantine court as seen by a hostile Latin envoy.

authors.aff: Priest and monk, founder of a monastery at the vicus Busiacus in the diocese of Le Mans
authors.sig: A priest and monk who founded a monastery at Busiacus in the diocese of Le Mans and gave it to Bishop Hadoindus in 625. His foundation charter describes how he left his pagan Alamannian parents and was baptized by Christians he met.

authors.aff: Holy Roman Emperor; King of Italy and Middle Francia
authors.sig: Holy Roman Emperor and king of Italy who rebelled against his father and fought his brothers before receiving Middle Francia at the Treaty of Verdun. His capitularies and letters survive as documents of church governance, among them a letter to Rabanus Maurus.

King of Lotharingia from 855 until his death at Piacenza in 869. He spent a decade trying to set aside his wife Teutberga to marry Waldrada, which drew opposition from Pope Nicholas I and his uncles. The divorce case produced the Sacramentum de Theotberga recipienda, his oath to take Teutberga back.

Holy Roman Emperor from 1133 until his death in 1137, after a reign opposed by Hohenstaufen dukes Frederick II of Swabia and Conrad of Franconia. Two documents survive under his name: a coronation rite dated 4 June 1133 and a sentence condemning Peter Leonis as a schismatic.

Canon of San Isidoro in León and then Bishop of Tuy until his death in 1249. He wrote the Chronicon mundi, a four-part world chronicle that draws mainly on Isidore of Seville. His Life of St. Martin argues that the merits and prayers of saints avail with God and that scriptural understanding comes by divine illumination.

Bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia, he defended Athanasius against Arian condemnation at Milan in 355. Exiled by Constantius II, he wrote polemical pamphlets from that exile. Among them are On Not Sparing Those Who Sin Against God and On Apostate Kings, which argue that kings who persecute the church face divine punishment.

Bishop of Rome from 1181 to 1185, he was driven from the city in 1182 and governed mostly from Velletri and Verona. His letters and privileges are decretals that assert papal protection over church property, monastic rights, tithes, and jurisdiction.

His Epistola ad omnem Ecclesiam is a principal Latin account of the discovery of St Stephen's relics, narrating Gamaliel's revelatory appearances and asserting that God revealed the relics' location by vision, that relics of saints must be revealed and honored, that God preserves the bodies of his martyrs, and that sharing with martyrs secures a share in resurrection.
His capitularies show a Carolingian king legislating directly on ecclesiastical morals, sacramental discipline, and the relation of royal to episcopal authority.

authors.aff: First Bishop of Münster; founder of Werden Abbey
authors.sig: His Life of Gregory is both a primary witness to the Utrecht monastic tradition from Willibrord through Boniface and a treatise on obedience to spiritual fathers.

Pope from March 1144 until his death in February 1145. He faced the invasion of papal lands by Roger II of Sicily and the Roman Commune under Giordano Pierleoni. His surviving letters and privileges defend monastery possessions and papal privilege against diocesan bishops and local magnates.

A Benedictine monk of the ninth-century Spanish March, according to Isaac Lampurlanés. He is known only through a Latin homiliary on parts of the New Testament, which argues against Arians and schismatics. Earlier scholars placed him in the sixth century.

authors.aff: Holy Roman Emperor and King of the Franks (r. 814–840)
authors.sig: The documents here show how a Carolingian ruler used imperial diplomas to define the legal standing of the Church — immunity from judges, monastic self-election, and protection of worship — making them primary evidence for early medieval church-state relations.

authors.aff: King of Italy and Holy Roman Emperor
authors.sig: Carolingian king of Italy and co-emperor with his father Lothair I until 855, who took Bari in 871. His charters at Pavia confirmed privileges to monasteries and patriarchates, and a historical chapter under his name argues that property assigned to evade justice falls under ban.

King of France from 1137 until his death in 1180. He led the French contingent on the Second Crusade, which ended in failure. A letter on his capture and liberation frames the defeat as divine punishment for sin and the slain crusaders as martyrs.

Archbishop of Mainz from 863 until his death in 889, he presided over the synod that condemned the Greek church for heresy. A letter to King Louis survives under his name, defending the primacy of Peter's see and warning that a silent bishop is a hireling rather than a shepherd.

authors.aff: Archbishop of Mainz; first abbot of Hersfeld Abbey
authors.sig: The letters here document the administration and disputes of Boniface's successor — questions of prayer, church order, worship, and discipline addressed to named correspondents such as Oswitha, Bernarius, Enred, and Willefrid — making them primary evidence for the Frankish church in the generation after Boniface.

A Carolingian Benedictine who was Abbot of Ferrières Abbey from 840 left over 130 letters that witness to intellectual life, book circulation and textual criticism. He also wrote On the Three Questions on predestination and free will and a Life of St. Wigbert.

Bishop in Gaul who joined the mission to Britain against Pelagianism. His letters present episcopal office as humble service to a suffering church. A sixth-century Life praises him as an ideal bishop and healer.

Wrote the Annales Lupi Protospatharii, a concise Latin chronicle of southern Italy covering 805 to 1102. Nothing is known of him beyond what the text shows: he wrote at Bari and drew on lost Bariot and Matera annals.

Fourth abbot of Cluny from 965 until his death in 994. He spread the Cluniac reform through Burgundy, Italy, and France. An account of Odilo's election as abbot survives under his name. It shows how Cluny grounded its authority in divine and papal foundations and in obedience to Benedict's Rule.

Archbishop of Reims and primate of France, he defied the Gregorian reform and was excommunicated by Gregory VII in 1080. A letter to the Morini survives under his name. He is remembered chiefly as patron of Fulcoius of Beauvais.

authors.aff: Presbyter at Vienne, brother of Bishop Mamertus
authors.sig: His De statu animae is the principal Latin patristic defense of the soul's incorporeality against Faustus of Riez, arguing from reason in book one, from philosophical and scriptural authority in book two, and by direct refutation in book three.

Canon regular and partisan of Pope Gregory VII in the Investiture Controversy. He wrote Ad Gebehardum liber against Wenrich of Trier's letter for Henry IV. His Opusculum against Wolfhelm of Cologne warns that schismatics from Rome lose eternal salvation and that pagan philosophers err without the Spirit.

Archbishop of Milan from 676 until his death in 685. He condemned Monothelitism at a synod in 679 and attended Pope Agatho's Roman synod of 680. A letter to Emperor Constantine IV against Monothelitism carries his name but was composed by Damian, later bishop of Pavia.
His one surviving letter is a witness to early tenth-century Gallican practice on clerical discipline and the hierarchical ordering of synodal judgment.

Bishop of Reims from 535 until his death in 550. Two letters survive under his name, one to Vilicus of Metz about pig prices and one to Nicetius of Trier excusing his absence from the Council of Toul. They are among the few sources for Merovingian episcopal politics and the dispute over royal intervention in excommunication.

authors.aff: Bishop of Rennes; formerly archdeacon and schoolmaster at Angers
authors.sig: Bishop of Rennes from 1096 and a Latin poet of the Angevin schools. He wrote verse lives of saints and letters. His moral and devotional pieces treat sin, repentance and grace.

authors.aff: Court of Constantinople; chancellor to Justinian
authors.sig: The extracts here come from his Chronicle, a chief Latin continuation of Eusebius covering the Eastern Empire from Theodosius I to Justinian's reign.

Bishop of Rome from 296 until his death in 304 during the Diocletian persecution. A short appendix printed under his name argues for equal sacrifice to Father and Son, but its citations of Hormisdas and Leo suggest it is probably spurious. Nothing of his own activity survives.

The single item held under this name, Appendix II of PL 7, is a four-page polemic against Maxentius defending persecuted bishops and procedural rights at synods (persecution of bishops is persecution of Christ himself; restitution must precede a bishop's trial at a synod; no condemnation without legitimate accusers and right of defense). It cannot be the pope's own writing — it cites authors such

A Frankish monk who compiled a handbook of model legal documents in the seventh century. His Formulary is dedicated to a bishop named Landeric. Its first book gives royal charters and its second gives private acts. It shows how kings, bishops and churches handled law and land in Merovingian Gaul.

authors.aff: Bishop of Avenches (Aventicum) from 574, later transferred his see to Lausanne
authors.sig: Bishop of Aventicum from 574, who later moved his see to Lausanne. He is remembered almost solely for his Chronicle, a terse continuation of Prosper of Aquitaine that uniquely transmits Burgundian affairs after 533/534 and reports contemporary events in Italy and the East.

A Roman legal advocate and one of the earliest Christian apologists to write in Latin. Jerome calls him an outstanding courtroom speaker, and he converted to Christianity. His one known work is a dialogue between a pagan skeptic and a Christian, borrowing chiefly from Cicero and the Greek apologists.

authors.aff: Recluse at St Martin's abbey, Mainz
authors.sig: Irish monk and recluse at St Martin's in Mainz, where he died in 1082 or 1083. His world chronicle counted the Christian era with a correction that Dionysius Exiguus had erred by 22 years. Its year-by-year history of councils, emperors and heresiarchs became a standard medieval source.

Taught rhetoric at Rome, where a statue was erected to him in the Forum of Trajan in 353. He translated Aristotle's Categories and On Interpretation into Latin before his conversion to Christianity around 355. Augustine recounts that conversion in Confessions 8.

Bishop of Rome from 30 October 942 until his death in 946. Alberic II of Spoleto helped secure his election during the Saeculum obscurum. His pontificate concentrated on administration, including clergy reform through legates and support for monastic development. A few privileges for monasteries survive in PL 133.

A Latin writer probably born in Northern Africa who attacked Pelagianism and Nestorianism while living in Constantinople from 429 to about 448. His Latin translations of Greek sources such as Cyril of Alexandria and Theodore of Mopsuestia preserved the documents of the Nestorian controversy.

authors.aff: Abbot of Dumio, later Archbishop of Braga
authors.sig: Monk who came to Gallaecia to convert the Suevi, then served as bishop of Dumio and Archbishop of Braga. He wrote moral treatises On Anger, On Pride and Exhortation to Humility. Gregory praised him as second to none of his contemporaries in learning.
He is venerated as a martyr and confessor for his uncompromising defense of Dyothelite Christology at the Lateran Council of 649 against Byzantine imperial policy.

authors.aff: Collegiate church of San Isidoro, León
authors.sig: His sermons and biblical expositions — on Revelation, the Catholic Epistles, and many doctrinal subjects — form a major twelfth-century Spanish homiletic corpus, notable for its extensive anti-Jewish polemic and its heavy reliance on Paul, Augustine, Gregory, and Isidore. He is also credited with the 'Concordia Veteris ac Novi Testamenti', a sermon compilation on which modern research has often fo

Bishop of Tours from 371 until his death in 397, he founded a monastery at Ligugé around 360. A Confession under his name argues for the unity of essence among the three divine persons, yet its attribution to him is open to doubt.
She was the primary political and military defender of the Gregorian reform papacy against imperial encroachments in northern Italy.

authors.aff: Pupil of Bernard Silvestris at Tours
authors.sig: A French Latin poet and rhetorician who studied under Bernard Silvestris. He wrote the Ars versificatoria, a metrical paraphrase of the Book of Tobit and the poem Piramus et Tisbe.

authors.aff: Cardinal bishop of Albano (from 1125), papal legate
authors.sig: Cardinal bishop of Albano and papal legate under Innocent II, he worked to restore monastic discipline in France and Germany. His letters rule that canons may present priests without simony and that monastic chapters freely elect abbots.

Bishop from 1160 to 1196, during whose episcopate Notre-Dame cathedral was built. Alexander III laid its cornerstone in 1163. Five pages of his letters and diplomas survive under his name, charters on monastic endowments and parochial rights.

Archbishop of Rouen from 1054 or 1055 until his death in 1067, appointed by Duke William. He presided over a council at Caen that imposed the Truce of God. A letter to the Bishop of Évreux argues that the Benedictine rule outranks secular law.

Patriarch of Aquileia from 811 until his death. He settled a long dispute with Venerius of Grado over Istrian bishoprics at the Synod of Mantua in 827. His Collectanea De Antiquis Ritibus Baptismi describes exorcism and salt, and sponsors who renounced on behalf of infants.
His single surviving epistle is a contemporary Latin witness to the two-wills, two-operations Christology affirmed at the Lateran Council of 649 and later at Constantinople III.

Bishop of Zaragoza from 592 until about 619 he held the Second Council of Zaragoza against Arianism. The Chronicle printed under his name in PL 80 was edited by Higuera in 1611 and is regarded as a forgery. Only 33 brief anonymous excerpts survive of any genuine chronicle.

The single work here is a crusading appeal written after pagans profaned churches and slaughtered Christians, arguing that war against Christ's enemies is a religious duty that saves souls and that contemplatives must take up active service in time of need.

His surviving exchange with Augustine is one of the clearest records of an educated pagan challenging Christianity in provincial North Africa after its official adoption, conducted with mutual respect rather than polemic.

First pope after the persecutions' end, whose name later attracted appended decretal material on Roman appellate authority; readers should treat the PL 7 appendix as attribution rather than certain authorship.

authors.aff: Bishop of Turin, then a suffragan see of Milan
authors.sig: His homilies and sermons here preach Christology, grace, and the church against pagans and Jews amid barbarian pressure on northern Italy, and they preserve an active authorship controversy over which texts are genuinely his.

authors.aff: Canon, correspondent of Rupert of Deutz
authors.sig: A canon known only from a letter to Rupert of Deutz, dated 1120 to 1129 in the source. The letter defends him against disparagers by arguing that error about God is dangerous while error about creatures is not.

authors.aff: Abbey of Saint-Aubin, Angers; cardinal-bishop of Palestine
authors.sig: Benedictine monk of Saint-Aubin at Angers, made a cardinal and bishop of Palestine by Pope Urban II. He attended the Council of Clermont in 1095 and later served as papal legate under Paschal II. Martène printed verses in Latin that he attributed, with some uncertainty, to this bishop.

His Life of Blessed Lanfranc and Life of William of Bec are the principal narrative sources for Lanfranc's career at Bec and Canterbury, including his teaching against Berengar and Roscelin and his death on 28 May 1089.

Abbot Abbo of Fleury was killed in a dispute at La Réole in Gascony on 13 November 1004. A single-page encyclical letter on his death survives under the collective name of the monks of Fleury. It treats his death as fellowship with the martyrs and commends the prayers of the saints for departed souls.

His Vita sancti Amandi is a Carolingian example of hagiography in Latin verse, arguing that Christ-centered poetry surpasses pagan models and that divine grace supplies an unlearned writer's insufficiency.

authors.n: Pilgrim Monks on the Mount of Olives
authors.aff: Monastery on the Mount of Olives, Jerusalem
authors.sig: The letter is an early witness to Western Filioque theology argued from Jerusalem itself, directed to Leo III and Charlemagne against Greek opposition from St. Sabas.

His Gesta Karoli Magni is one of the two principal early biographies of Charlemagne, mixing anecdote and moral judgment — it censures bishops more than it praises Charles, and condemns forced conversion as polluting sacred things.

His surviving letters are early witnesses to Visigothic-era Spanish discipline: they insist that no one may exercise sacred offices without holding them, reserve chrism and church consecration to bishops, treat usurpation of sacramental rites as schism, and attack Priscillianist remnants and presuming priests in his province.

The five works here are doctrinal treatises defending the divinity, lordship, and liberty of the Holy Spirit against Arians and Photinians, treating the Spirit's procession from the Father and his role in creation, baptism, and the distribution of gifts.

A monk of Cluny who rewrote an earlier, disordered Life of Saint Odo by one Joannes at the urging of senior monks. He chose a plain, domestic style because verbal confusion had buried the saint's deeds. His labor was meant for the future profit of readers.

authors.aff: Bishop of Brescia; educated at the school of Chartres under Fulbert
authors.sig: His Eucharist letter is a primary witness to eleventh-century sacramental teaching against Berengarius, arguing that the eucharist is the true body and blood of Christ and that patristic consensus binds in faith.

A Latin rhetorician and professor of rhetoric at Bordeaux, according to Ausonius. In 321 at Rome he delivered a panegyric praising Constantine as the exemplar of every virtue to his sons. A speech from 313 is often attributed to him, but differences of style and vocabulary argue against it.

The most important bishop of Trier in the age when Frankish supremacy began in Roman Gaul, remembered here chiefly for a treatise defending holy vigils as apostolic in origin and for letters engaging emperors and barbarian kings.

authors.aff: Clairvaux Abbey; later prior of Saint-Jean-en-Châtel
authors.sig: A Cistercian monk who served as secretary to Bernard of Clairvaux before Bernard dismissed him in 1151 or 1152. His letters survive, along with sermons on feasts such as On the Nativity of the Lord.

authors.aff: Clairvaux Abbey; later prior of Saint-Jean-in-Châtel
authors.sig: A French Cistercian who served as secretary to Bernard of Clairvaux until Bernard dismissed him in 1151. He later became prior of Saint-Jean-in-Châtel in 1160. He wrote a letter arguing that true liberality conforms to all without ambition, citing Cicero.

authors.aff: Prior of Worcester Cathedral priory (c. 1113 or c. 1116 – 1124)
authors.sig: English monk and prior of Worcester Cathedral priory until his death on 24 June 1124. He was taught by Bishop Wulfstan and studied under Lanfranc at Christchurch, Canterbury. His letter to Eadmer argues that York has primacy over the Scots and that York received its faith and orders from the Scottish church.

authors.aff: Archbishop of Magdeburg; founder of the Premonstratensians
authors.sig: Canon at Xanten and almoner to Emperor Henry V, he later became archbishop of Magdeburg. After a conversion to itinerant preaching he founded the Premonstratensian canons regular at Prémontré. Sermons printed under his name argue that schism is the devil's work, but the sources do not document that he wrote them.
A pivotal early medieval pope who established influential precedents for centralized papal authority, independence from secular control, and jurisdictional supremacy over all Christian churches.

Bishop of Rome from 1059 to 1061, he issued the decree restricting papal elections to the cardinal bishops. His letters and diplomas defend papal privilege and clerical immunity from lay jurisdiction. They date from the reforming papacy on the eve of the Investiture Controversy.

authors.aff: Bishop and first Prince-Bishop of Liège
authors.sig: Bishop of Liège from 972 and its first prince-bishop after he received the county of Huy in 980. He served three Ottonian emperors and wrote saints' lives, including a Life of Saint Remaclus and a Life of Saint Hadalin. In a preface to a life of St. Landoald, he defends earlier hagiographers against critics who find their matter incredible.

A Benedictine monk of Saint Gall called the Stammerer for his lifelong stutter. He composed sequences and hymns and wrote a martyrology and the anecdotal Gesta Karoli Magni. He also taught Solomon III, bishop of Constance.

authors.aff: Probably lay abbot of Saint-Riquier; counselor to Charles the Bald
authors.sig: The only layman of his time who devoted himself to writing history, he gives an eyewitness, partisan account of the Carolingian civil war that defends Charles the Bald against Lothair.

A Roman priest and the first Roman theologian to write in Latin, he defended Christ's full divinity in On the Trinity against Sabellians and those who made Christ a mere man. He later became a rival bishop of Rome in 251, opposing Cornelius over the readmission of apostates.

Fifth abbot of Cluny, who governed the abbey from about 994 until his death in 1048. He built Cluny up with daughter houses under his authority and promoted the Truce of God. He established All Souls' Day on 2 November, which the Western church soon adopted. His sermons and Life of Majolus show his reform of Cluny's devotional life.

authors.aff: Bishop of Bayeux; Earl of Kent
authors.sig: The charter here documents his governance of the Bayeux diocese; readers of his name should note he is known as a bishop-patron and administrator, not as a theological author.

His Exposition on the Psalms reads David christologically throughout: David as a type of Christ, Absalom's hanging prefiguring Judas, the synagogue disinherited for killing the heir, and the church inheriting the vineyard — a representative pre-scholastic allegorical psalm exegesis arguing chiefly against Jewish reading of the text.

authors.aff: Abbot of Corbie; Bishop of Beauvais
authors.sig: Abbot of Corbie before he became bishop, he served the Carolingian court on missions to East Francia and Rome. His Passion of Saint Lucian portrays Lucian as the founding bishop and presents each martyr's victory as Christ's own victory renewed.

authors.aff: Abbot of St Martin's, Tournai; Bishop of Cambrai (from c. 1105)
authors.sig: Abbot of St Martin's at Tournai and bishop of Cambrai, he refused investiture from Emperor Henry IV and was exiled in 1110. His On Original Sin uses a realist account of universals to explain how all sinned in Adam, and it locates sin as a privation in the will alone.

authors.aff: Abbot of Battle; monk, sub-prior and prior of Christ Church, Canterbury
authors.sig: Prior of Christ Church and later abbot of Battle, who defended church authority against royal encroachment after Becket's murder. His Epistle and Synodal Letter defend church property and the subordination of kings to bishops. Works under his name are hard to separate from those of Odo of Cheriton and Odo of Murimund.

Second abbot of Cluny, he led the monastic reform that spread from Cluny across Gaul and Italy after his authorization by Pope John XI in 931. He wrote moral reflections on Job modeled on Gregory's Moralia, a Life of Saint Gerald, sermons, and works on music.

A monk of the abbey of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés who served as copyist and scholasticus and returned to it around 1058. His Life of Burchard is his only surviving work, and it preserves details on the origin of the abbey.
A twelfth-century Cistercian writer whose surviving reputation rests on symbolic-number theology, represented here only by short sermons treating perfection, grace, and justification.

His synodal statutes are among the earliest episcopal legislation on liturgical practice in Paris, including the abolition of the Feast of Fools and reform of corrupted liturgy by episcopal authority.

His De profectione Ludovici VII in Orientem is a firsthand day-by-day account of the Second Crusade from France to Antioch, written as material for Suger's planned biography of Louis VII, and it blames the crusade's failure on human action — above all the Byzantines under Manuel Comnenus — rather than divine will.

His Chronicle and history of the translation of SS. Savinian, Potentian and their companions preserve Sens's monastic and episcopal traditions — including his assertion that the bishop of Sens held primacy in Gaul — while his minor works defend monastic religion against anthropomorphites and Amalarius of Lyons.
A prominent Cistercian spiritual author whose contemplative commentaries on the Gospels and Marian laments influenced medieval monastic devotion.

authors.aff: Archbishop of Tarragona; formerly Bishop of Barcelona and abbot of Saint-Ruf, Avignon
authors.sig: Archbishop of Tarragona from 1118 and earlier Bishop of Barcelona. A charter and two letters survive under his name. One letter is to Raymond, bishop of Ausona, and the other to Pope Innocent II. They treat sin and grace and ask whether a man who has killed by accident may receive minor orders.

authors.aff: Abbot of Ripoll and Cuixà; Bishop of Vic
authors.sig: One of the most important prelates of eleventh-century Iberia and considered a spiritual founder of Catalonia; his letters and sermons here show him defending ecclesiastical discipline: forbidding marriage within forbidden degrees, condemning divination and augury, and opposing usurpers of St. Peter's estates.

A monk of Saint-Evroul who worked there as script master, librarian and cantor. His Historia Ecclesiastica runs to thirteen books of universal history from Christ's birth to about 1141 and is a principal contemporary source for Normandy and Anglo-Norman England.

authors.aff: Priest, associate of Augustine of Hippo
authors.sig: Priest and historian who studied under Augustine of Hippo. He composed the Historiarum adversus paganos libri VII at Augustine's request to show that providence governs history against pagan claims that Christian times were worse.

authors.aff: Bishop of Augusta Ausciorum (Auch) — probable identification
authors.sig: The Commonitorium is his only work: an elegiac poem of 1036 verses in two books mapping the way to heaven and warning against its hindrances, treating sin, envy, avarice, almsgiving, prayer, baptism, and last things in verse.

His reply to Parmenianus is an early sustained Latin polemic against the Donatists; its arguments — the church spread through the whole world, the invalidity of schism and rebaptism — anticipate Augustine's later anti-Donatist case.

authors.aff: Catechetical School of Alexandria; Christian School of Caesarea
authors.sig: Taught at Alexandria and later founded the Christian School of Caesarea. The churches of Palestine and Arabia regarded him as an authority. His surviving works are mostly exegesis. They include commentaries on John and Matthew and homilies on Jeremiah.

authors.aff: Monk of Christ Church, Canterbury; described as its precentor
authors.sig: Monk of Christ Church, Canterbury, who wrote Latin saints' lives of Dunstan and Alphege. His Alphege life was written at Lanfranc's command around 1080, amid dispute over the saint's sanctity. William of Malmesbury praised his style but faulted his history.

Egyptian monk and hegumen of Tabennisi after the death of Theodore. A Latin translation by Jerome of his Doctrina de institutione monachorum grounds monastic discipline in running exegesis of Scripture.

Bishop of Corduba in Hispania and Constantine's chief ecclesiastical adviser on the Donatist question. He is credited with presiding at Serdica. Canons attributed to that council address episcopal translation and appeals to the Roman see. A letter to Constantius rebukes the emperor for Arian interference.

authors.n: Othloh of Saint Emmeram in Regensburg
authors.sig: A monk of St. Emmeram's in Regensburg who headed its monastic school and taught William of Hirsau. He wrote On the Spiritual Course and an autobiographical account of his temptations. He also wrote Visions, both his own and those of others.

A monk and cleric of St. Emmeram in Regensburg whose short musical treatise measures the monochord. He presents this measurement from a four-part figure and calls it a 'theorema troporum', or 'sieve of the monochord' ('cribrum monocordi').

authors.aff: King of Germany (from 936), Holy Roman Emperor (from 962)
authors.sig: These charters and council acts document how the Ottonian king exercised authority over councils, bishops, and even a pope, making them primary evidence for early imperial control of the church.

Bishop of Bamberg from 1102 to 1139, he was once imperial chancellor under Henry IV and later worked as a papal legate in Pomerania. His letters and diplomas argue that bishops owe the emperor fidelity while church property lies beyond secular power, and they attack Emperor Henry V and his court.

The pages here show imperial law regulating judicial combat, perjury, and ecclesiastical pleading through advocates — evidence of how civil magistracy and church procedure intersected under Ottonian rule.

authors.aff: Holy Roman Emperor, King of Germany and Italy
authors.sig: Holy Roman Emperor and King of Germany and Italy who took up rule himself after regencies under his mother and grandmother. He was crowned emperor in 996 and put down a Roman revolt. His Constitution of Pavia declares that church property alienated by bishops does not bind their successors and that laws against the church's utility are void.
He is a primary historical source for early Capetian France, the Peace of God movement, and eleventh-century liturgical music and hagiographical forgery.

authors.aff: Founder of the monastery at Tabennisi and head of the Pachomian federation
authors.sig: Egyptian monk who founded communal monasticism at Tabennisi and led a federation of such houses. His Rule is the earliest surviving monastic rule. A Latin version attributed to Jerome's translation survives, though some have denied that attribution.

authors.aff: Bishop of Auxerre, formerly Abbot of Saint-Germain
authors.sig: Abbot of Saint-Germain who became bishop of Auxerre in 622. He was known for charity to the poor and founded monasteries for nuns and for men. A single epistle survives under his name.

His extant works defend the Church's power to forgive post-baptismal sins against Novatian rigorism and give the famous line 'Christian is my name, Catholic my surname,' making him a key pre-Augustinian witness on penance, baptism, and the church's name.

authors.aff: Probably a professor of rhetoric at Bordeaux; proconsul of Africa (390); comes rerum privatarum (393)
authors.sig: A Gallo-Roman orator from Aginnum who delivered a panegyric in the Roman senate house in 389. The speech celebrates the defeat of a usurper and condemns his persecution of a religious movement, and it offers a contemporary Latin account of the emperor's rise.

authors.aff: Cardinal-deacon of SS. Cosma e Damiano under Antipope Anacletus II
authors.sig: Cardinal-deacon of SS. Cosma e Damiano under the antipope Anacletus II, and a native of Rome. He wrote a Life of Calixtus II and a Life II. He supported Anacletus in the schism after 1130.

His Life of Gelasius II is an eyewitness-adjacent account of the 1118 election and flight from imperial and Frangipani violence, written to defend canonical election against Henry V's opposition — and, per recent scholarship (Veneziani & Renzi), composed during the 1130 schism as Anacletian propaganda supporting Anacletus and delegitimizing his enemies.

Bishop of Helenopolis in Bithynia from 400. He spent nine years among the Nitrian monks of Egypt. His Lausiac History records the lives and sayings of Egyptian and Eastern monks and teaches on prayer and the defeat of demons.

A central figure in the Investiture Controversy, his turbulent negotiations with Emperor Henry V highlighted the tensions between papal and secular authority that culminated in the Concordat of Worms.

Bishop of Rome from 817 to 824, he dealt chiefly with the Frankish empire of Louis the Pious. His letters defend papal privileges, including the pallium as a sign of unity with the apostolic see and the exemptions of the Ravennate church. He also urged rulers to protect church property given in vows against Lombard and simoniac abuse.

authors.aff: Bishop of Lilybaeum, Sicily; papal legate
authors.sig: He is remembered chiefly as a leading papal legate at Chalcedon in 451 and as the author of an extant letter on the Easter reckoning.

His De corpore et sanguine Domini (written 831, revised 844) was the first monograph on the Eucharist and became the dominant medieval account of Christ's presence in the sacrament. Ratramnus and Rabanus Maurus criticized it. He answered them in a letter to Frudegard.

A deacon of the Roman Church around 500 who supported the antipope Laurentius until his death. Gregory the Great praises his two books On the Holy Spirit which defend the Spirit's full deity. Engelbrecht instead assigned them to Faustus of Riez.
He compiled the *Liber testimoniorum*, the standard early medieval catena of Gregory the Great's scriptural commentaries.
Patrick is recognized as the foundational missionary bishop of Ireland whose ministry established Christianity across the island.

Patriarch of Aquileia from 787, he had earlier been royal master of grammar at Charlemagne's court. He wrote Against Felix of Urgell, defending one person of Christ in two natures and the procession of the Spirit from the Father and the Son. His work On Salutary Teachings and his hymns also survive.

His six-book hexameter Life of St. Martin — books 1–5 versifying Sulpicius Severus' Life and Dialogues, book 6 recounting twelve posthumous miracles at Martin's tomb drawn from a document of Bishop Perpetuus — was a significant early verse epic on Martin, adapting Sulpicius' narrative for later readers.

Bishop of Nola in Campania. He gave up a senator's career after his conversion. His Poems and Letters chart the move from classical literary culture to Christian asceticism. They treat grace, the church and renunciation of self. He corresponded with Jerome and Augustine.

authors.aff: Notary/secretary of Ambrose of Milan; deacon after Ambrose's death, later in Carthage and Africa
authors.sig: Secretary to Ambrose of Milan and later a deacon in Africa. At Augustine's request he wrote a life of Ambrose dated to 422, the only biography of Ambrose resting on a contemporary account. In Carthage in 411 he drew up theses defining Pelagian teaching as heresy.

authors.aff: Mozarabic Christian community in the Emirate of Córdoba
authors.sig: He is one of the most important intellectual and literary figures of 9th-century Mozarabic Christianity, providing crucial firsthand accounts and theological defenses of the Martyrs of Córdoba.
His Life of Gregory VII is a major pro-papal biography of the Investiture Controversy, portraying Gregory as a new Elijah set against King Henry IV.
His history is a major source for the Visigothic Kingdom of Toledo and for the conflict between the Catholic and Arian churches that ended in the conversion of the Visigoths from Arianism.

Lombard Benedictine monk and historian at Monte Cassino, ordained deacon around 782. His History of the Lombards traces that people's origins to Scandinavia and runs through the eighth century. He also wrote a Life of Saint Gregory the Great, homilies, poems and letters.
Ambiguity in the heading prevents definitive identification among several historical figures named Paul I.

authors.aff: Bishop of Verdun; abbot of Tholey
authors.sig: Bishop of Verdun from around 630 under Dagobert I, who had been educated beside him at the court of Chlothar II. Letters under his name survive in PL 87 and cite a fellow bishop trained at the Merovingian court.

Bishop of Rome from 579 until his death in 590 during the Lombard siege of the city. His letters assert that the Roman see governs all churches. They negotiate the Istrian schism over the Three Chapters with Elias and the Istrian bishops and argue against Theodore of Mopsuestia.

authors.aff: Monk and spiritual director in Rome
authors.sig: Monk and spiritual director in Rome, probably of British birth. He taught that human effort and free choice are primary in salvation and denied original sin. His Letter to Saint Augustine and Books on Free Will are primary texts of the Pelagian controversy.

Bishop of Rome from 556 to 561, chosen as Justinian I's candidate and poorly received in the West. His letters defend coercing schismatics as an act of love and insist that separation from the apostolic see is schism.

Bishop of the church at Tours for thirty years, he instituted a fast from St. Martin's Day that became known as St. Martin's Lent. He wrote a Testament, a will that freed slaves for service to the church and endowed perpetual lights at saints' tombs.

authors.aff: Master of the cathedral schools of Paris (Mont Sainte-Geneviève, Notre-Dame); later monk of Saint-Denis and abbot of Saint-Gildas-de-Rhuys in Brittany
authors.sig: A founder of scholastic theology. His Sic et Non, which sets conflicting authorities side by side, shaped the medieval academic method of question and disputation.

authors.aff: Librarian of the Roman Church under Adrian II
authors.sig: Librarian of the Roman Church under Adrian II and a learned Greek scholar who stood briefly as antipope in 855. He wrote an Abbreviated History of the Franks. His account of the translation of St. Stephen defends relics that expel demons and work healing miracles.

authors.aff: Physician to a King Alfonso (sources differ on whether Alfonso I of Aragon or Alfonso VI of Castile)
authors.sig: His Dialogi contra Iudaeos, an imaginary twelve-part debate between his former self (Moses) and his new self (Peter), was among the most widely copied anti-Jewish works of the Middle Ages (over 160 surviving medieval manuscripts), and its Tetragrammaton-Trinity diagram influenced Joachim of Fiore and later Shield-of-Trinity schemes.
Archdeacon of Bath and a French-born cleric who studied at Tours and read Roman law at Bologna. His letters and sermons argue on sin, penance, and grace, and he wrote Against the Perfidy of the Jews.

authors.aff: Bishop of Chartres; formerly Abbot of La Celle and of St-Rémy, Reims
authors.sig: Benedictine abbot of La Celle and of Saint-Rémy at Reims, he became Bishop of Chartres in 1181. His sermons, letters and treatises teach a Christocentric monastic theology of grace, sin and penitence. He formed a lasting friendship with John of Salisbury while studying in Paris.

authors.aff: Chanter and canon of Notre-Dame, Paris
authors.sig: Chanter and canon of Notre-Dame in Paris, he was a theologian whom the popes employed as a judge. His Verbum Adbreviatum survives in long and short versions and urges readers to abbreviate their reading for the sake of their salvation. He also attacks pluralist prelates and monks who own private property.

Ninth abbot of Cluny, who ruled a congregation of some 2,000 houses from 1122. He wrote Letters and polemic in Against the Jews and Against the Sect of the Saracens. He sought to turn the crusading spirit from conquest toward dialogue and conversion. His defense of monastic revenues answered the Cistercian critics.

Archbishop of Milan from 1110 until his death in 1117. Pope Paschal II sent him to the Byzantine emperor, and his Latin oration on the Holy Spirit defends the filioque. It argues that denying the Spirit's procession from the Son diminishes the Son's glory.

Bishop of Ravenna from around 433, he preached short homilies on gospel parables and miracles. His sermons treat Christ, grace, faith, and the sacraments. Felix of Ravenna later gathered 176 of them, though some are interpolations.

authors.aff: Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia; monastery of Fonte Avellana
authors.sig: Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia and prior of Fonte Avellana, he worked for church reform against simony and clerical incontinence. He wrote the Book of Gomorrah on clerical vice for Pope Leo IX and the tract On Divine Omnipotence, which secured his place in medieval philosophy.

authors.aff: Chancellor of Notre-Dame and teacher of theology, Paris
authors.sig: Chancellor of Notre-Dame in Paris and teacher of theology. His Historia Scholastica retells Scripture from creation to the apostles' deaths. It relies heavily on Josephus and the Fathers rather than novelty. He also left sermons.
His work is a primary witness to twelfth-century liturgical practice and property arrangements inside the Vatican basilica.

authors.aff: Master of theology and Chancellor of the University of Paris (from 1193)
authors.sig: An early systematizer of Peter Lombard's theology. His Five Books of Sentences helped establish the scholastic quaestio method and the Sentences as the basic theological curriculum.

A Benedictine monk of Maillezais who wrote the abbey's founding history at the request of Abbot Goderannus. In On the Antiquity and Improvement of the Island of Maillezais he argues that providence founded and restored the monastery and answers opponents including Boso, count of La Marche.

The single work here is a legal-ecclesiastical document showing how an endowed clerical college was structured: stipends conditional on attendance at canonical hours, forfeitures reserved for pious uses, perpetual lamps or alms to the poor, and anniversary masses for founders' souls.

authors.aff: Bishop of Paris; school of Notre Dame
authors.sig: Bishop of Paris and teacher at the school of Notre Dame. His Sentences became the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages. Augustine is his most-cited authority, and he also wrote a Commentary on the Psalms and Collectanea on the Epistles of Paul.

The work defends Paschal II as true pope against Henry V and the antipopes Guibert, Albert, Theodoric, and Maginulf, arguing that papal election comes from God, that Guibert was never a true pope but a heresiarch, that the devil cannot confer the true pontificate, and that usurpers of the papal see fall by divine judgment.

authors.aff: Librarian (bibliothecarius) of the abbey of Monte Cassino
authors.sig: Librarian of Monte Cassino who continued Leo of Ostia's Chronicle of Monte Cassino. He wrote On the Holy Places and a Life of Saint Bruno, works that defend his abbey. He is judged a careless compiler and possibly a prolific forger so his texts need checking.

Founder and superior of a community of canons regular at Santa Maria in Portofuori, Ravenna. His Rule binds clerics to the model of levites and apostles. It draws on the rules of Benedict, Jerome, Augustine, and Paul.

authors.aff: Priest of Poitou; crusader in the army of Raymond of Saint-Gilles
authors.sig: Poitevin priest who took the cross in 1096 and marched with Raymond of Saint-Gilles to Nicaea, Antioch and Jerusalem. His Historia de Hierosolymitano itinere is an eyewitness account of the First Crusade that presents the campaign as holy war, where death against the Turks is martyrdom and victory is God's gift to faithful soldiers.

A Cistercian monk at Vaux-de-Cernay Abbey who joined the Albigensian Crusade around 1210. His History of the Albigensians is a partisan Catholic chronicle that reports Cathar beliefs and actions with more precision than some other anti-heretical writers.
