King of the Franks from 1060 until his death in 1108, whose reign saw a modest recovery of the royal domain. He was excommunicated by Urban II at Clermont in 1095 and resisted papal intervention in episcopal elections. His royal diplomas grant monasteries privileges and lands for the redemption of the soul.

The letter here is a royal act defending a one-time crusade tithe as valid by consent of churches and princes while denying that it sets any precedent — evidence of how crusade finance was negotiated between throne and clergy.

authors.aff: Premonstratensians (Order of Canons Regular of Prémontré), Abbey of Bonne-Espérance
authors.sig: He was a leading early theologian of the Premonstratensian Order, known for his extensive allegorical commentaries on Scripture and his treatises on clerical reform and spirituality.

Bishop of Brescia in the late fourth century, he took part in the Synod of Aquileia in 381. His On Heresies (Diversarum Hereseon Liber) catalogues twenty-eight pre-Christian and 128 Christian heresies and traces the New Testament canon through Hebrews and Laodiceans. Augustine cites it as a source.
His Against the Arians is an early Gallic defense of the Son's consubstantiality with the Father, written against the Blasphemy of Sirmium and naming Ursacius, Valens, and Potamius among opponents.

Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople from 858 to 867 and again from 877 to 886, he led the conflict with Rome known as the Photian schism. A short ascetic piece on unceasing prayer and stillness (hesychia) survives under his name and cites Anthony the Great.

Bishop of Toul from 1069 or 1070 until his death in 1107. He signed the renunciation of obedience to Rome at the Synod of Worms in 1076. His surviving diplomas defend church property against local exactors, and they show how he used written records and synodal judgment to protect it.

Pirmin is renowned as the founder of Reichenau Abbey and the author of the *Scarapsus* (or *Dicta Pirminii*), an important early medieval catechetical work containing one of the earliest preserved texts of the textus receptus of the Apostles' Creed.
He is renowned for authoring the *Liber de honore Ecclesiae*, one of the most prominent polemical and canonical treatises produced by the Gregorian reform party during the Investiture Controversy.

authors.aff: Imperial bureaucracy in southeastern Gaul under Valentinian III
authors.sig: Official in the imperial administration of southeastern Gaul under Valentinian III and a friend of Hilary of Arles. He compiled an annotated Julian calendar around 448–449, which replaced festivals regarded as pagan with Christian holy days.

Seventh Abbot of Cluny, serving from 1109 to 1122. Callixtus II made him a cardinal-deacon in January 1120. His Statutes and Pious Precepts set out the Cluniac doctrine of posthumous suffrage. Masses, monastic prayers and alms were held to aid the souls of benefactors after death.

His poem is one of the earliest poetic treatments of annalistic material and one of the earliest historical works centered on Saxony, presenting Charlemagne's rule as divinely granted and the Saxons' conversion as deliverance from error.
His letter to Justinian (PL 67) is a rare African episcopal protest against posthumous condemnation in the Three-Chapter Controversy, defending Chalcedon while resisting Justinian's edict.

Court poet of Constantine who was banished for reasons the sources do not state and recalled after writing a panegyric for the emperor's Vicennalia. His twenty-eight surviving poems include formally ingenious pattern poems that praise Constantine as a just, pious ruler renewing a golden age.
His Vita Cypriani is the earliest biography of Cyprian and the primary eyewitness narrative of his exile and martyrdom, prefixed to editions of Cyprian's works.

The unknown compiler of Leges ad mores corrigendos, a short code of penitential rules for priests dated to roughly 900 to 1000. It requires infants to be baptized within nine days and limits how often mass may be said.

Archbishop of Trier from 1016 until his death in 1047, chosen by Emperor Henry II. He traveled to the Holy Land with the monk Symeon, and on his word Pope Benedict IX canonized him. A letter to Benedict IX survives under his name, relevant to early medieval papal canonization.

His diplomas here are a record of an eleventh-century bishop defending monastic immunity and jurisdiction against a lay advocate, with theses on relic translation, intercession of saints, and the abbot's sole possession of the ban.

Bishop of Lisbon and the second earliest Christian prose writer of the Iberian Peninsula. He took part in the Council of Sirmium in 357 and is believed to have helped draft its creed. An anti-Arian treatise (PL 8) argues that the Son shares one substance with the Father.

authors.aff: Bishop of Hadrumetum, primate of Byzacena
authors.sig: Bishop of Hadrumetum and primate of Byzacena in North Africa, he sided with Pope Vigilius at Constantinople during the Three Chapters Controversy. He wrote a five-book commentary on the Apocalypse and commentaries on the Epistles of St. Paul.

Roman grammarian and critic of the 1st century AD. He turned to literary work after an unsuccessful bid for promotion in the army and marked the texts of Horace, Terence and Persius with signs after the Alexandrine grammarians. A Minor Work on Ancient Notes survives under his name, but is not identified with the De notis fragment.

authors.aff: monk of Marseille; later attached to Pope Leo I in Rome in a secretarial or notarial capacity
authors.sig: Augustine's most persistent defender against the Semi-Pelagians of Gaul on grace, predestination and free will. His Sentences, Epigrams and Responsiones distilled Augustine's teaching on grace for later readers. His Chronicle continued Jerome's universal chronicle into his own century.

Her Cento Vergilianus de laudibus Christi recast biblical history—Creation, Fall, Flood, then the life of Christ from the Gospels—in reassembled Virgilian hexameters, making classical epic verse carry Christian doctrine for a late-fourth-century Roman elite still attached to pagan letters.

Bishop of Besançon from about 613 and close to King Chlothar II. He is remembered for his care for the poor. A liturgical text attributed to him records that the bodies of Silvestre and Anian rest at the Saint-Agapit chapel.

authors.aff: Layman; former provincial governor and imperial official
authors.sig: A Hispano-Roman who practiced law and was twice provincial governor before turning to asceticism around 392. He then wrote Christian poetry, including hymns of the daily hours, Crowns of Martyrdom (Peristephanon), and Psychomachia. Psychomachia was the first completely allegorical poem in European literature.

Bishop of Troyes who wrote the Annals for the years 835 to 861. In the predestination controversy he defended double predestination in a letter to Hincmar and Pardulus. His On Predestination (851) was written at Wenilo of Sens's request against nineteen articles from John Scotus Eriugena.
His one surviving work here is a history concerning the city of Rome, transmitted alongside other Roman antiquarian texts such as those of Pomponius Laetus in later collections.

Bishop of Carthage and Augustine's correspondent on the cataloguing of heresies. His letters ask Augustine for a book on heresies and press him for a reply to Julian of Eclanum over new composition. Exiled to Naples when the Vandals took Carthage in 439, he died there around 450 to 454.

authors.aff: Monk of the Abbey of Reichenau
authors.sig: A monk of Reichenau who around 995 or 996 wrote the Gesta Witigowonis. The work is a dialogue poem in leonine hexameters between the monastery Augia and the poet. It praises Abbot Witigowo's decade of rule and defends his abbacy against the envious.

Monk of the Roman cloister on the Coelian Hill before his election as pope on 11 April 672. He worked to perfect monastic discipline and to repress Monothelitism. A privilege under his name exempts monasteries from episcopal and lay exactions and secures free election of abbots.

authors.aff: Abbot of Fulda; Archbishop of Mainz
authors.sig: Abbot of Fulda and later Archbishop of Mainz. He headed the monastic school at Fulda and wrote On the Universe (De rerum naturis), an encyclopedia. His commentaries on Ezekiel, Jeremiah and Matthew cite Paul, Jerome, Gregory and Augustine heavily.

His value for readers lies in the Vitae of Saints Medard and Godeberta — near-contemporary accounts of saints of his own diocese that defend their subjects' innocence through miracle narratives and assert themes of prayer, mercy toward enemies, and priestly absolution.

authors.aff: Abbey of the Holy Cross, Poitiers
authors.sig: Her Testament is a rare surviving text attributed to a Merovingian queen, recording her voluntary transfer from lay royal life to religious rule, her royal munificence in endowing the monastery of maidens, and how her nuns were governed by Caesaria's Rule.

authors.aff: Bishop of Utrecht (899–917), resident at Deventer
authors.sig: Bishop of Utrecht from 899 until his death in 917, he governed from Deventer after Norman raids destroyed the city. He wrote sermons on pastoral office and repentance, poems and a chronicle.
Archbishop of Canterbury from 1114 until his death in 1122, he succeeded Anselm and pressed Canterbury's claims over Wales and Scotland. A single letter to Pope Calixtus II survives under his name.

His two documents are evidence of crusader-era piety in practice: an estate pledged to a monastery to fund or secure a Jerusalem journey, preserved for what they show about land, vow, and monastic economy around the First Crusade.

His surviving charters show how an eleventh-century Provençal archbishop used legal instruments to enforce the Peace of God, protect monastic property, and frame Sunday observance and the truce as divinely binding.
His diplomas and letters are primary evidence for how an early twelfth-century metropolitan exercised authority over monasteries, church property, and unjust secular oppressors.

Fifth abbot of Cîteaux from around 1134, Rainard led the order through its incorporation of Obazine and Savigny in 1147. He is credited with compiling the Instituta generalis capituli apud Cistercium. One account dates its publication to c. 1150–1151 rather than 1134.

authors.aff: Chaplain to Richard I of England
authors.sig: Chaplain to Richard I of England through most of the 1190s. He preached exegetical sermons on grace, sin, virtue and penance. His homilies draw sharp distinctions and teach that late penitents still pass through purgatorial fire.

Benedictine monk of Fleury-sur-Loire who wrote Latin verse, comic tales and hagiography among them. His prose Miracles of Saint Benedict defends Fleury's claims about the saint's relics and feast against rival accounts.

authors.aff: Bishop of Verona (931–934, 946–948) and of Liège (953–956)
authors.sig: A Benedictine bishop who held the sees of Verona and Liège. While imprisoned near Pavia he wrote the Praeloquia. His sermons and letters argue for clerical discipline and that priesthood is conferred by God above kingship.

authors.aff: chaplain to Bohemond I of Antioch, later to Tancred of Antioch
authors.sig: Norman priest and chaplain to Bohemond I and Tancred of Antioch, who wrote a firsthand Latin account of the First Crusade centered on Tancred's campaigns. A copy in PL 155 names Radulphus of Acre as its author instead.

authors.aff: Canon of Le Puy; chaplain to Count Raymond IV of Toulouse
authors.sig: His Historia Francorum qui ceperunt Iherusalem is one of five eyewitness chronicles of the First Crusade; the copy here reads the campaign as providence — God preserving, correcting, and inspiring his army through defeat, visions, penance, and prayer.

Bishop of Nevers in the seventh century who attended the Council of Paris in 614 and the Council of Clichy in 627. He also attended the Council of Chalon-sur-Saône in 650 and signed a privilege of Clovis II for Saint-Denis in 654. A single epistle is printed under his name.

A monk of the eleventh century known only from one short letter to Bernard. The letter holds that good will is enough without a finished deed. It also defends the study of law as a way to protect monastic possessions.

Benedictine monk at Corbie who replied to his abbot Paschasius Radbertus on the Eucharist at the request of Charles the Bald. He argued that the bread and wine keep their outward appearance while their invisible substance is truly Christ's body and blood. He also defended double predestination and the filioque.
The single item here is a foundation charter for the Abbey of Vabres, preserved in PL 132 as an example of eleventh-century monastic patronage.

Archbishop of Reims from 1083 until his death in 1096. He presided over the Council of Soissons in 1092–93, which condemned Roscellin's nominalism. His surviving letters argue that papal and synodal authority governs episcopal consecration and discipline, citing Pope Urban II.

authors.aff: King of the Visigoths at Toledo (r. 586–601)
authors.sig: His conversion ended Arianism among the Visigoths; the edict printed here shows how he bound clergy and laity to the councils' decisions under penalty of excommunication and property loss.

authors.aff: Provost of St. John's, Liège; later dean of St. Lambert's cathedral chapter
authors.sig: Canon of the cathedral chapter of St. Lambert in Liège from 1101, he later served as provost of St. John's and then dean. His letters argue that flight from a city is allowed under necessity and that singular grace is made common to the faithful. A treatise on church orders is tentatively assigned to him, though its authorship is debated.

authors.n: Reiner of Saint Lawrence of Liège
authors.sig: He is an important figure in twelfth-century monastic historiography, best known for compiling one of the earliest specialized institutional author-catalogues in medieval Europe.

Second abbot of the Benedictine abbey of St. Michael at Siegburg from 1076 until his death on 4 November 1105. The Repertorium credits him with a Life of Saint Anno, a life of the Cologne archbishop Anno II. Only fragments survive. It is assumed he commissioned the work rather than wrote it.

authors.aff: Abbot of Prüm (892–899), then of Saint Martin's, Trier
authors.sig: Abbot of Prüm and then of Saint Martin's in Trier, where he died in 915. He wrote On Ecclesiastical Disciplines, a handbook of church discipline and penance drawn from capitularies and councils. His Chronicle is a principal source for late Carolingian history.

A Benedictine monk who taught at the abbey of Saint-Germain in Auxerre and succeeded Heiric as school master. His Expositions of the Psalms read the Psalms as spoken in the voice of Christ the head and allowed more than one prophetic fulfillment. They were widely used in twelfth-century Europe.

Archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen from 865 until his death in 888. His Life of Saint Ansgar is the chief source for the first mission to Scandinavia. It defends that mission against pagan idolaters and against critics such as Guntharius of Cologne.

authors.aff: Master of the cathedral school of Barcelona
authors.sig: Grammarian and master at the cathedral school of Barcelona, active in the eleventh or twelfth century. His verses on the Lord's body set out that bread becomes Christ's true body at consecration while keeping its appearances, and that worthy reception gives eternal life.

Archbishop and Latin Father of the Gallic tradition. He baptized the ruler in 496, an event that brought Nicene Christianity rather than Arianism. His Testament survives, defending manumitted persons as free and funding perpetual commemorative offerings from bequests.

Bishop of Chur in Raetia, attested from about 800 until his death by 820. Canons for his diocese are printed under his name, though some manuscripts give them to a 'Pseudo-Remedius'. They regulate sacramental practice, including the consumption of eucharistic remains and the burning of worn sanctuary vessels.

Archbishop of Lyon from 852 who defended Gottschalk against Hincmar in the ninth-century predestination controversy. He presided over the Synod of Valence in 855. Treatises on grace and predestination circulate under his name but are probably not his.
His letters show a Gregorian-reform legate exercising excommunication, interdict, and property sanctions against lay rulers and contumacious bishops in southern France.
The held prologue shows his method of preface-writing: he disclaims presumption before critics and credits wisdom to importunate prayer rather than to himself.

authors.aff: Abbey of Saint Victor, Paris; prior from 1162
authors.sig: Prior of the Abbey of Saint Victor in Paris from 1162 until his death in 1173. He wrote on contemplation in the Benjamin Major and on the Apocalypse, and his teaching rests on a biblical account of the human person.

Benedictine abbot of the Norman abbey of Préaux from about 1101 to about 1125. He wrote commentaries on Genesis, Deuteronomy, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. Fragments of his Genesis commentary read paradise as the church or Scripture. A letter to Anselm of Canterbury also survives.

Bishop of Soissons, he issued a constitution in 889 to correct the ignorance of his clergy. He assisted at the councils of Verberie in 892 and Rheims in 893, and he excommunicated the murderers of archbishop Foulques.

authors.aff: King of the Franks (Robert II, r. 996–1031)
authors.sig: A rare case of a reigning king writing theology: these texts show royal legislation on church order, sanctuary, and monastic defense alongside royal liturgical composition.

authors.aff: Abbot of Molesme; founder of Cîteaux
authors.sig: Abbot of Molesme who led a group of hermits there and left in 1098 with monks seeking stricter observance of the Benedictine rule, founding Cîteaux. His letters argue for a return to strict observance and for secular rulers to protect monastic reform.

Bishop of Metz from 883 until his death in 916 or 917, he repaired churches damaged in the Norman invasions. His surviving diplomas and letters set out how a Carolingian bishop should guard church property, holding that private oratories stay subject to their mother church and that precarium grants give use without the right to sell.

A monk of Saint-Remi who studied under Gerbert d'Aurillac. He wrote the Historiae covering 888 to 995 from Charles the Fat to Hugh Capet, drawing on Flodoard's annals. It is a principal source, but its rhetorical aims often strain accuracy.

A Benedictine of Saint-Remi at Reims who rewrote the Gesta Francorum in better Latin. His Historia Hierosolymitana became one of the most widely read accounts of the First Crusade. It supplies the most often quoted version of Urban II's Clermont speech. The works argue that the crusade is God's work and cast Adhemar of Le Puy as another Moses.

authors.aff: Archbishop of Vienne (consecrated August or September 860)
authors.sig: His Martyrology became a renowned standard Carolingian martyrology, and his hagiography and historiography made him a principal Frankish hagiographer and historiographer.

authors.aff: Founder and first abbot of Fontevraud Abbey
authors.sig: Itinerant preacher and hermit who founded Fontevraud Abbey in 1096 as a double monastery under an abbess. His rules for the nuns of Fontevraud govern the canonical office, common life, and poverty.

His chronicles — continuations of Sigebert of Gembloux and additions to William of Jumièges — are an important source for Anglo-French history and twelfth-century intellectual life, while his letters and treatise defend strict literal observance of the Benedictine rule against Cluniac practice and Cistercian expansion.

Abbot of Saint-Vigor at Bayeux from 1066 to 1084. He wrote a commentary on the Song of Songs that reads the three Solomonic books as stages of spiritual progress toward union with Christ, the true Solomon. Medieval English monastic booklists record copies, and some manuscripts carried Gregory the Great's name instead.

His Gesta Abbatum Trudonensium is a major monastic chronicle defending the abbey's property rights, canonical election against imperial confirmation, and Cluniac reform of discipline — a combative record of twelfth-century church–empire conflict from inside one abbey.

authors.aff: Cardinal and Chancellor of the Apostolic See at Rome; earlier master at Oxford
authors.sig: Oxford master who later became a cardinal and Chancellor of the Apostolic See at Rome. His key work is Sententiarum Theologicarum Libri Octo. Bernard's letters show him opposing Abelard's rationalistic tendency.

Archbishop of Bourges from 840 until his death in 866 and a saint venerated on 21 June. His Chapters is a manual of church law drawn from the fathers canons and capitularies including Theodulf's Capitulare on baptism penance and clerical conduct. It censures priests who exact unjust prices and penitentials that impose light penance on perjurers.
He is one of the essential contemporary chroniclers for the history, religious culture, and millenarian outlook of early eleventh-century Europe.
Abbot of Bec from 1149 to 1179. He rebuilt the abbey church and built a hospital there. A Latin poem on the contempt of the world is printed under his name.

He is a notable 12th-century monastic chronicler whose *Gesta Abbatum Trudonensium* provides critical historical documentation of medieval abbey life and regional politics during the Investiture Contest.

Subdeacon of the Roman church and fourth Bishop of Orléans under Constantine. He died there on 7 September, traditionally dated to around 340. A short work titled Revelation survives under his name, but no source confirms that he wrote it.

Elected pope in August 897 amid factional violence after the Cadaver Synod, he had Formosus' body retrieved from the Tiber and buried. His letters confirm church property and privileges for Grado, Elna and Gerona. He died or was deposed after about four months, a phrase often denoting deposition.

His Libellus Proclamationis is a first-person account of his deposition, arguing that an irregular deprivation of a bishop is invalid, that appeal to Rome suspends lower judgment, and that papal principate derives from Christ through Peter — a classic case of episcopal appeal against a metropolitan.

authors.aff: Monastery on the Mount of Olives, Jerusalem; later Aquileia
authors.sig: Translator of Origen and Eusebius into Latin as Greek learning faded in the West. He also wrote the History of the Monks and a Commentary on the Apostles' Creed. His quarrel with Jerome over Origen's orthodoxy in the 390s produced an Apology against Saint Jerome.

authors.aff: Monk of Fulda Abbey; schoolmaster there under Rabanus Maurus
authors.sig: A Benedictine monk at Fulda who succeeded his teacher as head of the abbey school and later served the German king as chaplain and confessor. His Life of Rabanus Maurus presents the abbot as governing his monastery in discipline. He also wrote a chronicle continuing Einhard and a Life of St. Leoba.

Abbot of Deutz near Cologne and a committed Gregorian. He defended the Benedictine tradition against the Canons Regular. His allegorical commentaries include On the Trinity and Its Works, which reads history as the moral reeducation of mankind under the three persons of the Trinity.

His Life of Bruno is a biography rather than a miracle-collection: it defends Bruno's combination of episcopal and military office, presents him as a peacemaker restored by divine grace against the rebels of 953, and is considered historically reliable by modern scholars such as Mayr-Harting.

The verses here are minor Carolingian Latin poetry by a ruling bishop, useful chiefly as evidence of how biblical exempla and classical authors were turned to moral and ecclesiastical instruction in his circle.
His surviving letters are a primary witness to the passage from Roman to Frankish Gaul and to the pastoral concerns—consolation, confession, discipline—of a late-fifth-century bishop.

authors.aff: Roman deacon, papal attendant of Pope Vigilius in Constantinople
authors.sig: The Contra Acephalos is a dialogue defending strict Chalcedonian Christology against a moderate Severan monophysite who is driven to speak of three natures in the Trinity; Rusticus also matters as an editor of conciliar acts.

authors.aff: Priest of Marseilles; associated with Lérins
authors.sig: A priest of Marseille who wrote On the Governance of God, defending divine providence against those who blamed God for Rome's disasters. His Against Avarice and letters condemn the greed of Christians in fifth-century Gallo-Roman society.

His allegorical readings of Solomon treat the king as a type of Christ — Solomon signifying Christ our peace, whose peaceful kingdom prefigures Christ's endless kingdom — making these among the earliest systematic mystical expositions of the Wisdom books.

Tradition makes him a rabbi of Fez who converted at Toledo about 1085. Scholarship treats the life and works ascribed to him as likely forgeries of a later date. His On the Past Coming of the Messiah argues from David, Isaiah and Jeremiah that Christ was born of Mary without human seed.

authors.aff: Bishop of Domhnach Sechnaill (Dunshaughlin), Co. Meath
authors.sig: Missionary bishop in Ireland in the fifth century and founder of Domhnach Sechnaill near Tara. Two Latin hymns are attributed to him, and they treat the Trinity and the church built on Peter's confession.

authors.aff: Bishop in southern Gaul (generally identified with Sedatus of Nîmes; printed here as Sedatus of Béziers)
authors.sig: A Gallo-Roman bishop in southern Gaul around 500, generally identified with the bishop of Nîmes. His Homily on the Epiphany reads the six jars as six ages of the world and the wine's failure as the law giving way to grace without perishing.

authors.aff: Colony of Irish teachers at Liège, under Bishop Hartgar
authors.sig: An Irish monk and grammarian who taught at Liège under Bishop Hartgar. He wrote a Collectanea on all the Epistles of St. Paul, a grace- and faith-centered exegesis citing Jerome and Augustine. His On Christian Rulers is one of the earliest medieval mirrors for princes.

authors.aff: Founder and first abbot of Chaumouzey Abbey, diocese of Toul
authors.sig: His History of the Monastery of Chaumousey is a primary record of a Benedictine foundation's origins, its episcopal grants, and its conflicts with Remiremont.

Bishop of Rome from 687 to 701, he refused to accept the Quinisext canons of 692 and resisted Emperor Justinian II's attempt to arrest him. A letter to Abbot Ceolfrid argues that learned study of disputed church questions benefits the whole church. A privilege threatens with anathema clerics who seize monastic cemetery rights or property.

Bishop of Rome from 844 until 847, consecrated without waiting for imperial ratification. His epistle defends papal oversight of provincial synods against Frankish kings. It asserts papal review of synodal decisions and eternal punishment for schismatics and persecutors.

authors.aff: Monk and missionary on the Danube frontier
authors.sig: A monk who preached and organized relief along the Danube after Attila's death in 453. Sources describe him as a stern ascetic revered by Romans and barbarians alike. A treatise on prayer, oaths, and almsgiving survives under his name. Its authorship is doubtful.

Roman of noble birth who took the papal throne from Antipope Christopher in 904 amid aristocratic feuding in central Italy. His letters and privileges confirm monastic electoral rights and forbid a bishop to leave his own see.

Bishop of Rome from 1009 to 1012, he issued papal privileges that protected church property. His grants declare that violating papal privilege incurs anathema and that tithes left to God must not pass to laymen. Several of his grants exempted monasteries from episcopal control.
His one surviving work is the earliest document on the Church in Menorca and a key source for a Mediterranean Jewish community under Christian pressure in 418.

Bishop of Minorca who sent an encyclical letter to bishops, presbyters and deacons across the world. It reported the riots of January 418, which burned the synagogue and led some 540 Jews to convert within eight days. His Epistola de conversione Iudaeorum argues that zeal for Christ justifies attacks on unbelievers.

authors.aff: Abbey of Gembloux, head of the abbey school
authors.sig: He taught for some twenty years at St. Vincent's abbey in Metz before returning to Gembloux about 1070. There he directed the abbey school until his death in 1112. His universal Chronicle runs from 381 to 1113. It became a standard source for later medieval historians.

His lexicon preserves, by quotation, Roman religious vocabulary and custom—numen (the nod and power of god), the temple as a place enclosed by augural formula, sacred tables standing in place of altars, mos as ancestral custom in religion—that would otherwise be lost, making it a primary source for Roman antiquities.

A Benedictine monk who ran the abbey school at Gembloux and wrote saints' lives and verse for houses that held their relics. His Chronicon ab anno 381 ad 1113 was widely used by later medieval historians. He backed Emperor Henry IV against Gregory VII in the Investiture Controversy.

His letters and poems are the principal surviving witness to the end of Roman Gaul from an insider's view — here including letters praising Theodoric II's civility while judging his Arian piety as custom rather than conviction, and opposing Euric and the Goths.

His Mitrale is one of the most important medieval liturgical treatises — read here alongside his Chronicle, it explains the offices, vestments, and church buildings allegorically and became a principal source for Durandus's Rationale.

His letters are Gregorian-reform polemic from a leading German metropolitan: they assert Peter's primacy and the pope's universal pastoral office, require difficult cases to be referred to Rome, hold that synods need papal authorization for judgment, insist that inferior clergy owe obedience to the pope, and defend canonical episcopal consecration; they argue directly against King Henry IV, royal
His lament on Fulk of Reims is both an elegy for a murdered archbishop and a polemic against Guinemarus, treating the church's judgment on the killer and prayer for the dead.

authors.aff: Abbot of Murbach and Bishop of Augsburg
authors.sig: Abbot of Murbach and bishop of Augsburg, appointed by Charlemagne in 778. His Regular Statutes argue that uncorrupted custom may stand as law and require every monk to practice lectio divina and to labor with his own hands. They direct abbots to share the common table and fare of their brothers.
His single surviving letter is a first-hand protest of a deposed pope against the usurpation by Vigilius and Belisarius, arguing that deposition by force does not extinguish episcopal authority.

Bishop of Rome from 468 to 483, a pontificate that spanned the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476. He defended the Council of Chalcedon against Eutychian partisans who seized the sees of Alexandria and Antioch. His letters show him defending Chalcedonian bishops and ruling on illicit ordinations by deposed bishops.
His letters are the earliest surviving papal decretals, establishing the form by which Roman bishops answered disciplinary questions on baptism, penance, ordination and clerical continence.

King of the Visigoths from 612 until his death in February 621, he campaigned against the remnants of Byzantine power in Spania. He wrote a Life of Saint Desiderius that blames Theoderic and Brunhilda for the bishop's martyrdom, and letters on church peace and pastoral negligence survive under his name.

His Vita S. Carilefi presents the hermit's life as a model of self-denial, prayer, and anchoritic struggle that surpasses coenobitic perfection; it holds that saints' lives edify believers toward imitation and that their merits glorify God alone.

authors.aff: Abbot of Saint-Mihiel Abbey, diocese of Verdun
authors.sig: Abbot of Castellion and later founder of Saint-Mihiel on the Meuse. Charlemagne sent him to Rome with the delegation that carried the Council of Aachen's decision on the filioque. His Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict was written for monastic reform. His Royal Way on princely virtue was addressed to Louis the Pious.

authors.aff: Abbot of Saint-Mihiel Abbey, diocese of Verdun
authors.sig: Abbot of Castellion and later founder of Saint-Mihiel on the Meuse. Charlemagne sent him to Rome with the delegation that carried the Council of Aachen's decision on the filioque. His Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict was written for monastic reform. His Royal Way on princely virtue was addressed to Louis the Pious.
Bishop of Rome from 432 to 440, who worked to reconcile Cyril of Alexandria and John of Antioch after Ephesus. His letters to the eastern bishops after the Nestorian controversy are conciliatory.

Archdeacon of the cathedral church who became its bishop and worked to reform church discipline and worship. In 625 he presided over a council of more than forty bishops that reissued earlier disciplinary canons in twenty-five articles. A disciplinary text under his name sets out sacramental teaching, penance, Sunday mass and marriage.

authors.aff: Abbot of Ilsenburg (c. 1070–1090); Bishop of Halberstadt (1090–1102)
authors.sig: Abbot of Ilsenburg and then bishop of Halberstadt. He could not enter his see during the Investiture Contest since partisans of Emperor Henry IV held the city. Pope Urban II consecrated him in Rome in 1094 and he died as a monk at Reinhardsbrunn Abbey in 1102.

authors.aff: Abbot of the Monastery of Santa Clara near Córdoba
authors.sig: Mozarabic abbot of the Monastery of Santa Clara near Córdoba under Muslim rule, who died in 853. A brief polemical tract against certain heretics survives under his name, defending the unity of the Trinity against tritheists.
His refusal to require rebaptism of heretics fixed the Roman position in the controversy with Cyprian and Firmilian and shaped later sacramental theology on baptismal validity.

First Christian king of Hungary, crowned in 1000 or 1001 with a crown sent by Pope Sylvester II. His laws and his Admonitions to his son Emeric set out how a new Christian kingdom should govern civil life by divine law and define royal authority over church and property.

authors.aff: Third abbot of Cîteaux Abbey, Burgundy
authors.sig: Third abbot of Cîteaux from 1110 until his death in 1134. He shaped the early Cistercian Order through its founding documents. These include the Charter of Charity and the Ancient Customs of the Cistercian Order.

Bishop of Rome from 768 to 772, elected amid factional strife after Paul I's death. He summoned the Lateran Council of 769 against noble interference in papal elections and iconoclasm. His letters appeal to the Frankish kings for the restoration of Peter's patrimony during the Lombard threat under Desiderius.
Due to multiple historical figures bearing the name Stephen II across various Christian traditions, a specific theological identification cannot be determined without further bibliographic details.

Bishop of Liège from 901 until his death in 920, and a hagiographer and composer. His Life of St. Lambert and his account of the miracles of St. Modoald defend relic cults and the intercession of saints against those who despoiled shrines and against pagan invocation of nymphs and Mercury.

His letters are primary evidence for episcopal resistance to royal and metropolitan pressure in twelfth-century France, arguing that the liberty of the church must not be annihilated and that a wronged bishop may use interdict and joint appeal to Rome.

authors.aff: Bishop of Tournai (1192–1203); formerly abbot of Sainte-Geneviève, Paris
authors.sig: Canon lawyer and bishop of Tournai from 1192 to 1203, he wrote a Summa on Gratian's Decretum that became a basic commentary for the French decretist school. His letters record the pastoral, polemical and jurisdictional work of a twelfth-century bishop.

Pope from 929 to 931 and the son of Teudemund. His letters and privileges claim monastic exemption from local bishops under papal protection. They also assert free abbatial election by common consent and immunity from diocesan synods.

His letters in PL 129 are short acts of papal government: confirming property grants by apostolic authority, shielding churches from secular courts and tolls, asserting that episcopal election belongs to the local church rather than kings, providing for metropolitan oversight of suffragan elections, protecting monastic property via papal privilege, and anathematizing violations of papal privilege.

Roman pope from 939 to 942, who had little room to act apart from Alberic II of Spoleto. He backed King Louis IV of West Francia against rebellious vassals under threat of excommunication. Letters printed in PL 132 under his name grant exempt monasteries protection from episcopal claims and let their abbots appeal to the apostolic see.
He is historically significant for his treatise on the Eucharist, which is recognized as one of the earliest texts to articulate and popularize the specific term and theology of transubstantiation.

authors.aff: Bishop of Rome, 3 August 1057 – 29 March 1058; formerly abbot of Montecassino
authors.sig: Bishop of Rome for an eight-month pontificate, continuing Leo IX's reform program until his death at Florence on 29 March 1058. His letters defend papal privilege, apostolic jurisdiction, and clerical exemption from secular judgment and tribute.
Stephen V is historically significant for banning the Slavonic liturgical language in Moravia and for crowning Guy of Spoleto amid the decline of Carolingian authority in Italy.

His Dicta et Facta preserves the sayings and ascetic teaching of Stephen of Muret, presenting the founder's renunciation of temporal goods, humility, love of God above all things, and deeds accompanying words as the pattern of Grandmontine sanctity.

authors.aff: Founder and first abbot of Fulda (abbot from 747 until his death in 779)
authors.sig: Founder and first abbot of Fulda. He was placed as a boy under Boniface and later studied the monastic practices of Subiaco and Monte Cassino. His Ancient customs of the Order of Saint Benedict forbid monks to swear and set out rules for silence and prayer.

Abbot from 1122, he rebuilt the abbey church and introduced the Gothic style in its west front and choir. He advised two kings of Capetian France and served as regent during the Second Crusade. His letters and his life of the king are primary sources for early twelfth-century Capetian history.
He is remembered as the spiritual founder of the Grandmontines, pioneering an austere twelfth-century reform movement centered on absolute poverty and contemplative solitude.

authors.aff: Benedictine monk, St Peter's Westminster Abbey
authors.sig: He wrote the first history of Westminster Abbey, tracing its foundation from Mellitus's day through Edward the Confessor's new church and promoting the cult of St Peter as the abbey's miraculous patron.

authors.aff: Ascetic writer in Aquitaine, disciple of Martin of Tours
authors.sig: Ascetic writer in Aquitaine who gave up work as a lawyer for monastic life under Martin of Tours. He wrote a chronicle of sacred history from creation to his own day and a Life of Blessed Martin. His Dialogues defend Martin's miracles against skeptics.

Bishop of Rome from 314 to 335 and the first pope to reign under the freedom the Edict of Milan guaranteed. Much that circulated under his name is apocryphal. The fragments printed under his name in PL 8 cover church unity, baptism, the date of Easter, and the condemnation of the Donatists.

His letters and synodal decrees here defend papal authority against Emperor Anastasius: church goods may not be alienated, privileges gained by subreption are void, nothing new may be ordained beyond ancient decrees, and successors must ratify their predecessors' acts — positions that shaped later claims for conciliar perpetuity and catholic unity.
The letters here show a tenth-century pope asserting papal privilege as the guarantor of monastic liberty against local bishops and lay powers.

authors.aff: Synod gathered in Mesopotamia under Archelaus, bishop of Carchar
authors.sig: The Actio records a synodal condemnation of Mani and his follower Diodoriades, 'refuted in many ways and cast out,' making it one of the earliest anti-Manichaean documents.

authors.aff: Urban prefect of Rome; consul in 391
authors.sig: Roman statesman and orator who served as urban prefect of Rome in 384 and 385 and as consul in 391. He defended the traditional cults of Rome against Christian emperors, and his protest against Gratian's removal of the Altar of Victory failed.

Bishop of Zaragoza from 651 to 664, he compiled the Sententiarum libri V at the request of Quiricus of Barcelona. The five books draw mostly on Gregory the Great and supplement him from Augustine. Through them Gregory's Moralia reached the Visigothic kingdom and later medieval readers.
His single surviving letter is a compact tenth-century treatment of faith and works in worship, argued from the structure of the divine office rather than from later scholastic categories.

authors.aff: Christian writer of Carthage; later associated with Montanism
authors.sig: Christian writer of Carthage and the first to write theology at length in Latin. He coined trinitas, persona, and substantia. He wrote Against Marcion, which defends the unity of creator and Christ against Marcion's two gods.

authors.aff: Monk writing under the Visigothic King Reccared
authors.sig: His one-page epistle is a polemic against the Caulianense monks, framed as an unwilling obedience to King Reccared.

authors.aff: Dean, notary, and librarian of Hildesheim Cathedral; earlier head of the cathedral school
authors.sig: Head of the cathedral school at Hildesheim and later its dean. He taught Bernward, Meinwerk, Benno and Emperor Henry II. He wrote the Life of Saint Bernward, which takes Hildesheim's side in the Gandersheim dispute with the archbishop of Mainz.

His Life of Louis (Gesta Hludowici imperatoris), written 836–837, is a principal source for the reign of Louis the Pious; it is a partisan defense of Louis that attacks Lothair and Ebo of Reims, and its theses on papal consecration of emperors and kings make it important for medieval political theology.

Norman Benedictine monk and abbot of Bec who became Archbishop of Canterbury in 1139. He defied King Stephen by attending Pope Eugene III's council in 1148 and refused to crown Stephen's son Eustace in 1152 on papal orders. His surviving works are the letters and testament in PL 188.

Bishop of Metz from 964 to 984, a Saxon nobleman and cousin of Emperor Otto the Great. He founded the abbey of St Vincent and gathered relics for it. His work The Finding of the Saints argues that incorrupt relics and miracles attest sanctity, and that a bishop's oath on the Gospels confirms a relic's authenticity.

A secular clerk who taught at Caen and then at Oxford, where he is the first scholar known to have lectured. His surviving letters argue that confession of the heart can stand in for vocal confession and that God judges by will rather than deed. He also attacks Roscelin and other innovating teachers.

Chancellor of the cathedral school at Chartres, he read Genesis through Plato's Timaeus in his Hexaemeron. He also compiled the Heptateuchon as a teaching text for the liberal arts, and John of Salisbury counted among his pupils.

Bishop of Cyrrhus from about 423 and a defender of the Antiochene side against Cyril of Alexandria. His Philotheus historia recounts the lives of Syrian ascetics and presents their intercession and discipline as models of true worship.

Bishop of Paderborn from 908 until his death in 916, a time of Hungarian invasions and conflict under King Conrad. He sided with Duke Henry the Fowler, and his exegesis On the Lord's Prayer argues that justification is by faith alone and that crying 'Abba' requires the Holy Spirit.

authors.aff: Abbot of Saint-Hubert (Andage), Diocese of Liège
authors.sig: His letter to the people of Liège survives in PL 157 as evidence of how an imperial-abbatial community under an Investiture-era abbot addressed the laity of its diocese.

authors.aff: King of the Ostrogoths and ruler of Italy from Ravenna
authors.sig: These four short precepts show an Arian barbarian king legislating on ecclesiastical discipline: councils must reconvene where first summoned, definitions made under discord are uncertain, bishops are the proper judges of doctrine, emperors must not judge ecclesiastical causes, prelates may not alienate church property by usufruct, and alienated church property must be reclaimed with its fruits ac

authors.aff: King of the Franks (Neustria and Burgundy in 673 and again 675–691; Austrasia from 679)
authors.sig: His precepts are primary evidence for how Merovingian kingship exercised piety through legal protection of monasteries and episcopal rights, including disputes with figures such as Duke Adalric and Bishop Chramlin of Embrun.

Archbishop of Canterbury from 668 to 690, he was chosen by Pope Vitalian while living as a monk in Rome. His chapters and penitential texts set English church law and penance, including graded fasts and the redemption of penance by psalms and alms.

The three letters here concern monastic exemption: they assert that the apostolic see grants privileges protecting monastic vows, that neighboring bishops have no power over exempt monasteries, that chrism and ministries come from prelates of the monastery's choosing, that the abbot is elected by his congregation and ordained within the monastery, and that correction belongs to the abbot and abbat

The chief exegete of the Antiochene school. His commentaries on the Minor Prophets and the New Testament treat sin, providence and Christology through conditional prophecy and literal reading, against Apollinarius, Julian and Jewish interpretation.

authors.aff: Bishop of Orléans (from about 798); abbot of Fleury (Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire) and other abbeys
authors.sig: Visigoth from Spain who joined Charlemagne's court and became bishop of Orléans around 798. He wrote On the Holy Spirit, defending the Filioque against those who called the Spirit a creature. His pastoral chapters to his priests reformed the clergy of his diocese.
His surviving epistle is a contemporary witness to the ninth-century translation and cult of Saint Memmius, patron of the diocese of Châlons.

authors.aff: Abbot of St. Georgen in the Black Forest; bishop-elect of Metz
authors.sig: Abbot of St. Georgen in the Black Forest and bishop-elect of Metz. He never took up that see because of the Investiture Controversy. A music treatise printed under his name defines strings, tones and intervals.

authors.n: Theuzo of Saint Mary of Florence
authors.sig: His single surviving piece is a mid-eleventh-century witness to how Benedict's Rule was glossed from patristic authorities, citing Gregory above all.

His Flores epytaphii sanctorum is among the few medieval theological discussions of relics and the bodies of saints, treating resurrection, sanctification after death, and the worship owed to God alone.

A writer at the abbey of Tegernsee whose only surviving work is a Latin letter of 1003 to Saint Adalbert, bishop of the Prussian church. The letter concerns the Prussian mission and cites Aristotle and Plato.

His chronicle is the most important narrative source for the Ottonian empire and for the foundation, dissolution, and re-establishment of the Merseburg bishopric, though it must be read with his episcopal partiality in view.
He is recognized only as an authority cited in external theological or historical sources.

Archbishop of Canterbury from 1162 until he was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral in 1170. His letters from his quarrel with Henry II argue that God must be obeyed rather than men and that priests are fathers and masters of kings.
He authored the first systematic Latin treatise on biblical hermeneutics, the 'Liber Regularum' (Book of Rules), which deeply shaped medieval scriptural exegesis.

Benedictine monk of Fleury who wrote a life of St. Aigulf (Ayoul) of Lérins. His works center on Benedict of Nursia and include a short eucharistic treatise against John Scotus Eriugena. They also include accounts of miracles at Fleury and of the destruction of Cassino, which fulfilled Benedict's prophecy.

His letter to Eumerius is one of the few surviving Gallic episcopal texts on baptismal discipline: it argues that doubtful baptism requires rebaptization without delay and that neglect of baptism endangers souls and blames pastors, citing Pope Leo I.

A presbyter possibly of Rome. He wrote a letter from Rome to the senator Faustus against the monk John the Scythian in 519 or 520. He argued that the formula 'one of the Trinity was crucified' is not found in the four councils and was already condemned at Chalcedon. This letter is his only surviving work.

authors.aff: Secretary to Baldwin VI, count of Flanders and Hainaut; connected to Hasnon Abbey
authors.sig: His single surviving work is a primary source for the 11th-century restoration of Hasnon Abbey under the counts of Flanders.

authors.aff: Consul of Rome, 494 (with Flavius Praesidius); earlier praefectus urbi
authors.sig: Roman consul in 494 under Theodoric who also corrected the codex Mediceus of Vergil. His epigrams on Sedulius's biblical elegiac verse argue for his authorship or editorship of that work, and some scholars have disputed the attribution.

authors.aff: Prior of Durham; later Bishop of St Andrews
authors.sig: Prior of Durham from 1087, he helped lay the foundation stone of Durham Cathedral in 1093. He wrote a Life of Bede defending the tradition that Bede's relics rest with Cuthbert at Durham against those who placed them in Rome.

A Benedictine monk of Saint Gall who taught the harp to noble pupils and also carved and painted. He is credited with inventing tropes for liturgical chant. His Latin poems on the Nativity and the feast of Saint Othmar are occasional and festal verse.

Bishop of Augsburg from 923, he reformed the clergy through visitations and held Augsburg in 955 before Otto I's victory at the Lechfeld. A charter on the Church and true worship survives under his name, a documentary witness to his administration rather than a theological treatise.

authors.n: Udascalcus of Saint Ulrich in Augsburg
authors.aff: Benedictine Abbey of St. Ulrich and Afra, Augsburg
authors.sig: He is an important regional chronicler whose historical and hagiographical writings preserve critical evidence for 12th-century Swabian church history and monastic-episcopal relations.
His surviving epistle is a witness to the anti-Priscillianist campaign in fifth-century Gallaecia and to the discipline Turibius sought to enforce as bishop.

authors.aff: Abbey of Cluny; ended his days at Zell (St. Ulrich im Schwarzwald) in the Black Forest
authors.sig: His antiquiores consuetudines of Cluny are an important surviving account of Cluniac monastic custom, treating true worship, prayer, the sacraments, and the Lord's Supper (Eucharist) as practiced at Cluny.
Urban II is best known for convening the Council of Clermont to initiate the First Crusade and for reinforcing the administrative and reforming policies of the medieval papacy.

Bishop of the see from 1125 until his death in 1148 or 1149, he carried on the Gregorian reform. His reports and letters argue that papal confirmation secures church grants and that long possession establishes a right to a chapel.

authors.aff: Presbyter of the church at Nola
authors.sig: Presbyter of the church at Nola and a friend of Paulinus, he was present at Paulinus' death in 431. He wrote a letter about that death at the request of Pacatus, recounting Paulinus' final communion with bishops Symmachus and Acindynus and the visions that came before and after it.
Ulfilas is celebrated for his pioneering translation of the Bible into Gothic and for establishing Arian Christianity among the Germanic peoples.

Abbot of Saint-Martin at Ligugé, credited with a Life of the martyred bishop Leodegar of Autun. The text defends Leodegar against Ebroin and presents episcopal election and clerical chastity as marks of holy office. Its original does not survive, and Bruno Krusch claimed to rebuild it from later Carolingian versions.
Insufficient documentation is available in standard theological reference works to determine their significance.

His one surviving work here is a hagiographic life of Arbogast that presents the saint's healings, exorcisms, and continuing patronage through Mary's intercession, modeling how a tenth-century bishop promoted his see's cults.

Almost nothing is known of this Latin writer. A two-page epistle survives under his name, arguing that grace is given apart from merit and that free will is healed by grace. It answers brothers who boast of free will.

authors.aff: Pope (25 November 1185 – 20 October 1187); formerly archbishop of Milan (1185)
authors.sig: Pope from 25 November 1185 until his death at Ferrara in October 1187. His letters and privileges defend tithes, monastic rights, church property and clerical immunity. They defend them against lay magnates and against Emperor Frederick and Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury.

Bishop of Cimiez in fifth-century Gaul, he preached twenty moral homilies in an ornate rhetorical style modeled on Seneca. In them he defends discipline as divine order, including judicial capital punishment against those who call it cruelty.

A Benedictine monk at Saint-Germain-des-Prés who traveled to Spain in 858 to collect relics of the Cordoba martyrs. At the order of Emperor Charles the Bald he compiled a Martyrology that became the model for every later Roman martyrology.

authors.n: Valerius of San Pedro de Montes
authors.aff: hermit in the Bierzo, connected with the Abbey of San Pedro de Montes
authors.sig: A Visigothic aristocrat who became a monk and then a hermit in the Bierzo. He resisted ordination to a proprietary church. He wrote a Life of Saint Fructuosus and minor works on prayer, perseverance, and faith.

Bishop of Liège from 1041 until his death in 1048 and a temporal prince active in imperial politics. He challenged the emperor's claims over the church and held that the pope may be judged by no one but God. A letter on heresy urges that dissent be tolerated rather than punished with blood.

Bishop of the Rutheni in Gaul, dated to 625. Two short letters survive under his name. One letter takes issue with a man the text addresses as 'the lord.' The fragments serve best as an example of seventh-century Gallic episcopal correspondence.

Bishop of Capua from 541 until his death in 554. He directed and corrected the Codex Fuldensis, a very early manuscript of the Vulgate. It replaces the four Gospels with a single harmony that he attributed to Tatian with some doubt.

authors.aff: Abbot of Montecassino (1058–1087); Pope (elected 24 May 1086, consecrated 9 May 1087)
authors.sig: Abbot of Montecassino before he became pope in 1086, he ruled briefly during the investiture conflict against the imperial antipope Clement III. His speech at the Synod of Benevento and his letters attack simony and defend election of bishops by clergy and people.

authors.aff: Bishop (see unnamed in source; traditionally identified as Carthage)
authors.sig: His surviving letters are evidence for how African bishops aligned with Rome against Monothelite innovation at Constantinople, affirming two wills and two operations in Christ.

Bishop of Tunnuna in North Africa and chronicler. He backed the Three Chapters and refused Justinian's edict of 544. He was imprisoned, exiled and confined in a Constantinople monastery. His Chronicle defends Chalcedon. Only the part from 444 survives.

authors.aff: Bishop of Rome, 13 April 1055 – 28 July 1057; formerly Bishop of Eichstätt (1042)
authors.sig: Bishop of Eichstätt from 1042, then pope from 1055 to 1057. He continued the reforms of Leo IX through synods that condemned clerical marriage and simony. His letters and diplomas protect monasteries and confirm their possessions under apostolic privilege.

Rhetor of Marseille, known through Gennadius of Massilia. He wrote the Aletheia, a hexameter poem on Genesis for the instruction of the young. It retells Genesis from creation to Sodom and argues for creation out of nothing against proponents of an eternal world.

authors.aff: Bishop of Vita, province of Byzacena (though some scholars argue he may have been merely born there)
authors.sig: His history is the principal contemporary witness to the Vandal persecution of African Catholics and preserves documents otherwise lost, including the anti-Arian confession drawn up by Archbishop Eugenius for the Carthage conference of February 1, 484.
He was the first known exegete to write biblical commentary in Latin, and his millenarian Apocalypse commentary shaped early Latin reading of Revelation.

Bishop of Rouen and a former soldier who refused military service after his conversion. He wrote In Praise of the Saints (De Laude Sanctorum) to defend the cult of relics against its critics. It argues that the saints' relics heal the faithful and that the saints repay their benefactors through intercession.

Bishop of Thapsus in Byzacium, probably summoned to the Vandal synod at Carthage in 484. He wrote Trinitarian polemics against the Arians, including Against Marivadus the Arian and Against Palladius the Arian. He is also credited with a work against Eutyches.

Bishop of Trent from about 380 until his death in 405. He worked to convert Arians and pagans in the Trentino and nearby districts. His letters argue that churches should be raised on martyrdom sites and that the faithful dead rest in Abraham's bosom.

A deacon in Gaul in the second or third decade of the fifth century whose only known work is a rule read aloud in communal assemblies. Holsten printed an Eastern Rule largely derived from Pachomius that covers the abbot's authority, silence and correction.

The fragmentary letters preserved in PL 67 concern church discipline: they argue that clerical sins must be publicly corrected rather than silenced, that laypeople may accuse clergy at synod, and that accusers bear the burden of proof — evidence of how conciliar procedure handled accusations against clergy in sixth-century Gaul.

Archbishop of Bourges who received the pallium from Pope Calixtus II in 1120. He attended the Council of Étampes in 1130 but quietly sided with the antipope Anacletus II. His letters argue for papal legitimacy against Girard II of Angoulême.

Ordained by Ebbo of Reims, he was abbot of Montier-en-Der and Soissons and tutored Carloman before becoming archbishop in 866. His Pastoral Letter (PL 121) covers sin and confession, the sacraments and lawful oaths.

His Commonitorium states the principle that what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all must be held as true, and argues that scripture and church tradition together guard the faith against heretics who cite scripture to cloak their errors.

The letters here show seventh-century Roman claims that sentences contrary to the canons are void, that appeals to the apostolic see may not be refused, and that Peter's binding and loosing grounds Roman authority.

Bishop of Rome from 537 to 555, he was arrested in Constantinople in 545 for refusing to condemn the Three Chapters. He later consented in writing to the Fifth Council's verdict. His letters and decrees document that contested submission and defend the four ecumenical councils.
His work here is a compact scholastic treatment of free will, arguing that voluntary consent judged by reason is the ground of all merit and that necessity destroys liberty and merit.

authors.aff: Benedictine Order, Abbot of Reichenau Abbey
authors.sig: A Carolingian intellectual who contributed to medieval liturgy, biblical commentary and Latin poetry.

authors.aff: Librarian of the Abbey of St. Gall, 905–909
authors.sig: Monk of St. Gall and librarian of the abbey from 905 to 909. He wrote Latin verse, including three poems to Dado of Verdun in 906 and a greeting poem for King Conrad I in 911. He also composed two hymns.

Frankish archbishop of the see of Sens from 887 until 923, he crowned Eudes, Robert I, and Rudolph as kings. His statutes set disciplinary rules for monastic common life and forbid nuns to deal in property without episcopal license.

His verse martyrology is one of the principal Carolingian reworkings of Bede's calendar, and his Life and Miracles of St. Goar preserve early testimony to a Rhineland cult centered on healing at a saint's memorial.
His capitulary is a working document of ninth-century diocesan reform and clerical discipline, showing how a Carolingian bishop enforced orthodoxy and sacramental order locally.

authors.aff: Priest of the church of Langres
authors.sig: His two passiones here are early Merovingian martyr narratives presenting martyrdom as wrought by love of faith and divine predestination, against pagan idolaters.

Bishop of Cambrai from 971 until his death in 972. He devised the ludus regularis seu clericalis, a dice game that replaces stakes with virtues. It was meant to keep clerics from gambling. The Deeds of the Bishops of Cambrai preserves his own account of it.

authors.aff: Antipope Clement III; Archbishop of Ravenna
authors.sig: Archbishop of Ravenna who was elected antipope against Gregory VII by the pro-imperial Synod of Brixen in 1080 and took the name Clement III. His letters and privileges assert papal privilege over church property and precedence for the archbishop of Ravenna. They aim polemic at Gregory VII's party and at Duke Wratislaus I of Bohemia.

Abbot of Stavelot, Malmedy and Corvey and councillor to Emperor Lothair II and King Conrad III. His letters defend Monte Cassino's property against lay encroachment, holding that church property may not be given to laymen as a benefice and that the emperor rightly protects the monastery.

authors.aff: 'Archdeacon of Toul' is a conventional label only; no such officeholder is attested
authors.sig: Readers should treat 'Wibert' as a conventional label for the anonymous eleventh-century Life of Leo IX rather than as an attested author; the work itself argues Leo's sanctity from his Benedictine profession and immediate posthumous veneration.

authors.aff: Dean/head of the Benedictine monastery of Feuchtwangen (Middle Franconia)
authors.sig: His surviving letters document the dependence of a small Ottonian monastery on episcopal protection against lay violence, and are a primary source for regional history.

authors.aff: priest in Francia who wrote at the command of Charlemagne
authors.sig: A priest in Francia who wrote a dialogue on the Octateuchum at the command of Charlemagne. He transmits verbatim passages from eight Fathers, mostly Jerome and Isidore on Genesis.

Benedictine abbot who rebuilt Hirsau Abbey on Cluniac lines and introduced lay brothers into German Benedictine monasteries. He wrote the Hirsau Constitutions and supported Pope Gregory VII against Henry IV in the Investiture Controversy.

authors.aff: Abbot of Æbelholt (St. Thomas of the Paraclete), Denmark
authors.sig: Augustinian canon and abbot who reformed the community on Eskilsø and moved it to Æbelholt, the largest Augustinian house in Scandinavia. His letters argue that labor for the neighbor's common good pleases God and that their solutions rest only on the saints' sanction.

His Deeds of the Saxons is often the sole authority for events of Henry I's and Otto I's reigns and a primary source for tenth-century Germany under the Ottonians. He imitates classical writers, especially Sallust. Although not a member of the royal court, he was extremely well informed about imperial politics, probably through imperial officers visiting Corvey.

A master of theology who served as bishop from 1228 until his death in 1249. He defended the mendicant orders and was among the first Latin thinkers to weigh Aristotle and Arabic philosophy against Christian doctrine. A Testament under his name urges almsgiving and monastic reform, though its attribution is uncertain.

Abbot of the Benedictine house of St. Blasien in the southern Black Forest from 1170 until his death there in 1178. A large patristic florilegium printed under his name sorts excerpts from the Fathers by doctrinal topic. Its sources include Augustine, Gregory, Ambrose and Bede. Its attribution to him rests on late testimony.
His Life of St Thomas is a primary witness to Becket's conflict with Henry II over the church's liberty, written by an eyewitness of the murder.

authors.aff: King of England (William I, from 1066) and Duke of Normandy (from 1035)
authors.sig: These PL 149 documents show how royal law and privilege shaped the English church after 1066; readers of the Laws and Diplomas see the king acting as guarantor of monastic rights against both local claimants and episcopal jurisdiction.

His Gesta Normannorum Ducum is one of the earliest histories of the Norman dukes and one of the first accounts of the conquest of England, written from a Norman point of view by a contemporary of 1066.

Benedictine monk and librarian of Malmesbury Abbey who wrote On the Deeds of the English Bishops and Deeds of the Kings of the English. His histories interpret events and draw on Bede, Gregory, and Aldhelm.

authors.aff: Chaplain to Duke William II of Normandy; archdeacon of Lisieux
authors.sig: Chaplain to Duke William II of Normandy and, by Orderic Vitalis's account, archdeacon of Lisieux. He wrote the Gesta Willelmi ducis Normannorum et regis Anglorum between 1071 and 1077. It is the fullest contemporary Norman account of the Conquest. It argues that Edward named William his heir and that Harold was a perjured usurper.

Chaplain to Emperor Conrad II, and possibly tutor to his son Henry III. His Gesta Chuonradi II imperatoris is a key source for Conrad's reign. It treats kingship as divinely appointed for the church's good.
His Vita Sancti Walpurgis is the principal ninth-century account of the Heidenheim abbess, arguing that saints intercede for bodily healings and that persevering prayer obtains what it asks.
His Vita Bonifatii (written probably between 763 and 768) is the earliest known biography from the Germanic-speaking world and the source for Boniface's felling of the Oak of Jupiter.

authors.aff: Abbot of Brauweiler Abbey near Cologne
authors.sig: Benedictine monk and third abbot of Brauweiler Abbey near Cologne from 1065 until his death in 1091. He wrote On the Sacrament of the Altar against Berengar of Tours and Verses on Both Testaments. Manegold of Lautenbach attacked him in the Liber contra Wolfelmum for mediating between Macrobius's Platonism and Christian doctrine.
His Vita Godehardi prior and posterior are mid-eleventh-century lives of Bishop Godehard of Hildesheim and continue Thangmar's Vita Bernwardi textually.

authors.aff: Monk, priest, and precentor at the Old Minster, Winchester
authors.sig: Precentor at the Old Minster in Winchester, he led the chant and trained the choir. He wrote the Life of Saint Ethelwold (Vita S. Aethelwoldi), which tells how Æthelwold restored monasteries by replacing secular clerics with monks. A letter to Alphege of Winchester discusses prayer and the state of the elect souls until the resurrection.

authors.aff: Benedictine Abbey of St. Pantaleon, Cologne
authors.sig: He is notable in the history of medieval exegesis for producing an extensive, allegorical commentary on the Song of Songs specifically directed toward a community of female monastics.

Bishop of Rome from 417 until his death in 418. His pontificate went to jurisdictional disputes over Gaul and Africa, and his letters and decrees on metropolitan authority and appeals to Rome remain primary evidence for early fifth-century Roman claims to jurisdiction.

authors.aff: Abbey of Saint Martin, Laon; formerly cathedral school (Saint-Jean), Besançon
authors.sig: His harmony of the four Gospels, descended from Tatian's Diatesseron via Ammonius of Alexandria, is a major twelfth-century work of grammatical and etymological Gospel exegesis.

authors.aff: Bishop of Verona (probably governing the see from about 362 until his death)
authors.sig: His ninety-three sermons (first printed in 1508), mostly Old Testament exegesis with heavy typology on Baptism and the Paschal mystery (63 of them), are among the earliest substantial sermon collections of the Latin West and show Western trinitarian theology still in an undeveloped state. He also insisted on Mary's complete virginity before, in, and after birth.
Adrian I solidified the decisive political and ecclesial alliance between the papacy and the Frankish monarchy and endorsed the Seventh Ecumenical Council (Nicaea II).
Adrian II is best known for ratifying the Fourth Council of Constantinople and officially authorizing the use of the Slavonic liturgy in the mission of Saints Cyril and Methodius.

Bishop of Rome from 884 until his death near Modena in 885. He issued a privilege and an epistle asserting papal protection of monastic donations and the binding force of predecessors' privileges on papal successors.

authors.aff: Papacy, Canons Regular of St. Rufus
authors.sig: He was the sole English pontiff and a pivotal figure in twelfth-century papal-imperial diplomacy, also traditionally associated with the papal bull Laudabiliter concerning Ireland.
